ady-candle-in-the-dark-english-1656:
Thomas Ady published A Candle in the Dark in 1656, in the middle of England's witch-hunting years. His treatise argues that most witchcraft charges rest on delusion, fraud, and wretched evidence. Ady writes as a Christian who believes Scripture, rightly read, condemns the accusers rather than the accused.

He takes apart the tests and tales used to hang supposed witches. Old women, melancholy, and spite make poor proof of a pact with the devil, he shows. His candle metaphor promises light in a dark business. The book is a brave plea for reason and mercy. It stands among the key English voices against the persecution.
arxiv-2512-00256:
Completely positive maps describe how quantum systems change while probabilities stay sensible. James Tian gives a self-contained derivation of two structure theorems for such maps in 2025, the Stinespring and Kraus representations. The derivation uses only scalar positive-definite kernels.

Textbook proofs of these theorems often rely on heavier machinery from operator algebras. A kernel-only route makes the results reachable for readers with a more modest background. The theorems underpin quantum information theory, where Kraus operators are the standard way to model noise in quantum devices. Kraus operators are the form in which noise models are usually handed to engineers. Stinespring's theorem explains why those operators must exist in the first place.
arxiv-2512-00356:
Quantized transport is famous in gapped topological materials, but it can also appear in metals. Fan Yang and Xingyu Li study quantized nonlinear transport in Fermi gases with Berry curvature in 2025, and where that quantization breaks down. An earlier proposal linked a nonlinear conductance to the Euler characteristic of the Fermi sea.

The authors consider two-dimensional noninteracting fermionic systems whose Fermi surface carries nonvanishing Berry curvature. Berry curvature acts like a magnetic field in momentum space and bends how carriers move. Knowing when the effect survives helps lab teams read such tests in new quantum materials. Such effects grow with the driving field, which sets them apart from plain conduction. For folks who probe such stuff in the lab, the gain is a clear line. They can tell a true odd effect from a plain one, and trust the test.
arxiv-2512-00556:
Language models can echo social biases in subtle ways that simple guardrails miss. Sina Salimian, Gias Uddin, Sumon Biswas, and Henry Leung present a framework for bias testing and mitigation in black box language models in 2025. It uses metamorphic relations, rules about how outputs should change when inputs change.

Indirect or contextually complex prompts often slip past existing safeguards. A unified framework for systematic evaluation and targeted mitigation addresses both detection and repair. Because the models are black boxes, the methods work from observable behavior alone, which suits the commercial systems most people actually use. Metamorphic testing needs no ground truth labels, only relations that outputs must obey.
arxiv-2512-00656:
Claims that language models flatter and agree with users, called sycophancy, have multiplied quickly. Jan Batzner, Volker Stocker, Stefan Schmid, and Gjergji Kasneci review those claims in 2025 and find a missing human in the loop. They identify five core ways sycophancy has been operationalized.

Sycophancy is inherently human-centric: it describes how a response lands on a person. Yet current research does not evaluate human perception of the behavior it labels. Without that check, the field may be measuring artifacts of its own prompts, and the paper urges grounding the debate in what users actually experience. The missing human in the loop is the paper's central complaint and its title.
arxiv-2512-00956:
Jiale Chen, Vage Egiazarian, Torsten Hoefler, and Dan Alistarh present WUSH in a 2025 paper on model compression. Quantization stores language model weights in very few bits, shrinking the model for cheaper use. A few extreme weights and activations stretch the range and waste the quantizer's limited steps.

A common fix applies a fixed rotation, such as a Hadamard transform, before quantizing, which tames the extremes. WUSH instead learns adaptive transforms tuned to the model. Near-optimal transforms could keep quality high at very low bit widths. That would let large models run on smaller, cheaper hardware.
arxiv-2512-01856:
Eric Joyce and co-authors ask if image-based pose estimation can support robot grasping alone. Their frame evaluates estimators of six-degree object pose. Inputs are single RGB images, with no depth sensor. Accuracy is one question. Grasp readiness is the sharper one.

Tests show how pose errors pass into grasp outcomes. An estimator good on benchmarks may still fail a gripper. Linking pose scores to grasp success sets a real bar. Single-camera grasping would cut robot cost if that bar can be met reliably. Grasp trials run in simulation and on hardware, so benchmark poses are graded by physical success, not by numeric error alone.
arxiv-2512-02056:
Training a large language model is slow and expensive, so most users fine-tune an existing foundation model instead. Eshed Gal and five co-authors introduce in 2025 reversible architectures for these models, designed to use far less memory during training and fine-tuning.

The designs borrow from symmetric and symplectic differential equations, structures that can be run backward exactly. Reversibility means intermediate activations need not all be stored, since they can be recomputed in reverse, which is where the memory savings come from. The authors also study the theoretical properties of these architectures, testing whether efficiency costs capability.
arxiv-2512-02356:
An Earth twin transiting a distant star dims it slightly and briefly, a signal easily lost in the star's own restless noise. Shuyue Zheng, Fabo Feng, and Yicheng Rui developed SPLS in 2025, an algorithm that fits the transit and the background trend at the same time.

Segmented polynomial fitting by least squares models the background in pieces with a double polynomial, so the shallow, long-period dip of an Earth-like planet is not fitted away. Detecting such twins is among astronomy's hardest data problems, since the signal hides inside stellar variability. A cleaner separation of planet from noise brings the census of Earth-like worlds closer.
arxiv-2512-02456:
A vision-language model must both see accurately and reason soundly, and weakness in either caps the whole. Sourabh Sharma, Sonam Gupta, and Sadbhawna present in 2025 a self-taught multimodal reasoner, built to improve its own perception and reasoning together rather than importing the skill from outside.

Earlier efforts strengthened reasoning while leaving perception to chance, so models reasoned elegantly about things they had mis-seen. A self-taught loop promises gains without proportionally more labeled data. Multimodal systems that check their own seeing before thinking could become markedly more reliable on visual questions.
arxiv-2512-02756:
Milla Åhlfeldt and a large team squeeze a common protein and watch how it responds at the nanoscale. Pressure can reshape a protein's folded state, and high enough pressure unfolds it. Hydrated lysozyme, a small enzyme often used as a model protein, serves as the test case here.

Using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, the team measures stress relaxation as pressure rises toward four tenths of a gigapascal. The motion of the protein reveals how its soft structure yields. Results inform food processing and preservation, where high pressure treats products without heat. Food plants use hard squeeze in place of heat, so a clear view of what squeeze does to food pays off fast.
arxiv-2512-02856:
Min Soe and co-authors simulate a light pulse striking the boundary between two clear materials, using a quantum style algorithm. A bounded two dimensional electromagnetic pulse travels onto a plane dielectric interface. How it reflects and refracts tests the simulation method itself.

The qubit lattice algorithm runs as a sequence of unitary collision and streaming steps. With suitable potential steps, it recovers Maxwell's equations in uneven dielectric media to second order accuracy. Such schemes may one day let quantum hardware simulate classical waves efficiently and accurately. Wave tests with sharp edges are a stern check. A code that passes them here can be put to work on waves in air, sea, and glass with trust.
arxiv-2512-03156:
An old star near the end of its life has a restless atmosphere. K. Ohnaka and co-authors image the star W Hya in sharp detail in this 2025 work. They use ALMA, a large array of radio dishes in Chile.

The team observed with the array's longest baselines, giving very fine views. They probe how gas moves and what chemistry occurs in the star's air and inner wind. Dying stars seed space with the raw material for new stars and planets. Close views show how that material leaves the star. W Hya is close and bright, which makes it an ideal target for such fine imaging.
arxiv-2512-03556:
Robots that learn in one place often fail in another. Yinzhou Tang and co-authors present RoboScape-R in this 2025 work. Imitation policies overfit to expert paths, while reinforcement learning lacks a unified reward across scenes.

Their model unifies reward and observation world models for training. A shared reward signal supports generalization across diverse scenarios. Robots trained this way may adapt to new rooms and tasks more readily. General skills are key if robots are to leave labs for homes and warehouses. World models let robots rehearse in imagination, cutting risky real-world trial and error.
arxiv-2601-06856:
Aswathy Menon Kavumpadikkal Radhakrishnan and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers probing the microscopic origin of prompt and non-prompt d 0 D^{0} production through. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Heavy-flavour hadrons are produced in the early stages of ultra-relativistic collisions at the LHC via hard partonic interactions and experience the whole system evolution.

The study of prompt and non-prompt D 0 D0 mesons provides. An independent avenue to test the theories of quantum chromodynamics and to investigate beauty hadron production. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07756:
Johannes Erdmann, Nitish Kumar Kasaraguppe, and Florian Mausolf automate a tedious choice in particle physics analysis: where to draw bin boundaries. Analysts sort events using discriminant scores, often from machine learning classifiers. Boundaries are still commonly chosen by hand. Simple habits include argmax projections of multi-class scores and evenly spaced bins for one-dimensional scores. Their 2026 preprint proposes direct optimization instead.

Their method optimizes binning for signal significance in multi-dimensional discriminants. Better bins can raise sensitivity without collecting more data. Hand choices may waste the information a good classifier provides. Automating the choice also makes analyses easier to reproduce. The paper speaks to high-energy physicists who build searches and measurements around binned data. It treats binning as part of the measurement, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-07956:
Harrison M. Bonner and Matthew R. Kirchner estimate the parameters of a general model of human pilot response. A human model is essential for analyzing the dynamics of piloted vehicles. Controllers and aircraft must be designed around how people actually respond. Their 2026 preprint presents a method for finding the single model that best fits response data. Data come from a simulator, with many trials combined.

Fitting one model across many trials separates steady pilot behavior from trial noise. Simulator data are safe and repeatable, unlike flight tests. The resulting model can predict pilot-vehicle behavior for new tasks. That prediction supports control design and handling studies. The paper serves aerospace engineers and human factors scholars. It treats the pilot as part of the dynamic system, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-08056:
Sibo Wang-Chen and Pavan Ramdya wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on neuromechanical digital twins. These are computer models that link a brain, a body, and the moves that body makes. The work spans models of humans, roundworms, rodents, zebrafish, and fruit flies.

Digital twins let researchers test how neural control and body mechanics shape behavior together. The models named include systems for walking and flying fruit flies, plus worm and fish models. For readers, the paper maps a fast-growing way to study movement without running every test on a live animal. It also shows how one approach can span very different species.
arxiv-2601-08256: Yilan Jiang, Cindy Xiong Bearfield, Steven Franconeri, and Eugene Wu study how data values themselves create visual groupings. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that reading a chart means weighing design and data together. Past work focused on affordances from design elements like color or chart type. How design interacts with data values to shape interpretation has stayed under-explored. The authors ask how readers find groupings that the data induce. Their results matter for chart designers who must predict what patterns viewers will actually see, not just what was encoded.
arxiv-2601-08456: Kiyoshi Sogo wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on two series in Entry 7 of Gauss's diary. Both series diverge, which means their sums run off with no bound in the plain sense. Sogo extends both series by adding new parameters to each. He then calls on three known tools: Rogers-Fine identities, Ramanujan's continued fractions, and Heine's relations for basic hypergeometric series. With those tools, he finds new series that match the old ones. The new forms let him compute the sums of the divergent series in question.
arxiv-2601-08956:
Satyaki Roy Chowdhury and Golrokh Mirzaei work on clean marks of brain growths in scans. True marks guide care and cuts. Deep nets can draw the marks, yet they oft leave rough, noisy edges where a growth seeps into sound tissue. Those rough edges are just where a doctor needs most trust in the mark.

The team adds a cost term that fines shaky marks. The term acts as a learned smooth rule, tied to a drop out trick used at train time. Marks that jump round from run to run get fined more. A reader in brain scans gets a way to calm edge noise. It may make auto marks more fit for real care plans.
arxiv-2601-09056:
Robert Dilworth writes on how to hide who wrote a text from style checks. Style checks can name an author from word picks and pace. They aid law work and fraud hunts. They can also harm a source who must stay hid, or a writer in a strict land. Dilworth seeks a way to mask style while it keeps sense.

His method is called StegoStylo. It stitches text in a way that keeps the facts, but shifts the style marks. The aim is not to lie. It is to stop a style print from name the hand that wrote the words. A reader in text safety gets a mask plan, and a warn on how strong style prints now are.
arxiv-2601-09356:
Emily Klass and six co-authors tackle a measurement problem in biophysics: finding the forces inside living, self-organizing matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats actomyosin systems, networks of actin and myosin that turn chemical energy into motion. They frame the task as an inverse source problem for the Stokes equation.

Knowing the forces is the key to grasping how these active systems work. Cells and tissues build order by spending energy and doing mechanical work. If the hidden forces can be read back from what is seen, experiments gain a direct window on that process. The paper sets up the math needed for such a recovery.
arxiv-2601-09456:
Stephan Ferenz, Oliver Werth, and Astrid Nieße design a metadata schema for energy research software. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets the findability and reuse of code in energy research. Good metadata lets other teams discover software and judge whether it fits their own work.

Many fields still lack a settled schema, and energy research is one of them. The authors built theirs from a requirement analysis, following the FAIR principles for research software. They then evaluated the schema through user testing. A shared schema would let catalogs index energy software the way libraries index books.
arxiv-2601-09656:
A. Arnold, S. Egger, V. Mehrmann, and E. A. Nigsch link two theories of how systems settle down. Their 2026 arXiv paper connects hypocoercivity with hypocontractivity through the Cayley transform. Both theories describe decay toward equilibrium for evolution equations in Hilbert spaces.

One theory works in continuous time, the other in discrete steps. The Cayley transform is the bridge that turns one setting into the other. The authors give new proofs that pin down the short-time decay, including the constants in the leading terms. Sharp decay rates matter for kinetic models, from gas dynamics to plasma physics.
arxiv-2601-09756:
David Brundage weighs synthetic data as a tool for cleaning veterinary health records. His 2026 arXiv paper studies de-identification of veterinary electronic health records under a fixed compute budget. Such records are rich for surveillance and research, but free-text notes often carry private identifiers.

The PetEVAL resource provides expert-labeled animal clinical narratives with identifier spans marked. That allows a fair test of de-identification methods in a low-resource field. Synthetic data may help train scrubbers without exposing real notes. The paper weighs the benefits, the limits, and the safety trade-offs of that route in full.
arxiv-2601-10056:
Jinyuan Shang and Haiping Hu study how quanta move in a near repeat lattice. Such a lattice is named quasiperiodic. Its sites follow a rule that near repeats but never quite does. The test case is the Aubry André Harper lattice.

The pair set the lattice in a two lead rig. The leads sit at zero heat. They work out the flow with a Green based method for out of balance rigs. Odd marks show up at band edges. Sharp points can form there. The flow can also wave in a log based beat as terms change. The work maps these odd acts.
arxiv-2601-10156:
Yutao Mou and co authors guard the tool calls of AI agents. An agent that can call tools can do real work. It can also do real harm if a call is wrong. A bad call may leak data or break a file. The risk grows with each step the agent takes.

The team built ToolSafe, a guard that acts step by step. It checks each call before the call runs. If a call looks unsafe, it can block or flag it. It also gives feed back to the agent. The aim is safe tool use with no need to wait for harm to show.
arxiv-2601-10356:
Mesut Ceylan, Alexis Tabin, Patrick Langer, Elgar Fleisch, and Filipe Barata explain pulse based health calls in plain terms. Wristbands track the pulse wave all day. Models read that wave to call heart rate, breath rate, and blood oxygen. A call with no grounds is hard to trust in care.

The team give counterfactual notes. Such a note says what change in the wave would flip the call. It is built for time data that map to a score. The notes help a pro see why a model made its call. They also flag when a call rests on a weak trait.
arxiv-2601-11056:
E. Garcia-Sanchez, D. Leung, M. Taylor, and P. Tradacete study Banach lattices. Banach lattices are spaces that mix order with a norm. Their 2026 preprint deals with upper p-estimates in such spaces. Two traits, p-convexity and p-concavity, sort these spaces into a scale.

Spaces on that scale act like the classic Lp spaces. Upper and lower p-estimates refine the scale with more care. They are modeled on Lorentz spaces, named Lp-infinity and Lp-one. The team studies new norms that fit the upper case. They also study how such spaces split into simpler factors. The work sits deep in functional analysis, a core of pure math.
arxiv-2601-11556:
Boyang Wang and five coauthors benchmark symbolic music reasoning in LLMs. Their 2026 preprint is named CSyMR, with MIR tool integration. Large language models now reason about music in symbolic form. Scores and chord symbols are text-like inputs for them.

Existing benchmarks stress isolated facts or atomic analyses. Real music thought connects structures across a whole piece. That integrative, compositional reasoning is the gap named here. The bench tests it with music information retrieval tools in hand. Models must combine tool outputs into joined judgments. The dataset is shared on Hugging Face for reuse. Such a bench can steer music AI toward deeper skill.
arxiv-2601-11956:
Yuyin Lu, Ziran Liang, Yanghui Rao, and their co-authors seek more trust in large language models. Such models can state false claims with full faith. Adding knowledge graphs can lift fact skill, but past tools do not gauge doubt in the proof they fetch or in the model's own steps.

Their frame, named DoublyCal in the work, rests on a double-calibration rule. It gauges doubt in both the fetched proof and the chain of thought. A model that knows its doubt can flag weak replies. That flag helps users judge when to trust an output.
arxiv-2601-12356:
Joel M Thomas and Abhijit Chakraborty study how Indian states differ in what they can make and do. They build a network that links each state to its industries. The links come from firm level data on firms on record and the paid up capital behind them.

The pair work out an index of economic complexity for each state. They also use a fitness and complexity method to score each place. These tools show how wide and how skilled the base of work is in each state. The study also covers two union territories. It gives a clear map of local skills that can guide plans for growth in each region.
arxiv-2601-12756:
Hiroyasu Ando analyzes how non adiabatic effects change convective modes in stars and fluids. A convective mode describes how buoyant blobs of fluid move and grow. In adiabatic analysis, no heat is exchanged, and a propagation diagram serves as a useful tool. That diagram shows how the mode behaves across a system.

Ando conducts a systematic analysis using a wave energy relation. For a strongly non adiabatic case, he finds a qualitative change. A monotonically growing convective mode becomes oscillatory instead. Heat exchange thus does not just tweak growth rates; it can change the character of motion. The result matters for stellar interiors, where convection carries energy.
arxiv-2601-13256:
Wenzhong Zhang, Zheyuan Hu, Wei Cai, and George Karniadakis survey deep nets as solvers for hard partial differential equations. Such laws rule heat, flow, and price moves. In high dims, grid based solvers collapse. The count of grid points blows up with each added dim, a flaw called the curse of dimensionality.

Deep nets give a mesh free swap. They can guess law answers in tens to thousands of dims. The team sets out how such nets are built and taught. They also weigh where the nets shine and where they fail. For maths and physics staff, the survey marks a path past a wall that blocked old tools for decades.
arxiv-2601-13756:
Adam Kaminer and co-authors prove a pattern in a tuned cell process in 2026. Their problem is an eigenvalue optimization tied to mRNA translation. In translation, ribosomes build proteins from mRNA code in the cell. The team studies the ordered list of optimal parameters for this model.

They prove a turnpike property for that list. The list has three parts: a short first part, a short third part, and a long middle. All values in the middle part are about equal. Such flat middles make control of the system far simpler to design.
arxiv-2601-14056:
Andrea Rigo and co-authors give image generation consistent 3D layout control in 2026. Text-to-image diffusion models can place objects in odd spots or warp their shape. Prior methods use 2D cues or copy-warp-paste steps to fix placement. Those often distort object geometry and fail to preserve consistency across edits.

Their POCI-Diff uses 3D-layout guided diffusion for placement. Objects can be positioned consistently and interactively, then edited in place. A scene that stays stable across edits suits design and story work. Users gain control that plain text prompts cannot give. The user can move an object and see the scene stay in shape. That kind of live control is what most text prompts lack.
arxiv-2601-14156:
A. W. Shaw and a large team report a rare dimming of the binary star system BG CMi in 2026. BG CMi is an intermediate polar, a white dwarf pulling gas from a companion star. They present multi-wavelength observations of its first recorded low state. Optical monitoring came from members of the American Association of Variable Star Observers.

The source faded by about half a magnitude for about fifty days in early 2025. X-ray and other data from XMM, Suzaku, Swift, and ground telescopes join the record. Low states reveal how accretion can stall in such systems. Amateur and pro data combined to catch this rare event.
arxiv-2601-14356:
Carlos Hernandez-Olivan, Hendrik Vincent Koops, Hao Hao Tan, and Elio Quinton work on music repair in this 2026 paper, set for ICASSP 2026. Audio restoration means undoing damage to a digital signal. The goal is to recover the pristine sound from before the damage. The task matters most for archives of old recordings.

Some archived music has high historical value. For those works, a clean version may be lost or may never have existed. The team's task is bandwidth extension, filling in sound detail that old recordings lack. They do it in a single step with flow matching, a generative method. Their method is also controllable, so users can steer the result.
arxiv-2601-14456:
Valerio Belcamino and three co-authors test what planning models really learn in this 2026 paper. Fine-tuned large language models can reach high valid plan rates on PDDL planning tasks. PDDL is the standard language for stating planning problems. It is unclear if the scores show transferable planning competence or mere memorization of one domain.

The team fine-tuned a 1.7 billion parameter model on 40,000 domain-problem-plan tuples from ten IPC 2023 domains. They then evaluated both in-domain and cross-domain generalization. Their title names the gap they study. The paper also tests verifier-reward reinforcement learning as a way to close that gap.
arxiv-2601-14556:
Andrew Crossman, Jonah Dodd, Viralam Ramamurthy Chaithanya, and their co-authors classify cyber-attack text in this 2026 paper. MITRE ATT&CK is a cybersecurity knowledge base. It organizes threat actor and cyber-attack information into tactics. Tactics describe the reasons and goals threat actors have for attacks. Each tactic has a set of techniques that describe the potential methods used.

Reports on attacks arrive as free text, and analysts must tag them by tactic and technique. The team constructs multi-label hierarchical classification models for MITRE ATT&CK text. Multi-label means one report can carry many tags. Hierarchical means the model respects the tactic-to-technique tree. Readers get an automated tagger for threat reports.
arxiv-2601-15056:
Maria T. Tagliaferri and Inseung Kang test a hip exoskeleton that helps people keep their footing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with falls, the top cause of injury-related hospital stays and deaths in older adults. A device that steadies the gait could cut that risk.

Lower-limb exoskeletons may help users stay stable while they walk. The team varies the help settings of a hip device in a planned way. They then test gait stability when the ground slips under the user. The goal is to find which settings guard best against a fall.
arxiv-2601-15256:
Ruichuan Zhang carries logarithmic geometry into the derived and spectral worlds. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with log geometry, which tracks spaces together with a record of their boundary-like parts. The derived version uses animated rings in place of plain ones.

Zhang develops deformation theory for animated log rings and for their spectral kin. He studies the stacks of derived and spectral log structures that arise. He then defines moduli stacks for these structures. The paper establishes that those stacks are representable, so they behave like genuine geometric objects in their own right.
arxiv-2601-15356:
Xiang Li, Xueheng Li, and co-authors teach a model to look closer before judging a photo's quality. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with image quality assessment. Reinforcement learning has helped multimodal models match human taste in scoring images.

But most such models judge from a coarse global view. Fine local flaws in a high-resolution image escape them. The authors present Q-Probe, which probes the image in context-aware steps. An agentic process picks where to zoom. Quality scoring then scales to high resolution without missing the small local image defects it finds.
arxiv-2601-15956:
Brant E. Robertson and a large team publish the photometric backbone of a major survey in a 2026 arXiv paper. The catalog is part of JADES Data Release 5. JADES provides deep imaging and spectroscopy of the GOODS-North and GOODS-South fields. Its wavelengths span the optical to the infrared, using JWST and Hubble instruments. The science reaches from nearby galaxies to the first few hundred million years. Photometry measures each source's brightness across filters.

A photometric catalog is the survey's phone book. Every later study starts by looking sources up in it. Brightness in many bands yields colors, distances, and rough masses. The care in such catalogs decides the quality of hundreds of papers. This release documents the measurements so others can build on them with confidence.
arxiv-2601-16256:
Mathias Driesse and coauthors sum how black holes bend paths when they pass. Their 2026 preprint works at fifth order in a key scale. The scale counts powers of the gravity pull in the pass. They also add the first self force terms at next order. The maths frame is world line quantum field theory, a line based tool.

The team finds the bend angle and push for a clean pass. Clean means no waves are shed in the sum, just the pass. Sharp sums test wave forms used for real black hole pairs. They also push maths tools to new depth. The work serves groups who model loud space wave events.
arxiv-2601-16356:
Simret Gebreegziabher and coauthors study how user values shape web agent acts. Their 2026 preprint deals with agents that run web tasks for users. Such agents now do more day to day tasks on their own. It is not known how user likes and values bend agent thought. Both clear likes and hid likes may shift each act.

The team tests agent acts as values in prompts shift. Shifts show which values move acts and which do not. Clear links help teams set guard rules for agents. They also help users know what cues to give. The work maps the act cloth of GUI agents.
arxiv-2601-16456:
Ferida Mohammad and coauthors build a test set for AI code help tools. Their 2026 preprint, named RubberDuckBench, deals with aid tools that reply to code asks. Coders now turn to such tools for help with their own code. Past tests oft use toy asks cut off from real work. Real asks rest on the full code base and its past.

The team draws asks from real GitHub pull threads. Each ask comes with the code and talk that frame it. True frame lets tests weigh if aids grasp real needs. Scores on real asks guide which aids earn trust. The work gives a sound test base for code aids.
arxiv-2601-16656:
More and more people turn to chatbots for comfort and company. Tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot now hear private fears and hopes. Trust sits at the heart of these talks. Yet we know little of how that trust grows. A 2026 preprint studies this new bond in depth.

Users chat with these tools with no guide at hand. The talks can feel close, like talks with a friend. The study asks how users come to trust the bot. It also asks what that trust feels like from inside. Such work can help set safe rules for care bots. It can also warn users of risks in deep trust.
arxiv-2601-16756:
Mauro Guerra and a large team refine the math for a rare atomic decay. Beryllium-7 atoms can grab one of their own inner electrons. That grab leaves the atom in a stirred state. Some stirred atoms shake off an electron as they calm. The shake-off forms a tail in the energy spread. Their 2026 preprint builds a sharp model of those tails.

Past models lacked key traits, like linked electron moves. They also skipped the skew that fast moves bring. New gauges with cold sensors now set the best bounds on ghost bits called sterile neutrinos. Bad tails blur those bounds. Sharp tail math thus guards a real hunt.
arxiv-2601-16956:
Avinash Maurya, M. Mustafa Rafique, Franck Cappello, and Bogdan Nicolae speed saves for vast AI models. Big models now train on thousands of chips at once. Their state must be saved oft to guard the run. A crash with no save can waste weeks of work. Saves of such sprawl are slow and hard to steer.

Their 2026 preprint builds DataStates-LLM for those saves. State parts come from plug-in providers that stack. The stack serves data, tensor, and pipeline splits at once. Fast saves guard runs and let teams pause and probe. They also help trace why a run went wrong.
arxiv-2601-17056:
Zahra Vaseqi and James Clark rethink tests for head-cam video tools. Head-cam shots show the world from the wearer's view. Tools must name acts in those shots in new homes. New homes shift light, gear, and scene in big ways. Past tests mixed two kinds of shift at once. Their 2026 preprint splits those shifts with a score rule.

Their rule, Ego4OOD, scores how far a test set has shifted. Input shifts split clean from sense shifts. Clean splits let teams grade true spread skill. Such grades matter for aid tools for the blind. They also matter for work and sport head cams.
arxiv-2601-17156:
E. Eduardo Sanchez-Karhunen, Jose Quesada-Moreno, and Miguel Gutiérrez-Naranjo open the black box of intent tools. Intent tools tag what a user wants from a query. Firms lean on them for sales and support work. Deep nets rule the field, but their guts stay opaque. Their 2026 preprint finds a new way to read those guts. It tracks how loop nets build their tags step by step.

Loop nets read a query in a chain of steps. The team traces which words steer each step. Clear traces let firms trust and fix their tools. They also show where a net leans on stray cues.
arxiv-2601-17456:
Bo Hou builds Lie bialgebras from dendriform D-bialgebras. Dendriform algebras split one operation into two linked parts. That split gives rich structure to work with. Hou studies how tensor products with perm algebras yield Lie algebras from them. He gives two such methods. One route runs through associative algebras.

The work also maps links to the classical Yang-Baxter equation. Solutions of that equation drive integrable systems and quantum groups. New sources of solutions widen both fields. Affinization is the thread that lifts small algebras to big ones. Hou's methods give algebraists fresh stock. Each new Lie bialgebra can seed whole families of models.
arxiv-2601-17956:
Kumar Gautam, Akshit Dutta, and Kumar Shubham describe a radar design based on quantum light. Their 2026 preprint uses the Born-Feynman path integral view to frame the system. The radar rests on five parts. A source based on quantum dots makes pairs of entangled photons. A transmission module sends one photon of each pair toward the target, while a delay line holds its twin.

A detection module then compares what comes back with the held twin. A signal unit works out what the match says about the target. Entangled pairs can help a radar pick weak returns out of noise. The paper lays out the full chain of parts and the theory that ties them. It is a design study for a young field.
arxiv-2601-18156: Anirban Mukherjee and Hannah Hanwen Chang propose a distributional test of distinctiveness for machine-generated works, aimed at intellectual property law. Their 2026 preprint moves beyond pairwise comparisons between single works. A test based on whole distributions can say whether a body of machine output stands apart as a class. The question matters as courts weigh the status of AI-made works.
arxiv-2601-18456:
Kohei Asai and three colleagues join two speech tasks that are most often done one by one. Real tapes mix many voices with noise, hiss, and room echo. That mix cuts both how much speech a lab can use and how clean it sounds. Teams can clean the tape first and then split the voices. In that chain, flaws from the first step pass to the next.

Their tool, Geneses, does both jobs in one pass with a model that builds speech anew. A build-anew model can fix harms that a plain chain cannot, such as echo on top of noise. The aim is one clean track per voice, fit for training new speech tools. More clean speech means speech tools that work for more people in more real rooms.
arxiv-2601-18656:
Sarika Aggarwal and three colleagues study how the length of a flood shapes the harm it does to health. Past work links floods to more ill health in the days and weeks that come next. But floods are not one thing. A flash flood hits in hours, while a slow flood can sit for weeks. That span may change who gets sick and how.

The team build a model that lets the health link shift with the length of the flood. Their model can show a short, sharp harm for fast floods and a long, slow harm for ones that sit. Such maps could help health teams plan for each kind of flood in its own way. They could also guide aid to the zones where harm lasts most.
arxiv-2601-18756:
Marko Maležič and Johann Ostmeyer hone a way to run the long tale of a quantum crowd with less drift. A crowd of bits that pull on each other changes in a smooth flow of time. Tools chop that flow into small steps. Each chop adds a small flaw, and the flaws stack as the tale runs long. Plain chops are easy to code but their stack grows fast.

The pair build chops of a higher grade that stack their flaws far more slow. Such chops can reach far times with the same count of steps. That reach is key for crowds whose tale must run long to show its marks. The work serves both plain and quantum tools that chase such tales. Less drift means claims about long runs can be made with more trust.
arxiv-2601-19456:
Simon N. Chandler-Wilde and Siavash Sadeghi study how sound and waves scatter off objects. The governing model is the Helmholtz equation, which describes waves of a fixed frequency. A common way to solve it is to rewrite the problem as an integral equation on the object's surface. These boundary integral methods are powerful, but their cost can grow as the frequency rises.

The authors derive estimates that show exactly how the method's operators depend on the wavenumber. The wavenumber measures how many wavelengths fit in a unit of space. Their bounds hold for general compact obstacles, not just simple shapes. Knowing the frequency dependence helps design solvers that stay fast at high frequency. Radar, sonar, and medical imaging all lean on such computations.
arxiv-2601-20156:
Velásquez-Toribio A.M studies a string-inspired model of the universe in which a field called the dilaton couples to all matter. In such models the equivalence principle, which says all objects fall alike, can be slightly violated. The author uses dynamical systems methods to track how the universe evolves in the Damour-Polyakov regime.

The work is set in a flat expanding universe filled with pressureless matter. Its aim is to make clear how cosmic relaxation drives any violations down over time. That link matters because tests of the equivalence principle are very precise, so the model must show why no violation is seen today.
arxiv-2601-20256:
Xuanyu Su, Diana Inkpen, and Nathalie Japkowicz present SoftHateBench, a benchmark for testing content moderation models against soft hate speech. Hard hate uses slurs and threats. Soft hate sounds reasonable on the surface but uses framing and value claims to steer readers toward blaming or excluding a group.

The authors test whether moderation models catch this policy-compliant hostility, which is driven by reasoning rather than insults. Many filters key on bad words, so they may pass text that is harmful in effect. A benchmark of this kind shows platforms where their tools are blind.
arxiv-2601-20356:
Debashree Priyadarsini Das and Sasmita Mishra study how a sterile neutrino, motivated by dark matter, would show up in neutrinoless double beta decay. This rare decay, if seen, would prove that neutrinos are their own antiparticles. In a type-I seesaw framework, an exact relation ties the active and sterile neutrino sectors through their masses and mixing angles.

The authors use a model-independent approach inside that setup. They trace the sterile contribution to the half-life of the decay. Experiments now push half-life limits ever higher, so theory must say what a sterile partner would do to the expected rate.
arxiv-2601-20656:
Diogo J. Paulo, Hugo Proença, and João C. Neves present FD-MAD, a frequency-domain method for detecting face morphing attacks. A morph blends two faces into one image that can match both people, threatening face recognition at identity enrolment and border control. The hardest case is single-image detection, where no trusted reference photo exists.

Despite much research, morph detectors struggle when tested on new datasets. The authors analyze residuals in the frequency domain, where blending leaves traces. Stronger morph detection protects passport and ID systems that now rely on a submitted photo.
arxiv-2601-20756:
Elizabeth Baker, Alexander Denker, and Jes Frellsen extend diffusion models to functions, not just finite data. Their 2026 paper works with score-based diffusion models on infinite-dimensional function spaces. Such models can help solve inverse problems that come from partial differential equations. An inverse problem asks what hidden cause produced a set of noisy observations.

In the Bayesian view, the goal is to sample from a posterior distribution over functions. That distribution blends prior knowledge with the observed data. The paper adds supervised guidance to steer that sampling. Guidance uses extra information to push samples toward answers that fit. The work matters wherever the unknown is a whole function, not a single number. It shows how modern generative models can serve classic inference tasks.
arxiv-2601-20856:
Seljon Akhmedli constructs examples that separate two views of order in dynamical systems. The 2026 paper concerns nilfactors, a key structure in ergodic theory. A system can be described through its measurable nilfactor or its topological nilfactor. The two need not match. Akhmedli asks which combinations of behavior can occur. The answer is all of them, and the paper builds systems to prove it.

The examples are minimal and uniquely ergodic. Minimal means every orbit fills the space. Unique ergodicity means time averages settle to one outcome. The construction adapts an idea from Furstenberg. He built a system on the two-torus that was minimal but not uniquely ergodic. The new work extends that trick to control both nilfactors at once. It completes a picture that theorists use to classify complex motion.
arxiv-2601-21256:
Tia Pandit and Bipin Singh Koranga review how the density of Earth affects long-baseline neutrino experiments. As neutrinos pass through Earth, its matter changes how they switch between types. The effect is strongest for the change from muon type to electron type, which sits under tests of a deep symmetry of nature.

The review shows that real changes in density along the path add structure that simple average-density models miss. It pulls together theory, past observations, and open questions for future work. Getting the density right matters because small errors can shift what experiments conclude about how neutrinos behave.
arxiv-2601-21656:
Tianqi Zhao, Guanyang Wang, Yan Shuo Tan, and Qiong Zhang cluster tabular data with a network fitted on synthetic tasks. Clustering tables is hard because columns mix types, the hidden generating process varies, and tricks rarely transfer between datasets. Prior-fitted networks have done well at supervised table tasks by mimicking Bayesian inference.

The authors extend that idea to clustering, where no labels exist at all. A network trained on a broad synthetic prior can cluster a new table in one pass. Transferable clustering would help analysts facing fresh tables daily, from hospital records to sales data, with no time to tune per dataset.
arxiv-2601-21756:
Alexey Orlov classifies supersingular elliptic curves in characteristic three. Elliptic curves over finite fields power much of modern cryptography and number theory. Supersingular curves are the special family whose point counts sit at the extremes.

The author lists the isomorphism classes of these curves explicitly in this characteristic. Formulae for the number of points on each curve are given as well. Explicit lists turn abstract theory into data that can be checked and used. Characteristic three is small enough to compute with directly, which makes a complete catalogue a useful test bed for broader conjectures.
arxiv-2601-21856:
Shujaat Khan and co-authors work on cleaning up ultrasound images without needing perfect examples to learn from. Ultrasound reading is hampered by speckle, a grainy noise built into the method, by blur from the imaging process. And by artifacts that vary with the scanner and the operator.

Supervised enhancement methods assume access to clean target images, which medical practice rarely provides. The team's 2026 preprint instead models the degradation itself, guided by the physics of ultrasound, and learns in a self-supervised way. Better images from ordinary scans could help clinicians in small clinics and low-resource settings most, where the machines are older and expert readers are scarce.
arxiv-2601-22156:
Yingfa Chen and co-authors make hybrid attention architectures practical for extremely long texts. Hybrid Transformers mix softmax attention blocks with recurrent networks, a pairing with an attractive balance of quality and speed for long-context work. Studies and adoption have lagged, though, partly for lack of efficient training recipes.

Their 2026 preprint tackles the problem with efficient distillation and effective architecture choices. Distillation transfers the skill of a full attention model into the faster hybrid, so quality survives the speedup. Long-context models serve law, research, and code, where documents run to hundreds of thousands of tokens. A hybrid that trains cheaply could move long-context ability from flagship systems to everyday tools.
arxiv-2601-22256:
Yinuo Yang, Ashley Ge Zhang, Steve Oney, and April Yi Wang built a tool to help teachers watch class coding work as it happens. Their 2026 preprint presents Spark, a live monitor for tasks with many linked steps. Such tasks have no fixed order and are hard to sum up at a glance.

Spark aims to show who is stuck and where the class shares the same snag. The work grows out of a real pain point for staff who teach coding. A clear live view can let a teacher step in early. It can also shape help for the whole room.
arxiv-2601-22356:
Kiwan Wong, Wei Xiao, and Daniela Rus teach robots to stay safe when rules clash. Their 2026 preprint, PoSafeNet, notes that safety rules are not all equal. Some can bend before others, but the order is only partial, not a full list from top to base.

Fixed orders or flat rules can freeze a robot or make it act in brittle ways. Their nets build the partial order into the learner itself. The robot can then trade rules off in a sane way when it must. The work targets robots that work near people. It aims for safe moves that still get the job done.
arxiv-2601-22556:
Weizhi Liu, Yue Li, and Zhaoxia Yin hide a proof of origin inside generated speech without spoiling its sound. Synthetic speech now sounds fully human, which raises the risk of misuse. Their 2026 preprint, VocBulwark, notes that past marks trade sound quality against strength, by noise overlay or deep model edits.

Their method injects a small set of added parameters instead. The mark aims to survive edits while the voice stays clean. Sound, lasting marks help platforms trace fake audio. The work seeks both goals at once. It is a guard for the voice era.
arxiv-2601-22856:
Yilong Zuo and five co-authors work on graphs whose nodes carry both text and images. Such multimodal graphs model many real systems, from products to papers. A problem arises when the meaning implied by node features clashes with the graph's own links.

Their method, OptiMAG, aligns the two views using a form of optimal transport that allows uneven matching. When features and links agree, tasks like labeling nodes work far better. The approach fits social, shopping, and science graphs where text and images meet. When structure and meaning line up, downstream tasks gain from both the graph links and the rich node content.
arxiv-2601-22956:
Boyin Tan and five co-authors add a planning step before AI writes code for a software issue. In practice, teams often draft several candidate fix proposals, then debate and pick one golden plan. Most AI research skips that step and jumps straight to code generation or repair.

Their system, SWE-Manager, selects and synthesizes the best proposal first, then codes from it. Choosing the plan before coding mirrors how careful human teams avoid wasted work. It could cut the common failure of fluent code that solves the wrong problem.

Their unsupervised method finds both the segments and the hierarchy among them. Skills learned from raw footage could let agents reuse past competence on new tasks. That ability matters for robots trained on large, unlabeled logs of experience. No action labels, rewards, or handcrafted annotations are assumed, which is what makes the discovery method unsupervised.

Analysts in January 1965 weighed Indonesia's main problems and prospects, with a hard question at the center: who might follow Sukarno. Sukarno's guided democracy balanced a large communist party against a wary army. The paper dates from months before the violent upheaval that remade Indonesia that autumn.

Country studies like this one tried to map factions, pressures, and likely turns before events forced choices. Readers see Washington judging an Asian leader's health, rivals, and support in real time. The estimate cannot know what is coming, which is part of its value. It preserves informed judgment made before history supplied the ending.

Postwar sightings of wreckage helped close cases that battle reports had left open. A crash location could point searchers toward graves or remains years later. The file also shows information still flowing months after the Paris accords. Officials kept collecting because hundreds of cases remained unresolved. This entry belongs to that patient, unfinished business.

Ludwig Erhard, the economist behind West Germany's postwar boom, became chancellor in 1963, and a CIA paper that November weighs his early rule. Erhard had just succeeded Konrad Adenauer, the republic's founding leader, whose shadow fell across everything he did. The professor, as many called him, was brilliant at economics and unsure at politics.

The paper judges his shaky start and his handling of party, parliament, and allies. It weighs doubts about his political touch against the prosperity he had built. The study captures a successor struggling to fill a giant's place, watched with concern from Washington.
