condillac-essay-origin-human-knowledge-1:
Étienne Bonnot de Condillac, a French abbé, published his Essay on the Origin of Human Knowledge in 1746. Thomas Nugent's English translation of 1756 is the text here, in both of its parts. Condillac meant the essay as a supplement to Locke, carrying the Englishman's project further than Locke himself had done.

His famous device is a statue, a marble figure given its senses one by one. From smell alone, Condillac builds memory, judgment, desire, and at last the whole life of the mind. Language, in his account, is the tool that turns sensation into thought. The Essay made Condillac the leader of French sensationalism, and its statue still walks through textbooks.
dermott-ahiman-rezon-1756:
Laurence Dermott published Ahiman Rezon in London in 1756 as the constitution of the Antient Grand Lodge. Its full title promises a help to a brother. Dermott's book is the founding charter of Antient Freemasonry, the rival half of the eighteenth-century Masonic schism that split the Craft for sixty years.

The Antients claimed the Moderns under Anderson had changed the old landmarks. Dermott answers with his own history, charges, and regulations, seasoned with wit at the Moderns' expense. This text is the complete first edition; the library elsewhere holds only an abridged version. Students of the schism need Dermott whole, since his book governed half the Masonic world.
emerson-english-traits-1856:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published English Traits in 1856, his travel book on England and its people. The book is the first great American comparative study of national character in the modern kind. Emerson had lectured through industrial England in 1847 and 1848, watching mills, mobs, and manners closely there.

He weighs English race, land, climate, and manners to explain the nation's power, wealth, and stubborn common sense. Chapters praise English truth-telling and pluck while they fault its materialism, caste, and cold reserve in society. His visits with Carlyle, Wordsworth, and De Quincey season the analysis with living voices of the age in Britain. America, the younger offshoot, measures itself against the parent stock on nearly every page of the study. The book remains a model of travel writing that thinks in nations and eras.
ermippo-redivivo-o-sia-il-metodo-di-prol: Ermippo redivivo, 1756. The revived Hermippus. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it.
europmc-pmc10120156:
Wang and a team report that a chemical change to the protein YY1 in microglia drives new vessel growth in the eye, in a 2023 study. Abnormal vessel growth in the retina is a leading cause of blindness. Microglia, the eye and brain's immune cells, help drive that growth when oxygen runs low, but the mechanism was unclear.

The change is called lactylation, a mark left by lactate on proteins. The team shows this mark switches on a growth factor gene, FGF2, in microglia. Blocking the path may offer a new way to treat blinding eye disease.
europmc-pmc10167356:
Jin and co-authors review how starving cancer cells of glutamine could serve as a treatment strategy, in a 2023 paper. Glutamine is an amino acid that fast-growing cancer cells consume in large amounts. They use it as fuel and as a building material for new cells, which makes it a point of weakness worth attacking.

The review covers the pathways by which tumors take in and use glutamine. It surveys drugs that block those pathways and trials that test them. It also explains why some tumors resist and how combinations might beat that resistance.
europmc-pmc10326056:
Shyam Sunder, Sharma, and Pokharel wrote a 2023 review on the harms of a class of cancer drugs. The drugs are called tyrosine kinase inhibitors, or TKIs for short. They block enzymes that drive cell growth. Since the early 2000s they have treated blood cancers, lung cancer, and some breast cancers.

Use of these drugs has grown, and so have reports of side effects. Shyam Sunder notes harm to the lungs, liver, gut, kidneys, thyroid, blood, and skin. Heart harm is among the worst, from high blood pressure to heart failure and sudden death. The review weighs what is known on causes and care, and notes that clear shared rules are still lacking.
europmc-pmc10478756:
Zoccali led a European working group review in 2023 on heart harm in chronic kidney disease. Kidney disease runs in five stages, with failure as the last stage. Heart and vessel disease is the top cause of death in these patients. Most die of it before their kidneys fully fail.

Early stages share classic risks, such as high blood pressure and blood fats. Later stages add salt and water load, anaemia, swelling, and bone and mineral faults. Zoccali notes that heart muscle thickens early and hits 70 to 80% of failure cases. New drug classes now cut heart risk in these patients. One class blocks sugar uptake in the kidney, the SGLT2 inhibitors.
europmc-pmc10480456:
Chen, Zhao, and Li reviewed in 2023 the constant reshaping of mitochondria, the cell's power units. These units split, merge, move, and get cleared away as cells need. That cycle, called mitochondrial dynamics, keeps energy supply and cell signals in tune. The review lays out how each step works at the gene level.

When the cycle slips out of balance, the power units falter. Chen ties such faults to brain decline, metabolic disease, heart disease, and cancer. Cells may then take wrong paths or die too soon. The authors weigh drugs and gene tricks that nudge the cycle back. Most ideas are young, but the targets are now clear.
europmc-pmc10499856:
Kapoor and Narayanan warned in 2023 that a common flaw taints machine learning work across the sciences. The flaw is leakage, where a model peeks at data it should not see in training. That peek can make results look far better than they are. The pair surveyed fields that have taken up machine learning.

They found leakage in 17 fields, in 294 papers in all. Some claims built on it were wildly too rosy. Kapoor sorts leakage into eight types, from plain errors to open puzzles. They propose a form, a model info sheet, to test for each type. A recheck of civil war forecasts then humbled fancy models: once fixed, they barely beat a decades-old plain method.
europmc-pmc1175956:
Eilbeck and colleagues present the Sequence Ontology, a shared word list for genome annotation, in this 2005 paper. Annotation means attaching biological knowledge to a DNA sequence. Biological terms are notoriously ambiguous: one word often names more than one thing, and each lab speaks its own dialect. The project aims to give all labs one set of terms, definitions, and links between them.

The paper describes how the list is built and used, with a focus on part-whole links between sequence features. Its practical use is shown on genome annotations from the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. Some questions have no right answer, such as whether a coding sequence includes its stop codon. But one shared usage is crucial when annotations from different sources are compared. The list covers features such as genes and transcripts in one language.
europmc-pmc12086256:
Lee and co-authors reviewed a growth signal that builds blood vessels. The signal is called VEGF, short for a vessel growth factor. It guides vessel growth in embryos and repair after injury. It also helps lymph vessels form and keeps tissues stable.

Too much VEGF activity feeds tumors and eye disease. Too little slows wound healing and harms blood flow. Drugs that block VEGF have changed cancer and eye care. Lee weighs their clear gains against resistance and side effects. The review spans basic signals to treatment outlook. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1262556:
Auvert and colleagues ran a randomized trial of male circumcision and HIV in 2005. Watching studies had hinted circumcision lowers HIV risk. The trial enrolled 3,274 uncircumcised men aged 18 to 24 in South Africa. Half were offered circumcision at once, half at study end.

The trial stopped early at an interim analysis. Twenty infections occurred in the circumcision group over follow-up. Forty-nine occurred in the control group. Incidence was 0.85 versus 2.1 per 100 person-years. Auvert gives the first trial-grade proof that circumcision cuts HIV risk. Follow-up visits came at months 3, 12, and 21.
europmc-pmc1392256:
Weinhold surveyed epigenetics, the science of gene control change, in 2006. The term surfaced nearly a century earlier. Evidence long hinted gene function changes without sequence changes. Recent studies thrust the field into fresh attention.

Epigenetic links now touch cancers of almost all types. Cognitive, respiratory, heart, reproductive, and autoimmune illnesses also appear. Suspected drivers include heavy metals, pesticides, diesel exhaust, and tobacco smoke. Hormones, radiation, viruses, bacteria, and nutrients join the list. Weinhold argues genome-wide epigenetic maps are essential for genetics overall. Stem cells, cloning, and aging research all depend on them.
europmc-pmc1414056:
Severe sudden kidney failure strikes some patients in intensive care, and its long-term toll was unclear. Bagshaw and co-authors tracked every case in the Calgary health region from 1999 to 2002. They counted 240 cases among one million adults. Risk ran highest in men, older adults, and people with past heart, lung, or kidney disease.

Just over half the patients died within a month, and 64 percent died within a year. Bagshaw found that liver disease, shock, and high illness scores raised the risk of death. Among those who lived a year, 78 percent no longer needed dialysis, the machine filtering of blood.
europmc-pmc1458356:
Knowing who died, and when, matters for studies of veterans' health. Sohn and co-authors checked four death record sources at the Department of Veterans Affairs in 2006. They drew 3,000 names at random from 8.3 million veterans. They then matched dates against a national death index, the gold standard.

The Social Security file caught 92 percent of deaths. The VA's own main file caught 77 percent. One hospital file caught just 12 percent. Dates that were present matched the index well. Sohn found that merging all four sources caught 98 percent of deaths. The merged file gives VA studies a far fuller base.
europmc-pmc1702556:
Brain tumors can switch on a growth receptor through faults outside its control center. Lee and co-authors sequenced the full EGFR gene in glioblastomas in 2006. Kinase-domain faults in this receptor were known to predict drug response in lung cancer.

They found new missense mutations, single letter changes, in the receptor's outer domain in 13.6 percent of tumors. The mutants came with extra gene copies. In lab cells they drove anchorage-free growth and tumor formation. Those cells stayed sensitive to small-molecule EGFR blockers. Lee suggests the mutations mark patients who may benefit from such drugs.
europmc-pmc1713256:
Bone-building signals called BMPs overlap so much that their separate jobs were blurred. Bandyopadhyay and co-authors untangled them in 2006 with mice lacking BMP2, BMP4, or BMP7 in limb buds. Removing genes only in the limb dodged early embryo death.

Contrary to earlier claims, BMPs did not pattern the front-back axis as helpers of Sonic Hedgehog, nor set digit identity. A threshold of BMP signaling was needed to start cartilage formation. Cartilage that did form matured normally without some pairs. But losing both BMP2 and BMP4 severely impaired bone formation. The loss split cartilage and bone roles apart.
europmc-pmc1783856:
Lucas and colleagues used one review in 2007 to compare two ways of blending study findings. Systematic reviews increasingly mix number-based studies with word-based ones, such as interviews. Blending the two fairly is still an unsolved craft problem.

Their test case reviewed lay views of infant size and growth, drawing on 19 studies of both kinds. They ran the same material through textual narrative synthesis, which sums up each study in words, and thematic synthesis, which groups findings by shared themes. Both routes reached similar conclusions about how parents view baby size. The narrative route handled study quality and variety better, but found shared points less well. The thematic route sparked new hypotheses, yet could blur quality differences between studies.
europmc-pmc1845156:
Pearson, Hattersley and co-authors showed in 2007 that a diabetes gene can make newborns unusually large and prone to low blood sugar. The gene is HNF4A, and faults in it cause a young-onset inherited diabetes. Fetal insulin drives growth, so the team studied birth weight in families carrying these faults.

They compared 108 people from HNF4A families with 134 from families with faults in a sister gene, HNF1A. Babies carrying the HNF4A fault were a median of 790 grams heavier than relatives without it. Over half of carriers were macrosomic, meaning oversized at birth, against 13 percent of non-carriers. Passing low blood sugar after birth hit eight carrier infants and none of the non-carriers. Mouse work on the pancreas backed the fetal insulin link.
europmc-pmc1939856:
Nielsen, Lundegaard and Lund presented SMM-align in 2007, a method that predicts how strongly short protein pieces bind to MHC class II molecules. Those molecules sit on antigen-presenting cells and show captured peptides to helper T cells. A foreign peptide that binds well becomes a candidate vaccine target, so prediction accuracy drives epitope discovery.

Class II grooves are open at both ends, so a peptide can sit in several registers, and finding its core is the crux. SMM-align uses a stabilization matrix method to align the peptide and predict affinity directly. On a large benchmark covering 14 human HLA-DR variants and three mouse variants, it beat four rival tools, including a Gibbs sampler and TEPITOPE. Pooling peptide data from different sources into training improved it further.
europmc-pmc1988856:
Del Cul, Baillet and Dehaene studied in 2007 why some flashed images reach consciousness and others do not. A target shown briefly, then covered by a mask, stays unseen unless the gap passes about 50 milliseconds. Models suggest conscious access needs lasting activity in looping brain circuits. The team asked which brain areas and timings mark that threshold.

They recorded dense electrical signals from the scalp while varying the target-mask gap in small steps. Early processing in visual areas below 250 milliseconds could occur without awareness. A later signal after 270 milliseconds spread widely across frontal, parietal and temporal areas. That late, broad activation matched whether subjects reported seeing the target. The findings separate hidden early processing from conscious report.
europmc-pmc2124756: A medical paper on the catalytic activity of the developing hen's egg. The chick's chemistry. This article preserves that embryology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2124856: A medical paper on the interference of inactive serum and egg-white in the phenomenon of complement fixation. The blocked complement. This article preserves that immunology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128356: A medical paper with studies on total bile, bile changes from pressure obstruction. The blocked bile. This article preserves that physiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131056: The pneumococcus carries a soluble marker all its own, and this third installment dug deeper into that specific substance. Lab workers purified and probed the compound. The germ's chemical signature, pinned down. The article preserves that bacteriology research for future study.
europmc-pmc2131156: A medical paper on varicella in monkeys, nuclear inclusions from varicella virus. The monkey chickenpox. This article preserves that virology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131356: Getting well from the germ takes more than luck, and this paper worked out how the body fights back. The team followed each step of the comeback. The healing, explained. The article keeps that body-defense study.
europmc-pmc2140356: A biology paper on influence of the concentration of electrolytes on electrification. The charged solutions. This article preserves that biophysics. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2140956: A biology paper on the prenatal growth of the mouse. The unborn mouse. This article preserves that embryology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2206356:
Le Maitre, Freemont and Hoyland tested in 2007 whether disc cells in the spine age prematurely during degeneration. Intervertebral disc degeneration is a major suspected cause of low back pain. Its features mimic ageing but appear faster. The team proposed accelerated cellular senescence, the state where cells stop dividing and change behaviour. They isolated cells from healthy and degenerate human discs and measured telomere length, ageing markers and growth capacity.

Telomeres, the protective DNA caps on chromosomes, shortened with age and with worse degeneration. Cells from degenerate discs showed more of the senescence marker P16INK4A and more ageing-related staining, even in young patients. Their ability to keep dividing fell. Higher P16INK4A also tracked with higher production of matrix-degrading enzymes, which chew up disc tissue. Senescence may thus drive the degeneration itself.
europmc-pmc2386456:
Griffiths, Christensen, and Jorm studied what predicts stigma toward depression in 2008. They separated two kinds: personal stigma, what a person believes about depression, and perceived stigma, what a person thinks others believe. The surveys covered three Australian samples, from 1,001 adults nationwide to 5,572 local residents.

Personal stigma ran consistently higher in men, in people with less education, and in those born overseas. It also rose with current psychological distress and fell with prior contact with depression and better knowledge about it. Perceived stigma followed a different pattern, sharing only the distress link. Living far from cities mattered for neither kind. The authors urged campaigners to treat the two stigmas as separate targets, since mixing them muddies both measurement and anti-stigma programs.
europmc-pmc2395256:
Robbins and a large team compared immune sentry cells in mice and humans in 2008. The cells are dendritic cells, which sample the body and alert the immune system. They come in subsets, chiefly conventional dendritic cells and a rarer kind called plasmacytoid, and matching mouse subsets to human ones was disputed.

The team measured gene activity across the whole genome in white blood cells from both species. Subset by subset, the activity programs matched: each mouse subset had a human counterpart running the same core program. That held for both the plasmacytoid and conventional families. The result means findings in mouse dendritic cells can be mapped onto human ones with more confidence. It also gives a shared naming frame for a cell family central to vaccines and immune disease.
europmc-pmc2478656:
Thomas and Harden set out a method for merging interview-based studies in 2008. Health researchers increasingly wanted systematic reviews of qualitative studies, the kind using interviews and observation, but had no standard synthesis method. Their answer, thematic synthesis, adapts the thematic analysis used inside single studies.

The method runs in three stages. First, reviewers code the findings of each study line by line. Next they group codes into descriptive themes that stay close to the original studies. Finally they build analytical themes that go beyond the sources, generating new explanations or hypotheses. The authors illustrate it with a review of children's views on healthy eating, which they combined with intervention studies. Interventions matching children's own suggestions, such as hands-on experience over health warnings, worked better. Software support and transparency are stressed throughout.
europmc-pmc2556656:
Lee and colleagues tested in 2008 whether inflammation across the whole body can drive the brain changes of Alzheimer's disease. Brain inflammation is a suspect in Alzheimer's, which features neuron loss and build-up of a protein fragment called beta-amyloid. The team injected mice with lipopolysaccharide, a bacterial molecule that provokes inflammation, and measured memory, brain chemistry, and cell survival.

The treated mice did worse on avoidance and water maze memory tests. Repeated injections raised beta-amyloid in the hippocampus and cortex. They did so by boosting the two cutting enzymes, beta- and gamma-secretase. These enzymes free the fragment from its parent protein. Three weeks of pre-treatment with an anti-inflammatory drug, sulindac sulfide, blocked the build-up. It also blocked the memory problems and neuron death. The same protection appeared in cultured neurons.
europmc-pmc2647156:
Gough and Simmonds reviewed in 2007 the HLA region, a stretch of DNA packed with immune system genes, and its links to autoimmune disease. In these diseases the body attacks its own tissues. Ties between this region and illnesses such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and Graves' disease had been known for over fifty years.

The strongest ties sit in one gene cluster whose products show foreign material to helper T cells, a step that can start an autoimmune attack. Newer studies, using big patient datasets and better statistics, found further ties in nearby parts of the region. These act on their own, apart from the main cluster. One gene, HLA-B, linked strongly to type 1 diabetes, and another, HLA-C, to multiple sclerosis and Graves' disease. The pattern hints that infections and killer T cells help trigger these illnesses.
europmc-pmc2684656:
Burton and colleagues proposed in 2009 that two pregnancy dangers, a baby growing too slowly in the womb and early preeclampsia, spring from one root at different strengths. Both are blamed on poor blood flow to the placenta, when the mother's arteries fail to widen as they should. The puzzle was why one pregnancy then sickens the mother while the other mainly starves the baby.

Placenta studies show stress inside the cells' protein-folding workshop in both conditions. That stress slows protein making, explaining the small placenta seen in each. In early preeclampsia, the blood flow failure runs deeper, adding oxidative stress, a chemical burning of tissue. The stressed placenta then spills inflammatory signals and debris into the mother's blood, causing her syndrome of high pressure and organ strain. Severity of the artery failure, the authors argue, decides which disease appears.
europmc-pmc2685456:
Coop and co-authors used worldwide genome data in 2009 to ask how much geography, rather than selection, shapes human adaptation. They compared allele frequencies, the shares of gene variants, across populations in two large collections. Variants under strong local selection should stand out sharply between places where conditions differ.

In practice, variants flagged as selected mostly followed the same map as random variants, sorting people into the usual continental clusters. Truly fixed differences between populations, where one group always carries a variant and another never does, proved surprisingly rare. Nearly all arose outside Africa, and most cluster in East Asia. The moral is restraint: selection in recent human history has often been weak, and migration plus chance drift have steered even useful variants. Extreme differences between populations, they conclude, need history checked before adaptation is claimed.
europmc-pmc2690656:
Kirk and colleagues reported in 2009 that rat mothers made obese by diet permanently rewire the appetite circuits of their pups. Earlier work had shown the offspring grow into overeating, fatter adults. The team tracked leptin, the hormone that reports body fat to the brain, through the pups' first weeks.

Pups of obese mothers showed a leptin surge that was both bigger and longer than normal, fed by extra leptin from their own fat. By day 30, before any overeating began, their blood leptin looked normal. The response was not. Leptin injections suppressed appetite only weakly. The arcuate nucleus, the brain's appetite control center, answered with a muted signal. A downstream appetite peptide in the target region also ran low. Flooding the young brain with leptin, the authors propose, teaches it to ignore leptin for life.
europmc-pmc2705656:
Supekar, Musen, and Menon studied in 2009 how large brain networks change as children grow into young adults. Most prior work tracked brain size or white matter, the wiring that links areas, not how areas work together at rest. They used resting brain scans and graph methods, which treat each brain area as a node linked to others.

Both children and young adults showed small-world networks, with tight local clusters and short paths across the brain. Wide rewiring with age still changed the layout, and a clear ranked, or hierarchical, order appeared only in the adult brain. Deep brain areas were more linked in children, while some outer areas grew stronger later.
europmc-pmc2759556:
Pilling, Fan, Huang, Kaul, and Gomer identified in 2009 marker combinations for human samples. Those markers distinguish fibrocytes from monocytes, macrophages, and fibroblasts. Fibrocytes are blood monocyte descendants that become fibroblast-like and help drive fibrotic disease, scarring that stiffens tissues. Telling these four cell types apart in lesions could reveal which cells a therapy should target.

Each type carried a unique marker signature. Only monocytes combined three specific markers, and only macrophages added a fourth. Fibrocytes shared part of that set but lacked one marker. Fibroblasts alone showed a wholly different set. Common markers such as CD34 and collagen failed to separate the types. Several immune signals also tuned marker levels on macrophages and fibrocytes in distinct ways.
europmc-pmc2807856:
Zanobetti, Franklin, Koutrakis, and Schwartz asked in 2009 whether the chemical mix inside fine air particles changes how much harm they do. Fine particles, called PM2.5, are a broad class tied to hospital visits, but their recipe varies by city and season. The team studied emergency admissions in twenty-six United States communities over four years.

A standard rise in particle levels brought roughly two percent more admissions for heart problems, heart attacks, heart failure, breathing trouble, and diabetes. The heart effects grew stronger when particles ran rich in nickel, chromium, arsenic, and bromine, elements tied to industry and traffic. The authors argue that source and recipe, not just total mass, shape the danger.
europmc-pmc2815756:
Safdie and colleagues reported ten cases in 2009 of cancer patients who chose to fast around their chemotherapy sessions. Mouse work had hinted that short fasting shields normal cells from high-dose chemo while leaving cancer cells exposed. Whether patients could fast safely during treatment was untested.

Patients fasted from about two days to nearly six days before treatment, and some for hours afterward, across an average of four chemo cycles. They reported hunger and lightheadedness but no serious fasting harms. Six patients who had chemo both ways felt less fatigue, weakness, and gut trouble in fasting cycles. Tumors still shrank as expected, though the authors stress only a controlled trial can settle benefit.
europmc-pmc2829056:
Wray, Yang, Goddard, and Visscher used genetics math in 2010 to explain what a common accuracy score can and cannot say about DNA-based disease risk tests. The score, called AUC, measures how well a test sorts sick from healthy people. Genome scans now feed risk profiles built from many small-effect variants, and AUC judges them.

The team derived an equation showing that even a perfect genetic test, explaining all inherited variance, has a ceiling on AUC. That ceiling depends on how common the disease is and how strongly it runs in families. Working backward, they estimate how much genetic variance a test must explain to reach a mid-level accuracy target across seventeen diseases. Answers ranged from about a tenth to about three quarters.
europmc-pmc2848556:
Bian, Xu, Lu, Xie, and Xi tested in 2010 whether Wolbachia, a bacterium living inside mosquito cells, can block dengue virus in Aedes aegypti, the main dengue carrier. Dengue threatens billions of people and has no vaccine or cure, so stopping the mosquito matters. Because Wolbachia and the virus crowd into the same tissues, the team compared infected and uninfected mosquitoes after dengue exposure.

Wolbachia sharply cut viral growth and spread inside the mosquitoes. Two weeks after infection it fully blocked transmission in well over a third of the infected mosquitoes tested. Infected mosquitoes also showed livelier baseline immunity and lived longer. The results support spreading Wolbachia through wild mosquito populations as a dengue control strategy.
europmc-pmc2868856:
Mealing and co-authors tested in 2010 whether health studies with very different designs and response rates still agree on risk relationships. They compared two New South Wales studies. One was a huge postal cohort where fewer than one in five invited people joined. The other was a state telephone survey that reached about three in five. Both covered the same population and asked many of the same questions.

Rates of smoking, diabetes, asthma, high blood pressure, and private insurance did differ between the two studies. Yet for questions worded closely alike, the links between exposures and outcomes came out almost identical, and formal tests found few real disagreements. The result reassures researchers that a low response rate alone does not wreck a study's risk estimates, even when raw rates are shaky.
europmc-pmc2970556:
Tremblay, Lowery, and Majewska examined how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, interact with synapses in the mouse visual cortex in a 2010 study published in PLoS Biology. In the healthy brain these cells constantly extend fine arms that touch nearby nerve endings.

Detailed microscopy showed microglial arms contacting every part of synapses, sometimes wrapping spines or swallowing small cell pieces, surrounded by pockets of open space. Dark rearing and renewed light exposure changed how actively the cells moved and touched synapses. The behaviour suggests microglia help tune connections in response to what the animal sees.
europmc-pmc3000156:
Boivin and colleagues measured how many young children hospitalised with breathing infections in Canada carried human metapneumovirus, in a 2003 prospective study over one winter and spring. The virus had only just been recognised as a human pathogen.

Among just over two hundred children under three, sensitive tests found the virus in about one in seventeen, far behind RSV and influenza A. Most of its cases were bronchiolitis, none needed intensive care, while a notable share of RSV and flu cases did. The picture is of an important but somewhat milder cousin of RSV.
europmc-pmc3102656:
Hollingsworth, Graham, and Little reviewed in 2011 the long effort to choose a standard DNA barcode for plants. A barcode is a short sequence that names a species the way a shop barcode names a product. Animals got a workable barcode early from one mitochondrial gene. Plants proved harder, since their mitochondrial DNA changes too slowly and their chloroplast genes each fall short in different ways.

The paper retraces how candidate regions were tested and combined, and what governs how well any barcode separates close species. It surveys early uses, from checking herbal products to sorting unknown seedlings, and the big shared library projects now under way. Tools for easy comparison against the library are still catching up. The authors' verdict is that a two gene chloroplast standard is workable today, with refinements to come. They wrote the review as a field guide for new users.
europmc-pmc3141456:
Aileen Clarke and colleagues checked a well-being questionnaire for use with teenagers in a 2011 paper in BMC Public Health. The scale, built to measure positive mental health in adults, had been approved only for ages sixteen and up. The team gave it to more than sixteen hundred pupils aged thirteen to sixteen in English and Scottish schools, alongside established comparison scales.

Scores filled the whole range and lined up with comparison measures in the expected directions, rising with family wealth and physical health. Repeat answers a week apart were fairly steady, and all items hung together as one scale. In discussion groups, pupils mostly found the wording clear and acceptable despite a few confusing items. The authors clear the scale for tracking teenage well-being from age thirteen.
europmc-pmc3149556:
Joseph Prejean and colleagues estimated new HIV infections in the United States from 2006 to 2009 in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Counting new infections, rather than diagnoses, shows where the epidemic is heading. The team used surveillance data from sixteen states and two cities with a refined statistical method that fills gaps and corrects for testing habits.

Yearly new infections held roughly steady at just under fifty thousand across the four years, with no significant change overall or in most groups. One pocket rose sharply: infections among people aged thirteen to twenty-nine grew by about a fifth, driven by young men who have sex with men, especially young Black men. That group also accounted for most new infections in 2009. The authors urge expanded, targeted prevention.
europmc-pmc3237356:
Stephanie Engel and colleagues studied prenatal exposure to organophosphate pesticides and children's cognitive development. They also asked whether a detoxifying enzyme changes the risk. The paper appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2011. The enzyme, paraoxonase 1, breaks down these pesticides, and people carry versions of it that work at different speeds. The study followed a multiethnic New York pregnancy cohort.

Mothers' urine during pregnancy carried pesticide breakdown products, and children were assessed at one and two years and again in early school years. Higher prenatal exposure was linked to lower mental development scores in infancy among Black and Hispanic children, with stronger effects where the mother's enzyme variant cleared the chemicals slowly. By school age, exposure tracked with weaker perceptual reasoning in one genetic group, in a dose-like pattern. The enzyme looks like an important susceptibility factor.
europmc-pmc3253456:
Robin Bernhoft reviewed mercury poisoning and its treatment in this 2012 article in the Journal of Environmental and Public Health. Mercury is a toxic heavy metal spread widely through nature. Most human exposure comes from eating fish or from dental amalgam fillings, and the metal occurs in several chemical forms that behave differently in the body.

Because its movement through the body is complex, mercury can produce a wide range of clinical pictures, which makes diagnosis genuinely challenging. Bernhoft explains how a reliable diagnosis can nevertheless be reached, weighing the exposure history and the available tests. The review then describes therapies reported to work for clinical toxicity. It serves as a compact reference for clinicians and public-health readers confronting a poison whose presentations are easy to mistake for other conditions.
europmc-pmc3266256:
Audrey Tyrka and colleagues tested whether childhood adversity leaves epigenetic marks on the stress hormone system that persist into adult life, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Animal work had tied poor early care to methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene and to exaggerated stress responses. The team measured methylation of that gene's promoter in blood DNA from ninety-nine healthy adults, alongside their childhood histories and a hormone challenge test.

Adults who reported parental loss, maltreatment, or low parental care carried more methylation on the receptor gene's promoter. Higher methylation in turn went with a blunted cortisol response in the challenge test. The authors read this as preliminary human evidence that early adversity can chemically tune the stress system, a possible route by which childhood hardship raises later risk of psychiatric illness.
europmc-pmc3283556:
Michael Delves and colleagues compared how current and experimental malaria drugs perform across the parasite's whole life cycle, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Medicine. Most drug testing concentrates on the blood stages that cause illness, yet malaria parasites also pass through liver stages in people and sexual stages that mosquitoes pick up. A drug blind to those stages cannot fully block transmission or prevent relapse.

The team tested fifty antimalarial compounds against the liver stage, the sexual blood stages, and the mosquito stages. Several Plasmodium species were used, including the main human parasite and two rodent parasites serving as laboratory stand-ins. Running the same panel across species and stages exposes which drugs work only on blood stages and which cover the full cycle. The authors offer the comparison as a guide for developing medicines that cure, prevent, and interrupt transmission at once.
europmc-pmc3323356:
Patrick and Williams examined how a theory of human motivation fits with a popular counseling style for health behavior, in a 2012 article. Habits such as eating well, exercising, and avoiding tobacco drive much of chronic disease and health spending. The theory, called self determination theory, holds that people change best when they feel their choices are their own, they feel capable, and they feel connected to others.

Motivational interviewing, a counseling approach that draws out a person's own reasons for change, grew up separately in clinical practice. The authors show the two overlap deeply, and argue each can supply what the other lacks. The theory gives the counseling style a firmer scientific backbone, while the counseling gives the theory concrete techniques. They call for studies testing where the two truly agree and where they part ways.
europmc-pmc3325956:
Byers, Wiles, Dunn, and Taft published a visual guide for telling where a female mouse is in her fertility cycle, in a 2012 paper. Breeding mice efficiently depends on spotting the stages when females will mate, which repeat every four to five days. A quick look at the vaginal opening works for the key stages, but coat color differences between strains can mislead the eye.

The paper presents photographs of the opening at each of the four stages for three widely used strains, black coated, agouti, and albino. When every stage must be pinned down, examining vaginal cells under a microscope remains the most accurate route, so the authors add an identification tool for that method too. The guide is meant as a teaching resource for animal facility staff.
europmc-pmc3420456:
Ochoa, Usall, Cobo, Labad, and Kulkarni reviewed in 2012 how schizophrenia and first-episode psychosis differ between men and women. The illness varies enormously between patients, and sex may explain part of that spread. The team summarized worldwide research across incidence, symptoms, functioning, substance use, and course.

Men develop schizophrenia more often and at younger ages than women. Symptom findings split: men may show more negative symptoms, women more emotional ones. Women generally functioned better before illness and socially, recovered more fully, and relapsed less, while men used substances more. Thinking skills showed no agreed sex gap, and family risk and birth complications showed none at all. Knowing these patterns, they argue, can sharpen care.
europmc-pmc3435256:
Gething and a large team drew the first world map of Plasmodium vivax malaria in 2012, the long-neglected second malaria parasite. Knowledge of where vivax spreads lagged far behind its cousin falciparum, blocking smart control plans. The team updated the transmission limits for 2010 and assembled nearly ten thousand geolocated surveys of parasite rates.

A statistical mapping model filled every five-kilometer square, dampened in Africa where a blood trait blocks the parasite. Vivax rates ran surprisingly low almost everywhere, rarely passing a small share of residents. Central Asia held the great majority of the roughly two and a half billion people at risk, with the hottest zones in Indonesia and Papua New Guinea. The map invites control plans tailored place by place.
europmc-pmc3483256:
Danzer and co-authors tracked how a Parkinson's-linked protein travels between cells, in Molecular Neurodegeneration in 2012. Clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein mark Parkinson's disease, and its harmful small clusters seem to spread through the brain over time. The team used a light-based test to find those clusters outside cells and ask how they get there and what they do.

Clusters turned up in two places outside cells: riding in tiny sacs called exosomes, and floating free. The sac-riding clusters entered new cells more readily and did more harm. The clusters sat both inside the sacs and on their surfaces. Danzer's team links release to the cell's recycling system: when recycling lags, sacs carry more clusters out. Boosting recycling might slow the spread.

europmc-pmc3702256: Pathways got Pathview. This 2013 paper launches Pathview for pathway data integration. The authors reveal the package. Their work spread through labs. Luo's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide. The study shaped pathway analysis.

europmc-pmc4055456: Plants got a light-and-heat-switch study. This 2014 paper finds a light-and-heat switch. The authors reveal the finding. Their work guides botany. Toledo-Ortiz's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped plant science. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc4056656: Sepsis got a blood-flow-kidneys study. This 2013 study links blood flow to kidney injury. The authors reveal the linking. Their work guides critical care. Legrand's team led the work. The study is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped ICU care.

frus-1861-d156:
On 14 October 1861, William Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a calm mid autumn report. The dispatch is document 156 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's mid October report comes from the heart of the autumn file. France still held its neutral course, and he could say so. A calm report from Paris was good news in itself for a cabinet beset on other fronts. Good news by silence was a phrase the cabinet learned to value that year. Silence from Paris, in that season, was a form of good news in itself.
frus-1861-d256:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands on 28 September 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 256 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d56:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 June 1861. The dispatch is document 56 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The longest day of the year found Adams reporting the state of play in London. Summer brought no break in the watch on shipyards, agents, and notes. His letter adds one more dated layer to the fullest run of letters in the whole 1861 volume. The Adams file is the spine of the 1861 volume, and this letter sits near its heart. Near its heart sits the summer when the post was won and held by paper.
frus-1862-d156:
Two Adams reports reached Washington under the date 3 October 1862; this second one is Document 156 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Envoys often split their news across two letters sent the same day, one for talks held and one for papers enclosed. The habit makes the printed file dense but rich. For readers now, paired dispatches like these show how much paper a single week of wartime diplomacy could produce at the London legation. Cotton hunger in British mill towns kept the war a kitchen-table topic across the North of England.
frus-1862-d256:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, answered Paris on 27 February 1862 with a dispatch to William L. Dayton, printed as Document 256 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The same date carries a Dayton report, so the two letters likely crossed.

Crossed letters were a fact of life before the Atlantic cable: each side wrote against stale news. Skilled envoys wrote for the situation they expected, not the one they last saw. The paired papers of 27 February show that discipline at work in the Paris file. With policy stated plainly enough to survive a fortnight at sea. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d356:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, on 7 February 1862. In a letter printed as Document 356 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

February brought the Union victory at Fort Henry, the kind of news that steadied Seward's hand with foreign envoys. France was then deciding whether to press deeper into Mexico after its allies wavered. A letter to Mercier in this month belongs to the quiet fencing by which Washington sought French restraint on both the war and Mexico. Mercier had served in Washington since 1860 and knew the capital's politics at close range.
frus-1862-d456:
On 20 January 1862 John Lothrop Motley reported from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 456 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Motley's January report covered the Austrian court's temper in the weeks after the Trent affair had nearly brought war with Britain. Vienna's rulers disliked rebellion on principle but distrusted republican success almost as much. His letters home weighed that balance for Seward. For the modern reader, the Vienna file shows the Union's diplomacy at its most patient. A famous historian, posted to a cool court, argues the case there. His client is a democratic government fighting to survive.
frus-1862-d556:
On 23 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister to Belgium. The instruction is Document 556 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Late May 1862 was the high-water mark of Union confidence that spring, and Seward's letters abroad carried that confidence to every post. Sanford in Brussels was charged with keeping Belgium's court and press on the Union's side. He was also charged with watching the Confederate agents. Those agents used Belgium as a base. The instruction is one of several that spring that treat Brussels as a working front. It was a front in the war of opinion, not a backwater. Sanford fought on it with real relish.
frus-1862-d56:
Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 2 May 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 56 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d656:
Late in his time as minister to Japan, Townsend Harris received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 19 November 1861. It is document 656 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. The two men had traded letters across the Pacific for years by then.

Much of Seward's outward mail that fall dealt with the war and the risk that other lands might back the South. His letters to Japan kept a smaller file in order at the same time. This one shows the reach of his desk. From a capital at war, he still wrote to a lone envoy on the far side of the world.
frus-1863p1-d156:
A stray comma rides in the title of this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 16 April 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date; the title of this one even keeps a stray comma in the printing. Adams was the American minister in London; the letter is document 156 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Mid-April mail from the legation kept the watch on Britain's yards and courts after the raider's seizure. Adams's reports stayed cool and exact, the style that had served the Union well. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day. The stray comma in its head is a small print quirk in a file of great weight.
frus-1863p1-d256:
On 31 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 256 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Read in sequence, these reports show a diplomat testing how far he could push a stronger power without provoking a second war. That balance was the heart of Adams's whole mission. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d356:
Washington's business with Britain on 9 January 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 356 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Britain had claimed neutral rights at sea, while the Union navy stopped British ships suspected of aiding the South. The friction from those seizures runs through this whole exchange. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d456:
Document 456 in the volume is a letter of 11 April 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d556:
Among the day's business on 8 June 1863 was a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d56:
On 28 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to Messrs. Fraser, Trenholm & Co. for the second time in four days. Memminger was the Confederate treasury chief; the Liverpool firm handled the South's money in Britain. The letter is document 56 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Two letters in four days to the same bankers point to fast-moving deals. Cotton, credit, and ships all ran through this firm's books, and Richmond's letters kept the flow in step with the war's needs. This one closes the treasury run in the printed group. It is a plain sheet with great weight behind it: the South's purse, held abroad.
frus-1863p1-d656:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State on 6 November 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d156: Minister Kirk wrote on November 21, 1943 to Hassanayn, chief of the Egyptian royal cabinet, and the letter is Document 156 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Host-government letters in the final hours before a summit dealt with the crown's part in the proceedings, though this record names no subject. The parties and the date are what the catalog gives. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d256: The facts given about this Cairo meeting, and the names of those who took part, come from the President's Log, the editors state. No record of the subjects discussed at the meeting has been found. The editors point the reader to their note on the Roosevelt and Churchill dinner meeting earlier in the volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d356:
An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume reconstructs a warning delivered at Tehran on 27 November 1943, for which no official record was made at the time. The account rests on a letter Ambassador Harriman wrote to the department's Historical Office in 1954, more than ten years later.

Molotov, Harriman recalled, summoned him and the British ambassador, Sir Archibald Clark Kerr. He told them that German agents in Tehran knew of Roosevelt's presence. The agents were planning a demonstration, which might involve an attempt at assassination. Stalin therefore urged the President to move into the British Legation or the Soviet Embassy, where a house stood ready. Harriman, General Connolly, and security chief Reilly agreed to recommend the Soviet compound, Roosevelt consented, and the move took place the next afternoon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d456:
On the last day of the Second Cairo Conference, December 6, 1943, American and British officials agreed the minutes of a joint meeting, later printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. An agreed text had to satisfy both delegations, so it states the version of events neither side disputed. The conference communiqué went out the same day.

Inside is the shared record of business done as the summit ended, when the decisions taken with Stalin at Tehran and refined at Cairo became the allies' settled course. Readers who want the conference's outcome rather than its gossip start with records like this one. They show what the two governments committed to, in words both approved.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d556:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on March 3, 1944, the same day two Churchill messages reached him. The exchange gives the day's correspondence a back-and-forth shape. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Roosevelt's style with Churchill mixed warmth, humor, and firm refusal when the two disagreed, as they often did over Mediterranean strategy that spring. His replies kept the partnership balanced between London's experience and Washington's growing power. For readers, this message shows the President holding his end of the alliance's central conversation in the last spring of preparation before the invasion of France.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d56: Secretary of State Cordell Hull set down a memorandum on October 25, 1943, during the Moscow Conference, and it stands as Document 56 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Memoranda of this kind fixed what was said and agreed while memories were fresh, and they anchor the official record. The catalog gives the author and the date and no topic. Hull's paper is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d156:
Joseph Grew, director of the Office of Far Eastern Affairs, sent Secretary Hull a warning memorandum on August 28, 1944. Behind the formal British request for a French mission in Southeast Asia, he reported, British secret operations in Indochina were already moving. His memo draws on a July cable from Colombo and an August report from Ambassador Murphy.

According to Grew, British SOE had already dropped a de Gaullist agent into Indochina using American facilities in China, keeping General Chennault in the dark. Two more drops were approved at a staff meeting the American coordinating officer was told had been cancelled. London meant to proceed without Washington's clearance, Grew wrote, though the operations were more political than military.
frus-1944-quebec-d256:
Future operations in the Mediterranean are the subject of C.C.S. 677, the United States Chiefs' paper of September 12, 1944. It answers General Wilson's progress reports with American preferences. Part or all of the Fifth Army, the chiefs held, should be transferred to France if it could be used effectively in the attack on Germany.

Timing and route, overland or by sea, would depend on the Italian offensive's outcome. If Eisenhower did not require the American forces in Italy, they should instead clear the Germans from Italy and assist British operations northeastward toward Vienna. The Twelfth Air Force's transfer would follow the same logic, while the Fifteenth Air Force could best perform its mission remaining at its Foggia bases.
frus-1944-quebec-d56:
Under Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius recorded this memorandum on September 6, 1944. Stettinius was fresh from the Dumbarton Oaks conference, where the plan for a United Nations organization had been drafted. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Six days before Quebec, the department's positions needed final shaping, and Stettinius's memoranda did much of that work. His interests ran to the peace organization as much as to the war's endgame. For readers, the paper shows the State Department preparing to argue, at a soldiers' and financiers' conference, for the political structure of the postwar world.
frus-1945-50-intel-d156:
The Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) addressed a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Board on 20 June 1946. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 156 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d256: The title "Department of State Briefing Memorandum" heads a text dated 17 December 1947. The State Department prints it as document 256 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. A new order was taking shape: the National Security Council now met at the top, with the CIA as its intelligence arm. Findings come first in a reader's eye, but the body of a report is where the proof sits, fact by fact.
frus-1945-50-intel-d356:
On 17 December 1948 the Intelligence Advisory Committee sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 356 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d56:
McCormack wrote to both Secretary Patterson and Secretary Forrestal on 15 December 1945. The State Department's intelligence chief addressed the two military secretaries together, as his own secretary had done five days earlier. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

McCormack's office at State and the military departments had to divide the work of the new system between them. December was the month of dividing. A letter to both secretaries at once kept the terms even: neither service could claim a private deal. Readers see the negotiation entering its drafting stage here, where courtesies thin and clauses thicken. The McCormack papers of December are the State intelligence office's last stand before the January settlement.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d156:
On 18 December 1944 the State Department told the public where the United States stood on Poland. The press release, printed in full in the Malta and Yalta volume, puts the policy in numbered points. It had already been passed to the governments concerned, Poland's included.

First, the United States stands for a strong, free, and independent Polish state. The Polish people keep the untrammeled right to order their own internal life. Second, boundary questions have always been left, in American policy, until the fighting ends. But if the nations directly concerned reach a friendly agreement first, Washington would not object. Such a deal could even help the war against the common enemy, the statement adds.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d256:
Stalin spoke with unusual frankness about the Pacific war on 17 October 1944, and Harriman cabled the President that night. Their long session with General Antonov covered detailed planning for Soviet entry. The report is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Stalin admitted his weakness in certain areas if Japan struck early. Against that, he set his plan for a strong land offensive to encircle and destroy the Japanese forces in Manchuria. One subject needs urgent American study, he said: help in building up supplies in the Far East through Pacific ports before the fighting starts. His list of needs, for ground and air forces, comes to about a million tons of goods.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d356:
Talking points, not treaty text, fill this American paper of February 6, 1945. It arms the Secretary of State with extra arguments for the United States plan on voting in the Security Council. The first point is blunt: the new world body might never be accepted if the American proposal failed.

American opinion, the paper warns, might reject a body that gave small nations an unfair place. The Latin American states and the British Dominions might do the same. It also cites the Tehran Declaration, where the three powers promised a peace commanding the good will of the world's peoples. The paper shows persuasion being prepared as carefully as policy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d456:
China's divided house prompts this memorandum from Stettinius to the President, dated February 10, 1945. As the day's meeting was likely the final plenary, Stettinius suggested Roosevelt find a moment to speak. He should urge Stalin and Churchill to see that their governments fully encouraged unity between the Kuomintang and the Communists in China.

The aim was China's war effort against Japan. United Chinese efforts, the memo says, must be important to all three governments. A penciled note by Hiss adds Bohlen's word: the President had already taken the matter up with Stalin, with satisfactory results. The memo shows Yalta reaching beyond Europe.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d56:
Weather, not politics, is the worry in Churchill's telegram to Roosevelt of 14 January 1945. He uses the code names of the day: Malta is “Cricket” and Yalta is “Magneto.” The message belongs to the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, which prints the leaders' private traffic.

Churchill reports that Anthony Eden is glad Edward Stettinius will reach Malta on 31 January if he can. Stalin, he says, expects him at Yalta on 2 February. But winter flying may force delays, and the two Western leaders might not meet Stalin until the 3rd. He closes by welcoming Harry Hopkins's trip to London.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d156:
Acting Secretary Grew briefed Truman on Palestine in a memorandum dated June 16, 1945. The memo is document 156 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Zionist representatives at the San Francisco conference had asked to meet the President before he sat down with Churchill, expecting Palestine to come up at the summit.

Grew says the Department is preparing material on Palestine for possible use at the meeting, since the British will soon have to decide that country's future. He does not think the question will need detailed discussion, or any decision by Truman, during the meeting with Churchill. Still, it would help to know the British government's intentions. The short memo is an early sign of the Palestine problem moving toward the center of American policy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d256:
A State Department memorandum set the American line on liberated Europe, in an extract dated June 30, 1945. The extract is document 256 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It states what the United States should propose under the agenda item on carrying out the Yalta Declaration on Liberated Europe.

For Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary, the three Allied governments should agree in principle to reorganize the present governments to include all significant democratic elements. Recognition and peace treaties should wait until that is done, and three-power consultation should work out the procedures, looking toward early free elections. For Greece, the paper proposes that the three governments send observers to supervise the elections due later in the year. France might join them. This builds on an Anglo-American approach already being made to Athens.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d356:
Edwin Pauley, reporting from Moscow on June 19, 1945, warned against fixing reparations totals too soon. In talk after talk, the Soviet negotiator Maisky kept returning to the twenty billion dollar figure discussed at Yalta. Of that sum, half would go to the Soviet Union, forty percent to Britain and America, and ten percent to all others.

Pauley had not openly resisted that basis, since the three leaders had agreed at Yalta to use it for discussion. But he judged it too early to name an exact amount before a first survey of what Germany could pay. Other claimant countries, he added, also had to be counted first.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d456:
Soviet troops massing in Bulgaria are described in Ambassador Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of June 29, 1945. General Oxley, head of the British delegation on Bulgaria's Control Commission, had just toured from Sofia to Varna. He went north of the Balkan mountains and returned by a southern route. Russian officers worked hard to keep his party from talking to anyone unwatched.

Oxley saw Russian troops in Lovech, Trnovo, and Shumen, perhaps advance parties for larger arrivals. Two Russian divisions stood near Varna and Burgas, and traffic through those ports ran to food and former prisoners out, cotton and planes in. His summary impression: Russian forces were massing in depth north of the Greek and Turkish frontiers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d556:
Cloyce Huston, who headed the State Department's Southern European desk, wrote to his colleague Walworth Barbour on July 11, 1945. The extract is document 556 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Attached is a long memo on Yugoslavia since the Crimea Conference.

The memo argues that Poland and Yugoslavia face the same core problem. Both are farming lands now ruled by governments under Soviet sway. It lists the Crimea terms for Yugoslavia one by one. The Tito-Subasic deal was to take effect at once, and a wider assembly was to form a short-term parliament. It also cites the Declaration on Liberated Europe and its pledge that peoples may choose their own form of rule.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d56:
President Truman answered Churchill's housing proposal in a one-line top secret telegram on June 11, 1945. The reply is document 56 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had asked that each delegation at Berlin have its own quarters and guards, rather than live as Soviet guests as at Yalta.

Truman's whole answer is that he agrees, and that he will instruct General Eisenhower to make the needed arrangements. A note in the volume shows the order moving the next day, when General Marshall passed Churchill's words to Eisenhower with the President's backing. The tiny exchange set the physical terms on which the three delegations would live and meet at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d656:
Washington explained to Ambassador Winant why Moscow need not sit in the Tangier talks, June 25, 1945. The secret wire is document 656 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It was signed by Grew and Loy Henderson.

The Department argues that leaving the Soviets out can be justified. Moscow, it says, has never shown any interest in the Tangier zone. It has kept no representative there and never claimed a party's rights under the Algeciras treaty. Imperial Russia had been a party to that treaty, but the Soviet state never acted on it. The United States, by contrast, kept a post in Tangier the whole time. It also kept exercising its treaty rights there, though it never signed the 1923 statute.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1056:
Nikolai Novikov, secretary of the Soviet delegation, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 25, 1945. Acting on Molotov's instructions, he encloses a Soviet aide-mémoire about German troops in Norway. Moscow has received reports that the terms of unconditional surrender are not being fully applied there.

The enclosure cites two bodies of troops: some 260,000 men between Mo and Trondheim, and 140,000 near Tromsö. These men, it claims, still hold their arms and light equipment. They have not been interned and move about freely. Since Allied command holds supreme control over surrendered troops in Norway, Moscow asks Washington and London to note the report.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1156:
Fetter, chief of the division for lend-lease and surplus war property, wrote to Clayton and to Collado on 28 July 1945. His division ran the books on the weapons and goods America had lent its allies. Collado directed the office for money policy and growth abroad.

As the war in Europe ended, the fate of all that gear became urgent business. Who kept it, who paid, and what was written off were choices with long shadows. This note shows the money-and-gear track running beside the summit. It is the ledger side of alliance war, kept while the leaders talked.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1256:
Sato cabled Togo on 27 July 1945, reporting again from Moscow. The day before, the Allies had issued the Potsdam Declaration, giving Japan terms for surrender. Tokyo's answer was not yet set, and its Moscow bid still hung in the air.

Sato's embassy remained Japan's last hope of a softer end through Soviet hands. His report reached Tokyo as its leaders weighed the Allied terms. What Moscow would or would not do bore straight on that choice. This cable is the Moscow thread at the declaration's moment. It shows the envoy still reporting, while the ground under his mission gave way.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1356:
The Soviet delegation laid a further proposal before the Potsdam Conference on 22 July 1945. Written proposals were the working tools of the summit, each one a draft the three sides could fight over line by line. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Every Soviet paper in the volume marks a point where Moscow stated its terms in fixed form. Comparing the run of Soviet proposals with the closing protocol shows readers the shape of the bargain that ended the talks. Some asks survived whole, some were cut down, and some vanished. This proposal is one tile in that mosaic, and its date places it in the summit's busy middle week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-156: Standing after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume, this editorial note is a piece of the volume's frame. The series' historians wrote notes like this to cite sources and link related papers. They keep a reader from mistaking a gap for a fact. The note does its work quietly, in a few lines.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-56:
A United States delegation memorandum of July 21, 1945, takes stock of the conference at its midpoint. Titled Status of Problems Before the Conference, it is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. Its first part lists the problems on which substantial agreement had been reached.

The Council of Foreign Ministers heads the list. The proposal stands substantially approved, with minor textual improvements to come. London is fixed as the meeting place, and September 1 as the latest date. On Germany, the revised paper on the Control Council's authority in political questions has approval. The German fleet and merchant marine will be divided in three parts, the memo records. A substantial share of the submarines will be destroyed, and all the merchant ships, Russia's share included, will serve the war against Japan. On Austria, Soviet consent for U.S. and British forces to enter Vienna is noted.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d756:
The British Chiefs of Staff set out their view in this memorandum of July 24, 1945. Document 756 brings the British military voice into the Potsdam record. London's chiefs advised their own leaders and worked with the American staff. Their agreed paper joined the second Potsdam volume.

Allied strategy was a shared product. A British chiefs' memo shows the other half of that partnership thinking. Readers can set it beside American staff papers of the same days. The pair reveals where the allies agreed and where they merely cooperated. The document keeps the volume honest about the alliance's joint mind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d856:
The Subcommittee on German Political Questions reported on July 19, 1945, in document 856. The group handled the political shape of beaten Germany: its government, parties, and borders of authority. Its report went to the conference's senior levels in the first week. The text joined the second Potsdam volume.

Political questions about Germany cut deepest at Potsdam. Who would rule, and under whose watch, shaped the continent's future. Readers find the experts' account of that argument in this report. The document shows the conference's layered method at its most serious. Staff wrestled the hardest topic first, so leaders could settle it last.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d956:
Edwin Pauley wrote to the Secretary of State on July 30, 1945, after reading William Clayton's reparations memorandum. The two men differ on one figure: how much movable factory equipment sits in the Soviet zone. Clayton says 40 percent. Pauley's own estimate runs near 45 percent, some 200 million Reichsmarks more.

Pauley lists seven reasons the gap could arise, from coverage of transport and utilities to wartime damage in the west. He then waves the dispute aside as beside the point. For practical purposes the Soviet zone holds about half of all reparations material, he says. The sides stand close enough to strike a bargain.
frus-1947v03-d256: A 1947 Foreign Relations of the United States document from the British Commonwealth and Europe volume. The Secretary of State's papers on postwar Europe. This entry preserves that diplomatic record. Writers of history may cite it later.
frus-1950v07-d756: A 1950 FRUS cable from the Chargé in Korea to the Secretary of State. The embassy reported from Seoul. This document preserves that telegram. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
frus-1977-80v29-d156: A 1977-1980 FRUS transcript of a telephone conversation on Panama. The leaders spoke. This entry preserves that transcript. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
gao-gaoreports-b-295956: Firma Hermann Leis doubled its May 2005 protest — two case numbers, one services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299156: Free&Ben Inc. took its February 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call on the claims. The firm challenged the award, and the ruling tests the protest. Small firms get the same formal process as the giants.
gao-gaoreports-b-299456: Lockmasters Security Institute took its May 2007 lock-and-key contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call. The firm challenged the award; the ruling tests the claims. Security-training deals get the same fair-bid law as any buy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1056: The U.S. had not restricted imports under the China safeguard in 2005, and GAO's report says the trade tool went unused. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the safeguard's use deserved honest assessment. The non-use had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-256: Immigrant investor visas drew few takers in 2005, and GAO's report blames pending regulations and other factors. The review counts the missing millionaires. The program's promise went unclaimed. The unclaimed promise was studied. The takers were few. The regulations were pending.
