gao-gaoreports-gao-05-356: Secure Flight's build needed risk management in 2005, and GAO's report says development and testing were underway, though risks had to be managed. The review checks the construction. The flyers' data deserved the care. The risks had to be managed. The flyers' data deserved the care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-456: Franchise funds' value to the Pentagon was unproven in 2005, and GAO's report says the convenience came without demonstrated benefit. The findings demand the proof. The report warns that the interagency buying deserved honest value. The value had to be shown.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-556: Military base upkeep money needed minding in 2005, and GAO's report says the facility funds had to be watched closely. The findings demand the attention. The report warns that the installations deserved honest budgets. The installations deserved honest budgets. The funds had to be watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-656: Medicare equipment suppliers needed stronger screening in 2005, and GAO's report says more effective vetting and enrollment standards were required. The findings demand the locks. The report warns that the fraudsters should not get paid. The screening had to be stronger.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-856: Federal health plan prices varied widely in 2005, and GAO's report says competition and other factors drove the differences. The findings do the comparing. The report warns that the workers deserved fair premiums. The variation had to be understood. The workers deserved fair premiums.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-956: Electronic voting security efforts were underway in 2005, and GAO's report says federal work had begun, though key gaps remained. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the voters deserved trustworthy machines. The efforts had to be completed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1056: The next-gen nuclear plant's status got a GAO check in 2006, and the report reviews the Energy Department's development effort. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the reactor of tomorrow needed steady progress today. The effort had to advance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-156: Big truck enforcement had strengthened since 2000, and GAO's 2006 report says federal efforts improved, though state grant oversight needed work. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the highways' giants needed watching. The oversight had to improve. The highways' giants needed watching.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-356: The Joint Strike Fighter was rushing to production in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon planned to build before testing proved performance. The findings sound the alarm. The report warns that the trillion-dollar jet should fly before it was bought. The testing had to come first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-656: Worker misclassification needed outreach in 2006, and GAO's report says better outreach could ensure proper classification. The findings demand the education. The report warns that the wrongly labeled workers deserved their rights. The outreach had to improve. The workers deserved their rights.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1156: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report surveys retiree benefits promised by state and local governments — pensions and health care for public workers. GAO examines benefit structures, legal protections, and the fiscal outlook for funding future costs. The report foreshadows the pension crises that would soon strain state budgets: promises made in good times coming due with too little saved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-156: The taxpayer's advocate was swamped in 2007, and GAO's report says the caseload had grown even as filers reported satisfaction. The findings balance the good news and the strain. The report asks whether the help desk for the harassed could keep up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-256: The SEC's computers needed steady hardening in 2007 — GAO's report says the market cop had to keep strengthening its controls year after year. The findings press for real persistence. The report's point: the guardian of the markets must guard its own gates.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-356: The coastal barrier lands got their status check in 2007 — GAO's report reviews the development and the federal aid that flowed there. The findings map the encroachment. The report's tension: the dunes the law meant to spare kept getting built on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-56: This 2007 GAO report takes a hard look at VA Health Care: Many Medical Facilities Have Challenges in Recruiting and Retaining Nurse Anesthetists. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gobineau-moral-intellectual-diversity-ra:
Henry Hotze published his English translation of Arthur de Gobineau's work as The Moral and Intellectual Diversity of Races in 1856. Gobineau's Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races had appeared in French in 1853 and 1855. Hotze, a Swiss-born editor in Alabama, shaped the English version for American readers.

Gobineau argued that race explains the rise and fall of civilizations, and that mixing of races brings decay. Hotze cut and framed the text to fit debates over slavery in the United States. The book became a foundational text of racialist ideology in the nineteenth century. Histories of racism cite it widely, and it is preserved here as a primary source for that record.
golden-bull-1356:
Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull in 1356 to fix how Holy Roman Emperors would be chosen. Named for its gold seal, the decree ended years of disputed elections and rival claimants. It named seven prince-electors as the only men allowed to choose the emperor.

The text spells out where electors meet, how they vote, and what rights each elector holds at home. It also regulates successions inside the electors' own lands, keeping those lands undivided. These rules gave the empire a stable frame for centuries. The bull stayed in force until the empire itself ended in 1806.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_openness:
Hungary's 1956 revolt against communist rule began with grief at a graveside. On October 6, Hungarians ceremonially reburied Laslo Rajk, a former minister who had been wrongly accused and executed. This briefing book, written sixty years later, traces the revolt's echoes in neighboring Romania.

The reburial drew out long-suppressed anger at a repressive, economically failing regime. On October 23 the discontent exploded in Budapest, in a mass demonstration demanding political and economic reform. Soviet tanks crushed the rising, but its example crossed borders. The Romanian angle matters because unrest there was watched and punished quietly, leaving a thinner record that postings like this help rebuild.
hesiod-callimachus-theognis-bohn-1856:
The Reverend J. Banks translated Hesiod, Callimachus, and Theognis into prose for Bohn's library in 1856. The volume joins three Greek poets of very different ages and tempers. Hesiod, the farmer poet of Boeotia, is the oldest voice in the book, from the eighth century BCE.

His Works and Days teaches farming, justice, and the myth of the five ages of man, while the Theogony orders the gods. Callimachus, the scholar poet of Alexandria, adds his polished hymns. Theognis gives short elegies of counsel, pride, and exile from old Megara. Banks's version was the road by which many English readers first met the Elegies of Theognis.
jami-salaman-absal-fitzgerald-1856:
Jami sang the soul's journey in Salaman and Absal, and Edward FitzGerald Englished it in Miltonic verse in 1856. The Persian poem tells of Prince Salaman's earthly love for Absal and the slow turning of his heart toward divine love. FitzGerald, later famed for the Rubaiyat, found in Jami a kindred spirit, and the rendering here comes complete from the 1909 centenary edition.

The allegory works on two levels at once, a love story that is also a map of the spirit. FitzGerald's stately English gives the Sufi tale a grave music of its own. The piece stands as the companion to his Rubaiyat, the other pillar of his Persian work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenthal-nauma:
Naumann Löwenthal (1819–1855) was a German teacher and writer born at Schmiegel, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling gives his short life. He studied philosophy, mathematics, and the natural sciences at Berlin and Breslau. He took his degree at Halle in 1841 and passed his teaching examination at Berlin in 1844.

Löwenthal then became the first Jew in Prussia appointed a head teacher, serving at a municipal technical school in Posen, where he died. The article notes his many treatises in technical periodicals and his one named book, “Die Physiologie des Freien Willens,” printed at Leipsic in 1843. That book’s title means the physiology of free will. The entry is brief, but it preserves a notable first in Prussian education and the outline of a career cut short at thirty-six.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-louis-107:
Louis Meyer, a Polish poet born in the village of Sluzewo in Russian Poland in 1796, is remembered in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Herman Rosenthal, published in 1906. Sent to Berlin at fourteen to prepare for business, he showed an unusual gift for poetry instead. In 1816 he went home to Poland and entered trade.

Business never crowded out his writing: Meyer kept studying and composed German verse for decades. In 1861 voters chose him for the County Assembly, though the Polish insurrection kept it from ever meeting. After his death in 1869 his collected writings appeared at Berlin in 1871, mixing epic and dramatic poems, scenes of Jewish life, and short prose aphorisms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montalto-filoth:
Filotheo Eliau Montalto, a Portuguese physician born at Castello Branco in the mid-sixteenth century, set one condition above all others: to live openly as a Jew. Gotthard Deutsch and Isaac Broydé tell his story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Raised in Judaism by Marrano parents, he left Portugal's Inquisition behind for Leghorn and then Venice.

At Venice he knew Concino Concini, whose word brought Maria de Medici's invitation to the French court. He had already refused the succession to Mercuriale's chair at Padua, fearing any post that might compromise his religious duties; from the queen he exacted complete religious freedom before accepting. He died at Tours in 1616, physician to a court that let him keep his faith.
keller-seldwyla-folks-1856:
Wolf von Schierbrand translated three tales from Gottfried Keller's Seldwyla cycle into English in 1919. Seldwyla is Keller's invented Swiss town, full of cheerful idlers and small dreamers. The best-known tale here is A Village Romeo and Juliet, drawn from a real event Keller read in a newspaper.

Two farmers ruin each other over a strip of land between their fields. Their children, Sali and Vrenchen, love in spite of the feud and get one perfect day together. The end is as sad as the day is bright. The other tales mix comedy with the same clear-eyed pity. Keller's Seldwyla stories remain the heart of Swiss prose fiction.
king-henry-vi-part-3-pg2256: York dies on the molehill in this edition: Margaret crowns him with paper before the stabbing, and the wars grind toward Towton. Father kills son, son kills father, in England's bleakest chronicle. The trilogy's blood-soaked climax.
las-casas-tears-of-the-indians-1656:
Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish friar, wrote his Brevísima relación in 1552 to accuse his own nation. The Tears of the Indians is the English translation printed in 1656. Las Casas had lived in the Indies and seen the conquest's cruelty at close range, and he wrote to lay it before the Spanish crown.

His short work lists, region by region, the killings and abuses that followed the Spanish landings. It became the founding text of the Black Legend, the dark fame of Spain's empire abroad. As the first broad indictment of conquest atrocities, it reshaped how Europe argued about empire itself. Its charges still start debate today.
motley-dutch-republic-1856:
John Lothrop Motley published The Rise of the Dutch Republic in 1856, a history of the Netherlands' revolt against Spain. Motley, an American, worked in archives across Europe. William the Silent, Prince of Orange, stands as the hero of the story. Sieges, massacres, and sea battles mark the Dutch fight for freedom.

Motley frames the revolt as a contest between liberty and tyranny. Philip II of Spain plays the villain in his vivid telling. The book won fame in America and Europe alike. Dutch readers embraced it as a national epic in English. It remains the American classic of Dutch history, dramatic and deeply researched for its time.
mr-culpepper-s-treatise-of-aurum-potabil: Mr. Culpepper's Treatise of Aurum Potabile, 1656. The drinkable gold. This book preserves that treatise. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Writers of history may cite it later.
openalex-w1989554956: Parasitic worms need right names — treatment depends on it. A 2009 study compared eyeballing and DNA barcoding for naming filarioid worms and related parasites. The head-to-head test judged which method names the worms right every time.
openalex-w2159170056: Sea turtles roam whole oceans, but conservation happens beach by beach — a mismatch this 2010 PLoS ONE paper tries to fix. The authors propose "regional management units," a framework for dividing wide-ranging turtle populations into biologically meaningful groups across scales. By mapping both the turtles and the threats they face, the system helps governments and researchers decide where protection and research money will do the most good.
openalex-w2168545956: Peatlands lock away enormous amounts of carbon — but warming could turn them from carbon vaults into carbon sources. This 2013 study reconstructs how peatlands accumulated carbon over the past thousand years, testing the assumption that heat simply speeds decay. The thousand-year record offers a reality check for predictions about what peatlands will do in a changing climate.
openalex-w2184278756: Before physicists can claim a discovery at the LHC, they must simulate billions of ordinary collisions — and those simulations need tuning. This 2016 paper builds new parameter "tunes" for three workhorse event generators (PYTHIA 8, PYTHIA 6, and HERWIG++), fitted to CMS measurements of the underlying event in proton-proton collisions. Better tunes mean cleaner comparisons between theory and data.
openalex-w2560801056: How many particles does a lead-lead collision make? This 2016 Physical Review Letters paper measures the charged-particle multiplicity density at midrapidity in 5.02 TeV collisions — the first such measurement at the LHC's top heavy-ion energy. For the most central 5% of collisions, the counts set the scale of the quark-gluon plasma created.
openalex-w2637985556: Drones are everywhere now — including over wildlife, at low altitudes in any terrain. This 2017 PLoS ONE systematic review asks whether unmanned aircraft systems disturb animals, synthesizing the evidence on a brand-new interaction. The findings matter for researchers and hobbyists alike: the eye in the sky has a footprint.
openalex-w2767362256: Multiple sclerosis drugs work — but do they work as well in older patients? This 2017 Frontiers in Neurology meta-analysis of randomized, blinded MS trials tests whether immunomodulatory therapies' effect on disability depends strongly on age. The answer reshapes how neurologists weigh treatment across the lifespan.
openalex-w2964483356: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and their kin share a dark thread: misfolded proteins that aggregate — tau's beta-structures among them — and the neuroinflammation that follows. This 2019 Frontiers in Pharmacology paper reviews neuroinflammation as a common feature of neurodegenerative disorders. The shared mechanism suggests shared therapeutic targets.
openalex-w4387452756: Nanotechnology could revolutionize cancer detection and treatment — protein engineering and materials science have spawned new nanoscale targeting techniques. This 2023 Molecular Cancer paper reviews progress and the hurdles to clinical implementation. The review tempers hope with the hard path to the clinic.
openalex-w7204275056: Young gum trees grow better with help from soil fungi. This tree-farm study tested giving young eucalyptus plants friendly root fungi plus fermented natural fertilizer. The team measured how fast the seedlings grew and how strong they got. Hands-on research for nurseries that want hardier young trees.
openalex-w7204586256: Every cooking oil has a smoke point, the heat at which it starts to break down. This study compares the smoke point of oil from the American bullfrog, Rana catesbeiana, with a common reference oil. The authors test whether the frog oil stands up to kitchen heat. An offbeat food-science experiment probing an unusual ingredient's culinary potential.
openalex-w7205008356: Placing a PICC line, a long catheter threaded into a central vein, is delicate work that nurses increasingly do with ultrasound guidance. This integrative review gathers what research says about nurses inserting these lines with ultrasound help. The authors assess safety, success rates, and training needs. A clinical review at the intersection of nursing skill and imaging technology, where steadier hands mean safer patients.
openalex-w7206176456: School cafeterias throw away astonishing amounts of food, and this article reports a project that tackled the problem with small children. The Prato Consciente program at an early-childhood school in Juazeiro do Norte, Brazil, taught kids to waste less and compost what remains. The authors analyze what the intervention changed in behavior and awareness. A practical example of how environmental education can start at the lunch table.
owen-mortification-of-sin-1656:
John Owen was the leading Puritan theologian of Cromwell's England, dean and vice-chancellor at Oxford. His Mortification of Sin in Believers, published in 1656, is a searching treatise on killing indwelling sin. Owen wrote it first for students, then for all serious believers.

He argues that sin, left alone, never fades but grows, so the believer must make its death a daily business. The work is God's Spirit's, Owen insists, yet it demands watchfulness, prayer, and honest self-knowledge from us. Puritan and evangelical readers still treat the treatise as the sharpest probe of the inner life.
paracelsus-supreme-mysteries-nature-1656:
Paracelsus reached English readers in force with the 1656 Turner collection, Of the Supreme Mysteries of Nature. The Swiss physician and alchemist had been dead a century, yet his fame kept growing. Spirits of the planets, the magical cure of wounds, and the secrets of the twelve zodiac signs fill these treatises.

Paracelsus taught that nature hides powers the bold physician can learn to use. Occult philosophy and hands-on cure mix freely in his pages, as they did in his practice. The volume stands as the key early-modern English Paracelsus, a door into Renaissance medicine and magic alike.
paracelsvs-of-the-supreme-mysteries-of-n: Paracelsus of the Supreme Mysteries of Nature, 1656. The Paracelsian mysteries. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
picatrix-castilian-alfonso-1256:
Astral magic fills the Picatrix, in the Castilian version made in 1256 for Alfonso the Wise of Castile. Talismans, planetary spirits, and the powers of the stars crowd its pages. The Arabic compendium, ascribed to al-Majriti, passed through the learned king's scriptorium into the most famous grimoire of the Middle Ages in any tongue.

Images are carved, fumigations burned, and hours chosen by the stars. Court scholars rendered the work as Buqratis in their Romance vernacular. Its lore shaped ritual magic in Europe for centuries afterward in secret. Readers meet medieval learned magic at its fullest, in the very dress that Alfonso's translators gave it at his command.
plos-pbio-0020356:
Daniel Hostetter, Sarah Rice, Sara Dean, and their team studied a slime mold motor protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. Myosin is the motor that pulls on actin in muscle and in many other cells. In the slime mold Dictyostelium, myosin strands bundle into thick filaments with two ends pointing outward.

The authors tested which parts of the protein, and which electric charges on it, drive that bundling. Getting the bundles right is vital for the cell to divide and crawl. Slime molds are a favored test bed for such motors. The fine rules found here help explain how myosin assembles in all cells, including the muscle cells whose failure causes some human myopathies.
plos-pone-0000056:
Paul Vigne and Christian Frelin reported a dietary surprise from fruit fly research in 2006. Drosophila, the fruit fly, is a stand-in for studying how bodies handle stress. Hypoxic tolerance is the ability to survive low oxygen, which matters in strokes, heart attacks, and high altitude. Diet is an unlikely lever for it.

Flies raised on a low protein diet showed increased tolerance to low oxygen. A simple change in food shifted a hard physiological limit. Findings like this do not transfer straight to people. But they reveal that oxygen survival is tunable by metabolism. They also give researchers a cheap model in which to find the tuning knobs.
plos-pone-0000156:
Hong J. Lee, Kwang S. Kim, In H. Park, and colleagues published this stroke study in PLOS ONE in 2007. The team used human neural stem cells engineered to over-produce VEGF, a factor that grows blood vessels. The cells were tested in a mouse model of stroke, where a blocked vessel starves part of the brain.

The title sums up the outcome: the treated mice gained protection for neurons, new vessel growth, and better functional recovery. Stem cells plus VEGF is a two-pronged approach, replacing support while rebuilding supply lines. The results encouraged work on cell therapy for stroke, where human treatments remain scarce.
plos-pone-0000256:
Michael J. Morgan, William McEwan, and Joshua Solomon published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When a person stares at the center of a textured patch, holes in the texture's edge rapidly fade from view, creating an artificial blind spot. The authors study the lingering effects of that artificial scotoma after the staring ends.

Vision fills in missing patches so smoothly that the brain hides its own gaps. This study measures what the filling-in leaves behind. The findings bear on how the visual system maintains a seamless world from a retina that actually has holes and interruptions in it.
plos-pone-0000356:
Gaëll Mainguy, Jan Koster, Joost Woltering, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hox clusters, the gene rows that pattern animal bodies, were thought to be read one gene at a time in the forward direction. The authors report extensive polycistronism and antisense transcription in the mammalian Hox clusters: long messages spanning several genes, and messages read off the opposite strand.

That messiness revises the tidy picture of Hox regulation. Long multi-gene transcripts and antisense copies add control layers to a famous system. The findings matter for developmental biology, where the precision of Hox activity builds the body plan.
plos-pone-0000456:
Y.-H. Percival Zhang and colleagues built an artificial enzyme pathway that makes hydrogen fuel from starch, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Hydrogen is a clean fuel, but making it without fossil energy is hard. Their synthetic enzymatic pathway uses a designed set of enzymes to convert starch and water into hydrogen at high yield.

Starch is cheap, renewable, and easy to store, unlike hydrogen gas itself. A high-yield route from starch could turn crops or waste biomass into fuel where it is needed. The study is a proof of concept for synthetic biology applied to energy: assembling enzymes from different organisms into a pathway nature never built.
plos-pone-0000556:
Nigel E. Raine and Lars Chittka asked why bumblebees prefer the flower colors they do, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The bee is Bombus terrestris, a common pollinator. The team tested the adaptive significance of sensory bias in a foraging context: whether innate floral colour preferences help bees find food faster.

A sensory bias is a built-in tilt of the senses, and it might be a leftover or a useful shortcut. If naive bees' color preferences match rewarding flowers, the bias speeds learning and earns its keep. Linking a mental quirk to foraging success is how behavioral ecology explains why animal senses are tuned the way they are.
plos-pone-0000656:
Emmanuel J. Chang, Rashida Begum, Brian T. Chait and colleagues worked on predicting where a key cell-cycle enzyme family acts, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cyclin-dependent kinases, or Cdks, add phosphate tags to proteins. That tagging sits at the center of the eukaryotic cell-division cycle. It steers processes such as DNA replication by switching regulators on or off.

Knowing a kinase's substrates, the proteins it tags, is the hard part. Prediction narrows thousands of proteins to likely targets for lab testing. Each confirmed substrate adds a wire to the cell cycle's circuit diagram. The work serves anyone mapping how division is controlled, and how it fails in disease.
plos-pone-0000756:
Jeffrey T.-J. Huang, F. Markus Leweke, Tsz M. Tsang and colleagues profiled spinal fluid from people in the earliest stage before psychosis. The initial prodromal state is an early phase before overt psychosis, marked by sub-threshold or unspecific psychiatric symptoms. Little was known about the biochemical changes during this period, when intervention might help most.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study measured metabolic and proteomic profiles in cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid around brain and spine. Patterns there could flag who is truly heading toward psychosis. Early, objective markers would change psychiatry, which still diagnoses psychosis mainly by symptoms that arrive late in the disease's course.
plos-pone-0000856:
Bruno Marques, Lavinia Liguori, Marie-Hélène Paclet and colleagues delivered a missing enzyme into cells using fat bubbles, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gp91 phox is a transmembrane protein and the catalytic core of the NADPH oxidase complex of neutrophils, the machinery that makes microbe-killing oxidants. Lack of this protein causes chronic granulomatous disease, a rare genetic disorder of severe, recurrent infections, because phagocytes cannot kill what they swallow.

Liposome-mediated delivery carried active gp91 phox into cells. Replacing a membrane protein is far harder than replacing a soluble one, since it must land in the membrane correctly oriented. Success here is a step toward protein-replacement therapy for CGD.
plos-pone-0000956:
Anjon Audhya, Ian McLeod, John Yates and colleagues identified a fourth subunit of a protein sorting machine, in PLOS ONE in 2007. After a receptor is pulled inside the cell, it can keep signaling from internal compartments. To shut it down, the cell buds it into tiny inner vesicles where it is cut off from the cytoplasm.

That sorting is run by the ESCRT machines. The team name a new part, MVB-12, as a fourth subunit of the metazoan ESCRT-I complex, and tie it to receptor downregulation. Each new part clarifies how cells silence signals on time. Failures in that timing are linked to growth disorders and cancer.
plos-pone-0001056:
Eva Sarndahl, Ida Bergstrom, Veronika Brodin and colleagues checked the activation state of neutrophils in stable heart artery disease, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neutrophils are fast response immune cells, and they have emerged as players in building artery plaques. In unstable angina they are highly activated in the blood.

A primed state had also been proposed for patients with stable angina, a milder claim needing a direct test. The team measured activation status in stable coronary artery disease. Whether quiet looking disease still runs hot immune cells affects how risk is judged. It also bears on whether calming neutrophils could help.
plos-pone-0001156:
Hosts and parasites evolve against each other over generations, often through matching sets of resistance and attack genes. Andy Fenton and Michael Brockhurst modeled a complication in that arms race in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The complication is epistasis, where the effect of one gene depends on another.

Fitness costs of resistance and virulence genes are thought to steer this gene-for-gene coevolution. The authors ask how interactions among several such genes change the dynamics when more than one locus is involved. Their model matters for predicting how resistance, in crops or in medicine, holds up or breaks down over time.
plos-pone-0001256:
Hormone-dependent breast cancers need estrogen to grow, so antiestrogen drugs are a mainstay of treatment, yet resistance is a major cause of failure. Hemant Varma, Andrew Skildum, and Susan Conrad report a route to that resistance in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their focus is pRb, the retinoblastoma protein, a brake on the cell division cycle.

The authors show that functional ablation of pRb activates the cell-cycle enzyme Cdk2 and causes antiestrogen resistance in human breast cancer cells. Losing one brake lets cells keep dividing despite the drug. The mechanism suggests where resistant tumors might be attacked.
plos-pone-0001356:
Why some trauma patients develop wound infections while others do not remains unclear, despite better understanding of trauma itself. Yiorgos Apidianakis and colleagues used a fruit fly infection model to hunt for host genes involved, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. A Drosophila melanogaster and Pseudomonas aeruginosa injury and infection model was used to identify host genetic components of susceptibility.

The authors report involvement of the skeletal muscle gene regulatory network in susceptibility to wound infection following trauma. Muscle genes are an unexpected place to find immune vulnerability. The fly model's speed lets such networks be screened in a way human studies cannot.
plos-pone-0001456:
Shannon Williamson and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study from a world ocean sampling voyage. Viruses are the most common life forms on Earth. In the sea they shape gene flow, species mix, and carbon cycles. The team read virus genes from water samples drawn from seas across the globe.

Their reads map which virus types live in each sea zone and how they differ. Most virus genes they found were new to science. That scale of novelty shows how little of the sea virus world is known. The data set gives a base map for ocean health and climate work alike.
plos-pone-0001556:
Aric Gregson and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot built on a hepatitis core shell. The shell bears parts of the malaria parasite's surface protein. The phase 1 trial enrolled 51 healthy adults with no past malaria, aged 18 to 45. Doses rose in steps to test safety first.

The team tracked side effects and immune replies at each dose. A shell that can carry malaria parts on a proven base is a draw for shot design. Clean safety and a firm reply would earn wider trials. Each such step tests the multi part shot idea for malaria.
plos-pone-0001656:
Rudolf S. N. Fehrmann, Hendrik J. M. de Jonge, Arja ter Elst, and their co-authors proposed a new way to read gene activity data in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A gene's output, they note, reflects the joint push of many regulators, which they call transcriptional system regulators. Measuring that joint push across the whole set of genes is hard.

Their approach, called TSR profiling, uses principal component analysis on gene activity data from 17 studies to extract broad regulatory patterns. The full text sets out the method, the data sets, and the profiles it produced. A profile of the whole regulatory system, rather than single genes, could help researchers compare cell states. It could also help them spot disease patterns and check how treatments shift a cell's program.
plos-pone-0001756:
Jay H. Russell and Kenneth C. Keiler screened a bacterium for proteins that sit in set places inside the cell, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Precise protein localization underlies motility, chemotaxis, cell-cycle progression, and cell division in bacteria. How many proteins are localized in any one species was unknown.

Their screen in Caulobacter crescentus used transposon mutagenesis to tag proteins. Caulobacter is famous for its asymmetric division, and the screen revealed which proteins gather at poles or other landmarks. The full text gives the screen design and the localized proteins found. A census of localized proteins shows how much internal geography even a single cell maintains, and gives targets for studying cell polarity.
plos-pone-0001856:
Bin Wang and co-authors studied a protein that steers stem cell fate after spinal injury, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Neural stem and progenitor cells can differentiate into neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. They are considered valuable for cell therapy of central nervous system injuries. Transplanted into the adult spinal cord, however, they mostly become astrocytes rather than neurons.

The team reports that Nogo-66 promotes differentiation of neural progenitors into the astroglial lineage through the mTOR-STAT3 pathway. Nogo-66 is a myelin protein known for blocking nerve fiber growth. The full text gives the cell culture results. Knowing what pushes stem cells toward scar-forming astrocytes is a step toward steering them toward repair instead.
plos-pone-0001956:
Shan Yu Fung, Hong Yang, and P. Chen studied tiny self-building peptides as drug carriers, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The cargo was ellipticine, a drug that kills cancer cells but hates water, so it clumps and fails to reach tumors in the body. Certain peptides fold and group on their own and can hold such drugs in a stable mix.

The team varied the peptide sequence and tested how each change shaped the drug complex and its cancer-killing power in lab cells. Sequence is the one dial they can turn freely. Learning which sequences hold the drug best is a step toward carriers that work in patients.
plos-pone-0002056:
Jun Xu and Colleen Clancy modeled burst firing in hippocampal neurons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Some neurons fire in bursts, tight volleys of spikes rather than single ones. In the hippocampus, bursts make signal relay more reliable, yet bursting can also sync networks in the runaway way seen in epilepsy.

The pair built a model of CA3 pyramidal neurons, a main hippocampal cell type, to find the ionic currents that create their inborn bursting. Knowing which currents set the burst points to drugs that could calm sync without silencing normal traffic. Models like this guide the search before lab tests.
plos-pone-0002156:
Jakob Brodersen, Anders Nilsson, Jeppe Ammitzbøll, and co-authors modeled how fish should swim when they migrate against a current, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Many fish travel long distances in winter, moving between habitats of unlike quality. Migration burns energy, so the best timing and speed depend on more than where food is best.

The authors worked out the swimming speed that should serve a fish best in a head current. How that choice changes the distance it can cover. Their model gives a benchmark for judging real fish: those that match it are spending their strength wisely on the journey north or south.
plos-pone-0002256:
Irina Harris, Paul Dux, Claire Benito, and co-authors asked at which stage of seeing an object's orientation gets fixed, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A standing debate in vision science concerns the shapes we store for recognition. Do they depend on the angle we saw the object from, or stay the same across angles? The answer may differ by stage of processing.

The team used repetition priming, where seeing an item once speeds its later naming, to probe each stage. Their results show orientation sensitivity varies across the stages of object processing. Work like this helps model how the brain recognizes a chair as a chair from any side.
plos-pone-0002356:
Kholiswa Ngumbela and co-authors measured how weak codon usage slows HIV protein making in T cells. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Wild HIV-1 strains carry genomes low in the letters G and C, with codon choices that human cells read inefficiently. Rewriting a gene with better codons is known to raise protein output in lab vectors.

The team quantified the effect for the viral gag gene inside intact T cells, the very cells HIV infects. Suboptimal codons cut the translational efficiency of the gag message. Knowing the size of that brake matters for vaccine design, where gag protein amounts decide how strong an immune lesson the vaccine teaches.
plos-pone-0002456:
Research by Balleza and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Enrique Balleza, Elena R. Alvarez-Buylla, Alvaro Chaos, and others. Its subject is critical Dynamics in Genetic Regulatory Networks: Examples from Four Kingdoms. The genes of an organism must switch on and off in a coordinated way for the organism to keep working.

That coordination must hold up even when random outside shocks hit the organism. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002556:
Sahin and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Annelise Sahin, Bertrand Daignan-Fornier, Isabelle Sagot, and others. Its subject is polarized Growth in the Absence of F-Actin in Saccharomyces cerevisiae Exiting Quiescence. Polarity establishment and maintenance are crucial for morphogenesis and development.

In budding yeast, these two intricate processes involve the superposition of regulatory loops between polarity landmarks, RHO GTPases, actin-mediated vesicles transport and endocytosis. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002656:
Work by Martin Widschwendter and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was epigenotyping in peripheral blood cell DNA and breast cancer risk: a proof of principle study. The catalog record names Martin Widschwendter first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Epigenetic changes are emerging as one of the most important events in carcinogenesis. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002756:
Work by Eric A. Zilli and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the influence of markov decision process structure on the possible strategic use of working memory and episodic memory. Authorship is credited in the record to Eric A. Zilli and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Researchers use a variety of behavioral tasks to analyze the effect of biological manipulations on memory function. The authors add a further point. This research will benefit from a systematic mathematical method for analyzing memory demands in behavioral tasks. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002856:
Work by Mary-Lee Dequéant and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was comparison of pattern detection methods in microarray time series of the segmentation clock. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Mary-Lee Dequéant, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. While genome-wide gene expression data are generated at an increasing rate, the repertoire of approaches for pattern discovery in these data is still limited. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002956:
Robin Lee, Lawrence Puente, Mads Kærn and co-authors found a non-death job for a yeast metacaspase in 2008. Caspase proteins are best known for carrying out apoptosis, planned cell death. In higher organisms they also shape growth, division, and specialization, beyond killing cells.

In baker's yeast, the metacaspase Yca1p altered cell cycle dynamics, the timing of cell division, the authors report. That is a role apart from death. Published in PLOS ONE, the study broadens how these old proteins are viewed and may inform work on caspases in human disease. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003056: Daniel DiGiulio, Roberto Romero, Harold Amogan and colleagues investigated microbes in amniotic fluid during preterm labor in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The title states the work combined molecular methods with culture-based methods, the two main ways to detect and identify microbes. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, while its abstract snippet repeats the title without further detail. The study reports microbial prevalence, diversity, and abundance in amniotic fluid from preterm labor cases, a topic tied to infection and early birth.
plos-pone-0003156:
Yana V. Bernatavichute, Xiaoyu Zhang, Shawn Cokus and colleagues map two linked marks on DNA in a model plant in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Methylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 is a hallmark of gene silencing in many organisms. In Arabidopsis thaliana, one form of that mark helps silence transposons and control DNA methylation.

The team built a high-resolution genome-wide map to test how this histone mark associates with CHG DNA methylation. Readers see the two silencing systems laid out across the whole genome. The work helps explain how plants keep mobile DNA quiet without harming normal genes.
plos-pone-0003256: Jie Zhong and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on a vaccine against human cytomegalovirus, a common herpesvirus. The title states its aim: to bring about broad protective immunity after vaccination with a chimeric vaccine, one built from mixed parts. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no results.
plos-pone-0003356:
Chihiro Hiramatsu, Amanda D. Melin, Filippo Aureli and colleagues test primate fruit finding in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Trichromatic primates have a red-green chromatic channel in addition to luminance and blue-yellow channels. It has been argued that the red-green channel evolved in primates as an adaptation for detecting reddish or yellowish objects, such as ripe fruits, against a background of foliage.

The authors assess importance of achromatic contrast in short-range fruit foraging of primates. Readers learn brightness contrast may matter more than colour at close range. That nuance revises a classic story about why primates evolved colour vision.
plos-pone-0003456:
Rahul Regulapati and co-authors proposed an origin for split genes in this 2008 paper. Genes of complex cells come in pieces, coding parts split by long non-coding stretches. Why genes took that fractured form stayed unsolved for thirty years. The authors focused on genes of the spliceosome, the machine that joins the pieces.

They argue the split structure could arise from random genetic sequences. Their solution claims to explain the pattern without special design. A random start would make split genes a byproduct of chance. The paper offers a testable story for a basic puzzle of biology.
plos-pone-0003556:
Semir Zeki and John Paul Romaya scanned the brain during hate in this 2008 study. Hate is a strong emotion that science had barely explored with imaging. Seventeen volunteers lay in a scanner for the tests. Each viewed the face of a person they hated.

They also viewed faces of acquaintances who stirred no strong feeling. Comparing the two sets mapped the neural correlates of hate. The active pattern was distinct from neutral face viewing. Mapping base emotions helps explain behavior driven by them. Hate drives real-world violence, which makes its brain roots worth mapping.
plos-pone-0003656:
Yuh-Man Sun, Megan Cooper, Sophie Finch, and colleagues published this development study in PLOS ONE in 2008. As stem cells become neurons, whole sets of genes must switch off and on in order. REST is a protein that shuts down neuron genes in non-neural cells.

The team found REST also controls genes for the extracellular matrix, the mesh that surrounds and supports cells. That control proved crucial for neural development to proceed well. The study widens REST's role beyond switching genes off inside the cell. It also shapes the scaffold the growing brain builds around itself.
plos-pone-0003756:
Christian Krintel, Peter Osmark, Martin R. Larsen, and colleagues published this enzyme study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hormone-sensitive lipase is a key enzyme that frees fatty acids from stored fat. Its activity is switched on by phosphorylation, the adding of phosphate tags. Protein kinase A does much of that switching.

Working on the human enzyme, the team found two serine sites, 649 and 650, matter most. Those spots are the major determinants of activation by protein kinase A against fat substrates. The precise mapping shows exactly where the body flips its fat-release switch.
plos-pone-0003856:
Eduardo R. Ropelle, Maria Fernanda A. Fernandes, Marcelo B. S. Flores, and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2008. AMPK and mTOR are key regulators of the cell's energy balance and of how leptin, the satiety hormone, curbs food intake. Acute exercise makes animals more sensitive to leptin.

The team asked whether exercise acts in the brain's control centers on those energy sensors. They found exercise increases the AMPK and mTOR response to leptin there. The result shows physical activity rewiring appetite control at the molecular level, not just burning calories.
plos-pone-0003956:
Dennis Eckmeier, Bart R. H. Geurten, Daniel Kress, and co-authors studied how zebra finches use vision in flight in 2008. Fast-flying animals read optic flow, the motion pattern across the eye. Flow from straight flight carries depth cues about the surroundings. Flow from turning carries no such depth information.

Their PLOS ONE article asks how free-flying finches solve that mix. The birds must separate turning from straight motion to judge space. Their gaze strategy likely steadies the image during key moments. The work explains how small birds navigate clutter at speed. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004056:
Christine Stabell Benn, Ane Bærent Fisker, Amabelia Rodrigues, and co-authors studied birth vaccines in Guinea-Bissau in 2008. Oral polio vaccine at birth was policy in many low-income countries. The policy aimed to raise coverage of the vaccine. Its effect on overall infant survival was never studied.

During a vitamin A trial there, some newborns missed the polio vaccine at birth. That accident created a natural experiment on the policy. Their PLOS ONE article reports effects that differed between boys and girls. Such non-target effects matter for vaccine schedules worldwide. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004156:
Karli Watson, Jason Ghodasra, and Michael Platt published this primate study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Serotonin signalling shapes social behaviour in humans and other primates. In humans, a variant near the serotonin transporter gene affects social anxiety and how strongly the amygdala reacts to social cues.

The team asked whether the same gene variant changes how rhesus macaques respond to social reward and punishment. Linking gene variants to social choices in monkeys helps separate biology from upbringing. The study gives a controlled animal window on how one gene can tilt social life.
plos-pone-0004256:
Rachel Lubong Sabado and colleagues published this HIV immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. What it takes to prime HIV-specific T cells, and why those responses look the way they do in infected people, remained undefined. In lymph nodes, T cells must touch dendritic cells to activate, and that same contact can pass HIV between cells.

The team recreated priming in the lab, in vitro, and compared it with responses in the body. Their system recapitulates in vivo responses, and it reveals a rapid loss of virus-reactive CD4 T cells in acute infection. That early loss is one reason the immune system never gains the upper hand.
plos-pone-0004356:
Ana Pérez-Berná and colleagues published this membrane study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team had recently identified the membranotropic regions of hepatitis C virus proteins E1, E2, core, and p7. They did so by watching how peptide libraries disturbed model membranes. Those regions are the parts of the virus that interact with cell membranes.

Here they screened a peptide library by two physical methods, DSC and SAXD, and compared the results with the biological function of the parent proteins. Checking whether lab behaviour matches real function validates the shortcut of studying virus pieces instead of whole viruses.
plos-pone-0004456:
Two kinds of small players in human genes may have evolved together, argue Stefan Lehnert, Peter Van Loo, Pushpike Thilakarathne, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. One player is the microRNA, a short RNA that dials gene activity down after genes are read. The other is the Alu repeat, the most common repeated stretch in the human genome.

The team showed that the seed part of some human microRNAs matches Alu sequences well enough to pair with them. That pairing could let microRNAs control genes that carry Alu copies. It also suggests the two spread through the genome in step with each other. The claim adds a new chapter to how repeated DNA, long dismissed as junk, may shape gene control.
plos-pone-0004556:
Chemical marks that keep a herpesvirus asleep are loosened when it wakes, show Zhangsheng Yang, Haidong Tang, Hai Huang, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gammaherpesviruses share a life pattern: latency, hiding quietly in cells, and lytic replication, bursting out to make new virus. In murine gammaherpesvirus 68, a mouse virus of this family, the balance is controlled by one gene, called RTA.

The team studied the promoter, the on-switch region, of the RTA gene during reactivation. They found its demethylation, the removal of silencing marks, and changes in histone acetylation, a loosening mark on DNA packaging. Those changes help explain how a sleeping virus throws its master switch. Related viruses cause human cancers, so the mechanism matters beyond mice.
plos-pone-0004656:
A Golgi protein folds into an unusual armadillo shape, show Harald Striegl, Yvette Roske, Daniel Kummel, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is p115, a general vesicular transport factor. The golgin family gives identity and structure to the Golgi apparatus, the cell's shipping and sorting station, and forms part of a complex protein network at its membrane.

P115 is targeted by the GTPase Rab1a and contains a large globular head and a long coiled-coil stalk. The team solved its head's structure and found an unusual armadillo fold, a curved stack of repeating units. That shape is a scaffold for binding partners. Knowing it helps explain how the Golgi grabs incoming cargo sacs and holds its own shape.
plos-pone-0004756:
Matthew Gegg and colleagues found that silencing the PINK1 gene harms mitochondrial DNA and energy output in dopamine cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Faults in mitochondria, the cell power plants, are tied to Parkinson disease. Damage to the energy chain and extra deletions in mitochondrial DNA have both been reported in the illness.

PINK1 is a gene whose loss can cause inherited Parkinson disease. The team silenced it in dopamine producing cells and watched the effects. Energy output fell and mitochondrial DNA suffered. The result ties one gene to the power failure seen in the disease. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004856:
Justin Remais, Lin Chen, and Edmund Seto studied leveraging rural energy investment for schistosome control in rural China, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cooking and heating are the most energy intensive activities among the world poor, and clean energy access is key to Millennium Growth Goals. Anaerobic digesters convert waste to biogas while also inactivating schistosome eggs in human and animal waste fed into household systems.

Energy and health benefits arrive together in one investment. Digesters cut indoor smoke and parasite transmission simultaneously. Co benefits strengthen the case for subsidies. Rural growth can bundle goals efficiently. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004956:
Linking a trait to a nearby DNA marker usually requires pedigrees. Family trees are often missing, though. Shuhei Mano, Takaho Endo and Akira Oka offered a workaround in PLOS ONE in 2009. They detect linkage in a randomly mating population. No pedigree record is needed at all.

Standard linkage methods lean on extended family trees. Those trees must be reconstructed from records. The new approach draws the needed information from population data itself. If it holds up, gene mapping widens greatly. Populations where pedigrees can never be built become fair game for trait studies.
plos-pone-0005056:
Some images can be seen two ways. The brain flips between the interpretations. That flipping is called bistability. Gijs Joost Brouwer and colleagues studied what controls it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used a bistable stimulus with incongruent depth cues. Volunteers watched while the team measured brain activity.

Metric changes in the incongruence changed the flipping rate. Cortical responses changed along with it. Mismatched senses tune the brain's switching. The work maps how conflicting clues steer perception. It shows perception as an active negotiation. The brain weighs evidence, then commits, then reconsiders. Such studies help explain illusions and, more broadly, how stable vision emerges from unstable input.
plos-pone-0005156:
Malaria parasites live inside red blood cells. They devour the hemoglobin there for food. Shoba Subramanian and colleagues mapped that meal in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two parasite enzymes do much of the cutting. They are falcipain-2 and falcipain-3, both cysteine proteases. Hemoglobin digestion was thought to follow an ordered process.

The study pinpointed each enzyme's cleavage site specificity. The two falcipains cut at different, precise spots. The maps reveal the parasite's dining rules. They also flag the enzymes as drug targets. Blocking digestion starves the parasite inside its host cell. Other proteases start the process, but these finish key cuts. Precise cut maps help chemists design blockers.
plos-pone-0005256:
Recognizing an object means joining what the eyes see with what the ears hear, while ignoring rival objects. Suied and Viaud-Delmon timed that joining process in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their results suggest the brain handles animal sounds in a special way.

Knowing an object's category helps the brain bind its cues together. Reaction times pointed to specific processing for animal sounds compared with other sounds. Fast, dedicated handling of animal calls makes sense for survival, and it shows how meaning shapes basic perception. Fast tracks for the sounds of beasts make sense in a world where a growl or a cry can mean food, threat, or a mate close by.
plos-pone-0005356:
Variants in mitochondrial DNA are suspected of shaping risk for many diseases, including cancer. One common variant, written A10398G, had conflicting evidence behind it. Pezzotti and colleagues tested its link to breast cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009, including interaction with alcohol.

Alcohol use is itself tied to breast cancer risk, so a gene and lifestyle interaction is plausible. Testing the variant alone and together with drinking gives a fuller picture. Careful studies like this sort real risk factors from noise in a crowded field. Mito genes come from the mother alone, so a risk tied to them would pass down the female line. A point that changes how a family should be told of its risk.
plos-pone-0005456:
Melanie Rauch and colleagues studied what keeps mature B cells alive, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. B cells make the antibodies that fight germs. A signal called BAFF, working through its receptor, was known to help young B cells grow past an early stage.

The team showed that the same signal is also needed to keep full-grown B cells alive and in place. Without it, two major B cell groups fail to form or fade away. That finding helps explain some immune defects and informs drugs that block BAFF in diseases where B cells cause harm.
plos-pone-0005556:
Suomeng Dong and co-authors identified a disease gene of a soybean pathogen in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. A water mould called Phytophthora sojae causes root and stem rot that can ruin soybean crops. Whether a strain can infect a soybean variety depends on matching genes in mould and plant.

The team found the mould gene Avr3c and read what it makes. The protein it codes for is sent into plant cells and varies between strains. Matching these genes to soybean varieties helps breeders keep ahead of the mould. Soybean is a major world crop for food and feed, so even small losses to this mould carry a high cost.
plos-pone-0005656:
Matti Uusitupa and co-authors reported ten-year outcomes of the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. That trial had shown that lifestyle change can prevent type 2 diabetes in people at high risk. Whether it also cut deaths and heart disease over a decade was the open question.

The authors followed the trial groups for ten years and counted deaths and cardiovascular events. The lifestyle group had already gained years with lower diabetes rates. Their long follow-up tells health systems what sustained prevention is worth. Diabetes prevention by lifestyle had already been proven; the open ground was death and heart outcomes over time.
plos-pone-0005756:
Jonathan Song and co-authors built a tiny vessel model in 2009 to study how breast cancer cells stick to vessel walls. Cancer spreads when stray cells leave the blood and seed new tumors. Modeling that sticking step well is key to blocking it.

Their microfluidic device lines a small channel with living endothelium, the vessel's inner skin, under flow. Cancer cells tumble through as they would in blood. Watching which cells grip, and why, names targets for anti-spread drugs. The device gives a controlled stand-in for a step that is nearly impossible to watch inside a body.
plos-pone-0005856:
Zhou Xing and co-authors showed in 2009 that a booster shot up the nose greatly strengthens TB protection in guinea pigs. A virus-vectored TB vaccine had already worked well in mice, alone or as a boost after BCG. Guinea pigs, though, model human lung TB more faithfully.

Animals first primed with BCG, then boosted through the nose, resisted lung infection far better. Delivering the boost at the airway surface, where TB enters, likely explains the gain. The result supports mucosal boosting as a strategy. It moves the vaccine platform one step closer to human relevance.
plos-pone-0005956:
Gene therapy often parks new DNA inside a patient's own genome, where it lands at random. Romain Desprat and Eric Bouhassira took up a known risk of that approach in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. A parked gene can switch on a nearby cancer gene, and a DNA stretch called the chicken HS4 insulator may act as a shield.

The question was whether the shield works for all genes or only some. Their answer points to gene-specific effects, so the same shield does not guard every case alike. That nuance matters for making gene therapy safer: a guard that works in one spot may fail in the next, and each use must be checked on its own.
plos-pone-0006056:
Eating a particle is a cell's way of clearing debris and germs, but the meal has stages. Craig Blanchette, Youn-Hi Woo, Cynthia Thomas and colleagues pulled those stages apart in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies epithelial cells eating beads coated with InlA, a bacterial protein, using dyes that sense acidity to follow the act step by step.

Taking the bead in, turning its compartment acidic, and merging it with the cell's digestion sacs can each run on its own clock. Older studies often blurred those stages into one. Parting them lets researchers assign each drug or gene to the exact stage it touches, a gain for cell biology and for infection studies alike.
plos-pone-0006156:
Fear learned in one moment binds a sound, a place and a shock into one memory. Sabiha Barot, Ain Chung, Jeansok Kim and colleagues imaged the neurons where those strands meet in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses functional imaging of stimulus convergence in amygdalar neurons during Pavlovian fear conditioning, the classic model for studying learning and for understanding phobias and anxiety.

Showing which amygdala cells receive both the harmless cue and the shock names the memory's meeting point. Fear conditioning is among the best-mapped forms of learning, and each mapped point sharpens it further. The work also serves anxiety research, where the same circuit fires without a real threat.
plos-pone-0006256:
The human body gives off light far too faint for eyes to see. Masaki Kobayashi, Daisuke Kikuchi, and Hitoshi Okamura imaged that glow in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The light comes from energy changes in metabolism and is about a thousand times weaker than what eyes can detect.

Sensitive cameras captured the emission rising and falling across the day. A diurnal rhythm in body glow ties light output to the body clock. The pictures make an abstract fact vivid: metabolism literally shines. Tracking the glow could one day offer a non-invasive window on metabolic state.
plos-pone-0006356:
Gene shape bears marks of both random mutation and natural selection. Salvatore Camiolo, Domenico Rau, and Andrea Porceddu examined Arabidopsis genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Features of gene expression profiles had been associated with build features of genes across many taxa.

Selection acting through expression patterns appears to shape gene structure, alongside bias in gene change. Highly used genes evolve different architecture from rarely used ones. Arabidopsis, the lab workhorse plant, gives clean data for such tests. The findings add to a picture of genomes fine-tuned by their own activity. The plant is small and fast to grow, which makes it a clean test case for such claims.
plos-pone-0006456:
Michael McCoy, Andrew Allen, and James Gillooly asked how much of genome layout is chance, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Open reading frames are stretches of DNA that could code for proteins. Knowing their size and number across genomes may reveal what controls genome complexity. The team examined how these frames are spread out in full genomes.

They studied the pattern of start and stop signals that bound each frame. From that pattern they built predictions of how frames should be distributed. If chance explains much of the layout, genome design looks less finely planned. The work gives a baseline for spotting where natural selection truly shapes genomes.
plos-pone-0006556:
Niels Høgslund and co-authors read gene activity in a model legume plant in PLOS ONE in 2009. Work on plant mutants had found key genes in the talk between legumes and Rhizobium bacteria. Those bacteria live in root nodules and give the plant nitrogen. The genes also guide how the nodules form and work. The team read all active genes at once in Lotus japonicus mutants.

By comparing mutants, they could pull apart the steps of this partnership. Legumes gain nitrogen from their bacteria, so farms need less fertilizer for them. Knowing the partnership gene by gene could help spread this trait to more crops. The plant is a main model for this field.
plos-pone-0006656:
Ana Martins and co-authors studied drug efflux pumps in resistant E. coli in PLOS ONE in 2009. Resistance-nodulation-division efflux pumps of Escherichia coli extrude antibiotics and toxic substances before they reach their intended targets. Whereas these pumps protect bacteria in many settings, their activity varies with pH. The team examined pH modulation of efflux pump activity in multi-drug resistant E. coli.

Their title highlights protection during passage through acidic body compartments. A pump that works harder at low pH helps bacteria survive the stomach or urinary tract. Understanding that modulation suggests ways to jam the pumps. Pump jammers could restore antibiotic power.
plos-pone-0006756:
Matthew B. Hale and colleagues tracked signaling errors in a mouse model of lupus in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lupus is a complex autoimmune disease of unknown cause. Many cell types and cytokines interact in its development. The starting events remain poorly understood. The authors focused on cytokine signaling through STAT proteins.

They found regulation of that signaling goes wrong in stage-dependent ways. Early and late disease showed different signaling faults. A fault that changes with stage needs stage-matched treatment thinking. Mapping when each error appears helps explain disease progression. It may also reveal windows where intervention works best in lupus.
plos-pone-0006856:
William Y. Y. Lai, Trevor Lane, and Alison Jones audited medical news on American newspaper front pages in PLOS ONE in 2009. Front-page medical stories reach a wide audience. How they are prepared and distributed had not been systematically studied. The authors quantified the visibility front-page medical stories achieve. They also traced where the stories come from.

Source tracing shows how much front-page health news starts as press releases. Coverage patterns reveal which institutions and journals dominate. Readers often treat front-page placement as a mark of importance. Knowing the pipeline helps readers judge health claims critically. It also presses newsrooms to check the origins of medical stories.
plos-pone-0006956:
Jennifer Bromberg-White, Elissa Boguslawski, and Nicholas Duesbery studied anthrax toxin in mouse eyes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Anthrax lethal toxin includes an enzyme called lethal factor. That enzyme cuts and disables signaling proteins known as MEKs. In cell and animal studies, the toxin targets the cells lining blood vessels.

The team disturbed eye development with the toxin and watched the result. They tracked how retinal blood vessels formed under its influence. The eye offers a clear window on vessel growth. Their work helps explain the vascular damage seen in severe anthrax infection.
plos-pone-0007056:
Erika Mileti, Gianluca Matteoli, Iliyan Iliev, and colleagues compared probiotic bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Probiotics have been proposed to treat inflammatory bowel disease. So far, their clinical benefits have been limited. The team tested three Lactobacillus strains in complex lab culture systems that mimic the gut.

They compared how strongly each strain calmed immune activity. The goal was to predict which strains would work in the body. Lab systems that forecast real effects save wasted trials. They may also explain why probiotic results vary so much between products and patients.
plos-pone-0007156:
Araceli Castillo-Romero, Gloria Leon-Avila, Armando Perez Rangel, and colleagues studied the cell skeleton of a parasite in PLOS ONE in 2009. Giardia lamblia is a gut parasite that causes diarrheal disease. Its microfilaments, built from actin, drive movement, division, and uptake. Yet these structures are poorly understood in this organism. The team stained actin and viewed it with confocal microscopy.

They found actin takes part in both growth and encystation. Encystation is how the parasite forms the hardy cysts that spread infection. Blocking that step could break transmission. Basic cell biology of a parasite often reveals its weakest points.
plos-pone-0007256:
Margaret Kweku, Jayne Webster, Martin Adjuik, and colleagues tested ways to deliver malaria prevention to children in 2009. Intermittent preventive treatment gives children antimalarial doses at set times. It is a promising intervention, but delivering it widely to families is a practical challenge in many regions.

The authors ran a community randomized trial in Ghana. They compare coverage achieved by two different delivery systems for the treatment. Their PLOS ONE paper measures what each system can actually reach. Health planners can use those coverage figures to choose delivery routes that reach more children.
plos-pone-0007356:
Salama A. Salama, Marwa W. Kamel, Shaleen Botting, and colleagues studied an estrogen byproduct in uterine tumor cells in 2009. Uterine leiomyomas are common benign tumors, and optimal medical treatments remain a significant challenge. A compound called 2-methoxyestradiol is an endogenous estrogen metabolite with anti-tumor activity in several models.

The metabolite is formed by enzymes including catechol-O-methyltransferase, called COMT. The authors examine COMT expression and the metabolite's effects in leiomyoma cells. They report effects on microtubule dynamics and on steroid receptor signaling. Their work supports developing this natural metabolite pathway for fibroid treatment.
plos-pone-0007456:
Yuqi Wang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on signaling control in baker's yeast. A transcription factor called Tec1 governs invasive growth in yeast. It works within MAP kinase pathways, the signaling chains cells use to respond to their surroundings. Part of the Tec1 protein carries a small tag called SUMO. The team studied what that tag does.

They mapped how sumoylation of Tec1 is regulated and what it changes. The tag alters how Tec1 interacts with the MAPK pathways it serves. In effect, the cell gains a subtle dial for adjusting growth behavior. Small chemical tags like SUMO are easy to overlook, yet they fine-tune major decisions. The study clarifies one such dial in a model organism used worldwide.
plos-pone-0007556:
Antonio Julià and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on predicting who benefits from the arthritis drug infliximab. The drug blocks TNF alpha and is a treatment of choice for rheumatoid arthritis patients who fail standard therapy. Yet a considerable share of patients show no real response. The team searched blood gene activity for a signature that separates responders in advance.

They found an eight-gene expression profile that predicts the response. Eight genes is few enough for a practical blood test. Such a test could spare non-responders months of costly, ineffective treatment. It could also move likely responders to the drug sooner. Personalizing treatment this way is a central goal of modern medicine. The study shows it can be done with a compact signature.
plos-pone-0007656:
Ingrid Müller and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how Staphylococcus aureus manages vitamin B1. In its active form, B1 is an essential helper for key enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism. Mammals cannot make it and must salvage it from food. The human pathogen, by contrast, runs its own B1 production. The team examined how the bacterium controls that production.

Control operates at two levels: the enzymes themselves and the transcription of their genes. Two-layer control keeps the vitamin supply steady under changing conditions. It also gives drug designers two kinds of targets in one pathway. Blocking a pathway the bacterium needs but humans lack is a classic antibiotic strategy. The study maps the control points that such a strategy would strike.
plos-pone-0007756:
Norbert Mucke and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares microscope images of thread-like molecules with computer models of the same threads. Filamentous biopolymers, such as protein fibers, have stiffness that shapes cell life. One measure of stiffness is persistence length.

Scientists often gauge stiffness from flat images of molecules stuck on a surface. How a filament lands can follow two main scenarios. The authors used atomic force microscopy images and Brownian dynamics simulations. Matching the two tests whether image-based stiffness values can be trusted. That matters for all work on biological fibers.
plos-pone-0007856:
Sophie Javerzat and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It links gene regulation to blood vessel growth in the chick embryo. Building vessels requires many genes to act in concert. Their activity must be tuned by place, timing and dose.

Finding which genes drive vessel maturation is crucial for medicine. Blocked or excess vessel growth drives many diseases, from cancer to blindness. The authors correlated global gene patterns with angiogenesis in the chick's extra-embryonic vessels. This accessible system lets them watch vessels form in real time. The gene lists point to new therapeutic targets.
plos-pone-0007956:
Xiaomei Niu and colleagues measured blood signs of heart and lung strain in young people with sickle cell disease, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease bends red blood cells into stiff shapes that harm vessels over time. High lung pressure and a stiff heart are two feared results.

Blood samples from children and teens were checked for signs tied to vessel growth and inflammation. Some signs rose in step with the heart and lung changes doctors could measure. Such marks could flag the young patients who need close watch and early care, before harm turns grave.
plos-pone-0008056:
Ravi Kavasery and colleagues ran routine HIV testing inside a men's jail for PLOS ONE in 2009. Millions of people pass through United States jails each year, and health officials urge testing for all unless a person opts out. Jails resisted, citing cost and disorder.

Their controlled trial worked out the steps in a real facility and counted what the testing found. Undiagnosed infections came to light, and the process ran without wrecking the jail's routine. The trial gives other jails a tested script for a policy that can catch illness early.
plos-pone-0008156:
Wen Zhang and colleagues looked for pig-to-human spread of hepatitis E in central China and found none in PLOS ONE in 2009. The virus infects people and several animals, with pigs named the main source for human cases worldwide. Close gene kinship between pig and human strains backed that view.

In this region, human and pig strains did not show the kinship that fresh crossover would leave. Local spread may run through other routes, or older shared strains. A negative result with clear bounds still guides action: control efforts there should not rest on pigs alone.
plos-pone-0008256:
Guifen Chen, L. Phillip Wang, and Joe Z. Tsien recorded memory activity in mouse brains in PLOS ONE in 2009. A core goal of neuroscience is to watch memory traces form and return in real time. The hippocampus is a brain region central to associative memory. Its CA1 area is a key site for these traces. The team recorded groups of neurons there as mice experienced events.

They described short-lived ensemble patterns that tracked specific memories. Population-level traces linked neural activity to later retrieval. Watching memories at the group level bridges single cells and behavior. The work advances real-time study of how the brain remembers.
plos-pone-0008356:
Matthias an der Heiden, Udo Buchholz, and Gérard Krause modeled influenza policy in PLOS ONE in 2009. On June 11, 2009, the World Health Organization declared a pandemic of novel influenza A/H1N1. By late September the virus had reached all continents. Impact in most northern countries had stayed limited so far. A larger wave was expected in the coming season.

Their model estimated how public health measures could defer the epidemic peak. Delaying the peak spreads cases over more time. That relieves hospitals and buys time for vaccination. The study, titled Breaking the Waves, guides pandemic planning.
plos-pone-0008456:
Rebecca Smith and co-authors use mice to study father's age in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Human studies link older fathers to higher risk of some mental disorders in children. Those links cover autism, schizophrenia, and early bipolar disorder. But human data alone cannot prove cause. A mouse model lets the team test age apart from other factors.

Pups of older mouse fathers show flaws in social acts. They also explore less than pups of young fathers. The pattern backs a causal role for father's age. It gives a model for tracing how age changes sperm and brain growth.
plos-pone-0008556:
Jose Abisambra and co-authors study a cholesterol receptor in Alzheimer models in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Alzheimer disease is the most common form of dementia. The major genetic risk for late-onset disease is the epsilon-4 allele of apoE. ApoE is the main cholesterol transporter in the brain. The low-density lipoprotein receptor, LDLR, helps cells take up cholesterol cargo. The team examine LDLR in mouse and human cell models of the disease.

They find LDLR expression and localization are altered in those models. The receptor is made in wrong amounts or sits in wrong places. Such changes could disturb brain cholesterol handling in Alzheimer disease. They add a trafficking flaw to the disease picture.
plos-pone-0008656:
Maximiliano Rapanelli and co-authors link gene expression to learning in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Plasticity in the medial prefrontal cortex plays a key role in learning and memory circuits. Several genes, like BDNF, support that plasticity. The team train rats on an operant learning task, where actions earn rewards. They measure prefrontal gene expression as learning proceeds. Then they link those changes to a computational theory of learning.

Their model explains how gene-driven plasticity supports the learned behavior. Expression shifts track the stages predicted by theory. Bridging molecules, behavior, and computation strengthens both sides. The work offers a template for studying learning disorders.
plos-pone-0008756:
Shuzi Zhang, Hehua Dai, Ni Wan, and colleagues found a way to teach mice to accept foreign tissue. Their transplant study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Donor MHC antigens mark tissue as foreign and provoke attack. Showing those antigens early can sometimes train tolerance instead. A growth signal called IL-2 shapes which T cells respond. Its availability during training was the lever tested here.

Adjusting IL-2 while donor antigens were presented changed the outcome. Regulatory T cells grew, and attack responses faded. Calmer immunity means grafts might survive with fewer harsh drugs. The recipe offers a path toward transplant tolerance.
plos-pone-0008856:
Filip Simunovic, Ming Yi, Yulei Wang, and colleagues compared gene activity in dopamine neurons from men and women with Parkinson disease. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Men develop Parkinson disease more often than women. Symptoms and disease course also differ by sex. The substantia nigra, rich in dopamine neurons, is where the disease strikes hardest. Molecular reasons for the sex gap were largely unknown.
