Transcription profiles split clearly along sex lines in their samples. Different genes dominated the male and female patterns. Separate profiles suggest treatments may need sex-specific tuning. Parkinson research gains a reason to analyze men and women apart.
plos-pone-0008956:
Maik Grohmann and colleagues catalogued the many edited forms of a brain enzyme's messages, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, TPH2, is the rate-limiting step in making serotonin in the brain. Serotonin helps regulate mood, and its faults are tied to several mental illnesses. TPH2 was the second form of this enzyme to be discovered.

The team found that the gene's RNA messages are cut and rejoined in varied ways. On top of that splicing, the messages are also edited at many points. Each variant could tune how much enzyme the brain makes, or how well it works. That variety may help explain links between TPH2 and mood disorders.
plos-pone-0009056:
Hung-Chung Huang, Daniel Jupiter, and Vincent VanBuren sorted genes by the shape of their activity data, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some genes behave like switches, either fully on or fully off. Finding those switch-like genes reveals the logic of gene control networks. They also make promising biomarkers, since their state is easy to read.

The team's method uses distribution metrics on expression profiles. Instead of averages alone, it reads how values spread across samples. Switch-like genes stand out by their two-humped pattern. The classification should sharpen models that treat genes as on-off circuits.
plos-pone-0009156:
Arthur Talman, Andrew Blagborough, and Robert Sinden engineered a malaria parasite that glows through its whole life, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plasmodium falciparum causes most malaria deaths worldwide. Its life spans human blood, liver, and the mosquito gut. Tools to watch the parasite at every stage were badly needed.

The new strain expresses green fluorescent protein throughout the life cycle. Researchers can now follow it in mosquito and mammal alike. A glowing parasite exposes stages that drugs and vaccines might attack. The strain is a workbench tool for the whole malaria field.
plos-pone-0009256:
Ekaterina Kotelnikova and co-authors published this bioinformatics paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microarrays measure the activity of thousands of genes at once. A single experiment can flag hundreds of genes that change in a disease. Turning that long list into biological meaning is the hard part.

The authors built an atlas of cell signaling pathways for that job. Researchers can map their gene lists onto the atlas to see which pathways are involved. Instead of staring at raw gene names, they get a picture of the cell's wiring at work. The tool aims to make expression data quicker and easier to interpret correctly.
plos-pone-0009356:
Ivo Francischetti and co-authors published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cyr61 is a protein that works outside cells, in the matrix that holds tissues together. It belongs to the CCN family, whose members carry four working modules in a row. One partner of interest is vitronectin, a blood and tissue protein.

The team found that Cyr61 binds vitronectin with high affinity. The grip lands on one specific stretch of vitronectin, its somatomedin B domain. A tight, mapped grip suggests the pair works together in processes like wound repair and blood vessel growth. The study pins down one contact in a web of matrix signals.
plos-pone-0009456:
Tanya Cunningham and co-authors tested two natural mineral mixes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some mineral products sold for health use can kill bacteria. Why they do so was not clear. The team put the mixes in liquid with bacteria and measured the effect. They varied the acidity of the liquid as they worked.

Killing power rose and fell with acidity. The minerals release metal ions that can poison bacteria, and acidity controls that release. So the same mix can be strong in one setting and weak in another. The work turns an old folk remedy into a process that can be measured and tuned.
plos-pone-0009556:
Eva Kucerova and colleagues sequenced the genome of a food borne germ in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cronobacter sakazakii can contaminate powdered infant formula. Infections in newborns can be deadly. The team read the full genome of one strain, called BAA-894. They then compared it with other members of the Cronobacter group by a hybridization method.

The genome gives a full parts list for a germ of real concern to food safety. Comparisons show which genes the harmful species share and which they do not. Those details can improve tests that detect the germ in factories. They can also point to the genes that make it dangerous.
plos-pone-0009656:
Wuyang Zhu and co-authors studied how Sindbis virus enters cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sindbis is a mosquito borne virus used widely as a model. Its coat carries a protein called E2. That protein makes first contact with the cell it will infect. The team tested whether E2 binds heparan sulfate, a sugar chain found on cell surfaces.

The binding proved crucial for the virus to infect cells. Without that grip, infection faltered. Naming the handshake gives antiviral work a clear first target. A drug that blocks the grip could stop the virus before it gets inside, a strategy of interest for related viruses too.
plos-pone-0009756:
In times of hunger, people may eat wild plants they would normally avoid. Emily Gurley and colleagues investigated a fatal outbreak in northeastern Bangladesh tied to one such plant. Their report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The plant was Xanthium strumarium, and people had eaten its seedlings during a time of food scarcity. The investigation traced the outbreak to that food source. Cases like this show how hunger can turn a toxic plant into a meal. The report helps health workers prevent repeat poisonings in lean seasons. Food scarcity was the backdrop to the whole event.
plos-pone-0009856:
During a flu pandemic, emergency medical workers must decide whether to report for duty. Daniel Barnett and colleagues gauged that willingness across the United States. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The workers surveyed staff ambulances and emergency calls nationwide.

The assessment framework weighed threat and efficacy, what workers fear and what they think helps. Willingness to respond decides whether ambulances keep running in a crisis. Knowing what sways the choice helps agencies plan staffing before disaster hits. The results speak to every service that must hold during pandemics.
plos-pone-0010156:
The authors were Mark Bain, Emily Cornwell, Kristine Hope, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study mapped a fish virus across the Great Lakes. The virus causes viral hemorrhagic septicemia and kills cultured and wild fish. Native to northern oceans and European fresh waters, it had become established in the Great Lakes, with large wild die-offs.

The team related the virus distribution to shipping, a likely route for spread between waters. Knowing how an invasive pathogen travels helps managers target inspections and ballast rules. Early mapping can slow the next waterway invasion before it takes hold.
plos-pone-0010256:
The authors were Makoto Kuroda, Harutaka Katano, Noriko Nakajima, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study read the 2009 pandemic flu virus with new sequencing tools. The H1N1 virus had emerged worldwide the year before. The team used a next-generation sequencer to read all RNA in lung tissue. The sample came from a patient killed by viral pneumonia.

Reading everything present, without targeting one germ, can reveal unexpected pathogens. They characterized quasispecies, the swarm of near-identical viral variants inside one host. That swarm view matters, because drug resistance and severity can hide in minor variants.
plos-pone-0010356:
Lucia Talamini and colleagues studied memory in early schizophrenia for PLOS ONE in 2010. People with the illness often struggle to recall past events well. An earlier model from the same group blamed weak use of context. In that view, memories are stored without enough of the surrounding detail. Retrieval then fails because the cues are too thin.

The team tested people in a first episode of the illness. Results fit the model's prediction: context effects on recall were reduced. Testing early cases matters, since long illness and medication can muddy results. If context binding is a core problem, training could target it directly. The study links a computer model of the mind to a real patient test.
plos-pone-0010456:
Qin Wang and colleagues found a new job for a calcium-based Wnt signal in prostate cancer for PLOS ONE in 2010. Wnt signals guide development and, when faulty, fuel disease. Their workings in prostate cancer were little known, though the cancer kills many men. The team measured a Wnt protein across human tissue samples first. They then tested the calcium branch of Wnt signaling in prostate cancer cells.

That branch reshaped the cells' inner skeleton and changed how they move. Cell movement underlies metastasis, the spread that makes prostate cancer deadly. A signal that drives movement is a candidate drug target. The study also connects a developmental pathway to a common adult cancer. It widens the map of what to block in advanced disease.
plos-pone-0010556:
Heleen Slagter and co-workers used brain imaging to watch conscious targets compete over time in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mind can only handle so much at once. That limit shows in the attentional blink: a second target seen too soon after a first is often missed. Theories agree the blink reflects competition for conscious access. The team scanned brains while subjects faced rapid streams with two targets.

Imaging revealed how brain activity for the targets rose and fell against each other. Neural competition, not simple erasure, seems to cause the blink. That view helps explain why the second target sometimes survives. It also links a classic psychology effect to measurable brain dynamics. Consciousness research gains a timed map of a bottleneck.
plos-pone-0010656:
Rebecca Baron and colleagues tested a compound that calms severe inflammation in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. During endotoxemia, a body-wide reaction to bacterial toxins, inflammation itself can kill. A protein called HMGA1 helps switch on many inflammatory genes at once.

The compound distamycin A blocked HMGA1 from gripping its DNA targets. With that grip broken, inflammation in lung and liver eased. Survival-related measures improved as well. Targeting a master switch, rather than one inflammatory signal at a time, offers a different strategy for treating runaway inflammation in critical illness.
plos-pone-0010756:
Steven Teo and Barbara Block compared tuna catches in the Gulf of Mexico, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Gulf is the main western Atlantic spawning ground for bluefin tuna. Directed fishing for bluefin there has been banned since the 1980s, yet longlines set for other species still catch them.

The team related yellowfin and bluefin catches to water conditions. The two species answered the same ocean in different ways. Temperature and depth patterns that drew one did not draw the other. Those differences are practical: fleets can adjust where and how they fish to keep yellowfin while sparing spawning bluefin.
plos-pone-0010856:
Anatoliy Kravets, Hong Qin, Ausaf Ahmad and co-authors published this yeast study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Candida albicans, a fungus that can infect people, sometimes survives harsh conditions by gaining or losing a whole chromosome. That trick creates a gene imbalance, and the authors asked how the fungus copes while the imbalance lasts.

They compared gene activity in normal cells with two copies of chromosome 5 against cells left with only one copy. At least two-fifths of the genes on the single chromosome were fully boosted back to normal output levels. Only a smaller share stayed reduced. Kravets and colleagues call this dosage compensation, a genome-wide balancing act. Understanding it may expose weak points in a pathogen that already resists many drugs.
plos-pone-0010956:
François Normand-Lauzière, Frédérique Frisch, Sébastien Labbé and co-authors published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fat in the blood after meals is suspected of damaging tissues and seeding type 2 diabetes. People whose parents both have diabetes showed abnormal fat handling when fat was infused, and the team asked whether the same fault appears after real eating.

They traced labeled fat through healthy offspring of two diabetic parents, healthy people without diabetic relatives, and patients with diabetes, during fasting, insulin infusion, and steady oral intake of a standard meal. In the offspring, the abnormal pattern seen with infusions was not fully established after food. Normand-Lauzière and colleagues map how an inherited diabetes risk develops step by step, before disease itself arrives.
plos-pone-0011056:
Benny Chen, Divino Deoliveira, Ivan Spasojevic and co-authors published this radiation study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Few drugs can rescue victims after lethal radiation exposure, a gap for both accidents and attacks. The authors tested human growth hormone, given after irradiation, in mice and then in monkeys.

Irradiated mice treated daily with the hormone survived at several times the rate of controls. Even a five-day course helped. Blood counts came back faster across white cells, T and B cells, natural killer cells, and above all platelets. Chen and colleagues extend the result toward monkeys, the needed step before human stocking decisions. A familiar hormone that is easy to make, and that buys survival after exposure, would fill a clear hole in radiation care.
plos-pone-0011156:
Chiavolini, Rangel-Moreno, Berg and colleagues tested a tularemia vaccine in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Tularemia is a severe infection that can be inhaled. After nasal vaccination, the team looked at immune tissue that forms in the airways and whether its presence tracked with survival.

Mice that formed this airway immune tissue were more likely to survive infection. That makes the tissue a useful sign that a vaccine is working. Vaccine makers can use such a sign to judge designs without waiting for full challenge tests. The work guides vaccines given through the nose, the route this germ naturally takes.
plos-pone-0011256:
De Meijer, Sverdlov, Popov and colleagues tested liver enzyme blockers in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Enzymes that remodel tissue can drive both injury and healing in the liver. Blocking the whole family curbed inflammation and liver injury in their mouse experiments.

Yet the same broad blockade made liver scarring, called fibrosis, worse. That paradox warns against blunt drugs in a system where the same enzymes do harm and good. Finer drugs that block only the harmful members may be needed. Liver doctors gain a clear caution for designing safer therapies.
plos-pone-0011356:
Matt Bianchi and co-workers examined in 2010 how sleep apnea changes the way sleep itself unfolds. In obstructive sleep apnea, the airway keeps closing during the night, and sleep breaks into short, restless pieces. Standard sleep scores count how long each stage lasts, but they miss how often the brain jumps from one stage to another.

The team tracked those stage-to-stage jumps and found that apnea alters the pattern of transitions through the night. Sleep in apnea patients does not just get shorter; it flows along different paths, with more abrupt shifts. Measuring transitions gives sleep doctors a richer picture of broken sleep than stage totals alone. It may help explain why patients still feel unrefreshed and could sharpen how treatment success is judged.
plos-pone-0011456:
Jun Song and co-authors profiled in 2010 the most dangerous minority inside head and neck tumors. These cancers contain a side population of cells that behaves like cancer stem cells, able to renew the tumor and survive treatment. The team isolated those cells and measured how they differ from the bulk of the tumor.

The side population proved highly invasive, resistant to chemotherapy, and marked by abnormal activity in the Wnt signaling pathway. That triple profile explains much treatment failure: therapy kills the ordinary cells while the toughest ones persist and rebuild. Profiling them gives drug hunters precise targets. A treatment that cannot kill this subpopulation will likely watch the tumor return, so future trials should be judged by whether they clear these cells too.
plos-pone-0011556:
Andreas Sjödin and co-authors read whole genomes in 2010 to compare lab-raised and wild strains of a feared bacterium. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia and is watched as a possible bioweapon, so knowing whether an outbreak strain came from nature or a laboratory has forensic weight. The team sequenced closely related strains with different histories: laboratory propagation versus natural circulation.

The two histories left distinct mutational patterns in the genomes, like different handwriting from different lives. Lab passage, with its bottlenecks and rich food, mutates a genome differently from survival in animals and ticks. Those signatures could help investigators attribute an outbreak correctly, a task where a wrong answer has political and medical consequences. The study also warns lab scientists that their strains drift from wild reality faster than they may assume.
plos-pone-0011656:
Michael Stern explored why people differ in their appetite for risk, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Willingness to take risks has a genetic component, and specific genes contributing to it have been found. Since risky choices often look irrational or harmful, it is puzzling that natural selection would favour them at all.

Stern argues that inherited wealth, or patrimony, changes the pay-off of gambling across generations. What a family stands to lose, or has to fall back on, shifts which risks are worth taking. His account links economic inheritance to the evolution of risk-taking behaviour in a fresh way.
plos-pone-0011756:
Matthew Angel and Mehmet Yanik found a way to make stem cell reprogramming with RNA work better, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Making patient-matched pluripotent stem cells without using DNA would be safer for therapy. Delivering lab-made RNA into cells can express reprogramming proteins directly, but cells sense foreign RNA and raise innate immune alarms.

By suppressing that innate immune response, the authors enabled frequent repeated transfection with the RNA. Repeated doses are what reprogramming requires. Calming the cell's alarms thus opens the door to efficient, DNA-free production of stem cells for future treatments.
plos-pone-0011856:
Federico Degrange and co-authors analyzed in 2010 how an extinct terror bird fed, using the skull of Andalgalornis steulleti. Terror birds were flightless South American predators with huge hooked beaks and no close living match. This species was mid-sized for the family, at roughly forty kilograms, and built for life on the ground.

The team applied engineering-style mechanical analysis to the fossil skull, testing how it handled stress while biting and striking. Those tests suggest how the bird killed and processed prey without risking its own beak. Rebuilding feeding mechanics from bone turns a silent fossil into evidence about how one of South America's top predators actually made its living.
plos-pone-0011956:
Guanghou Shui and co-workers examined in 2010 which raw materials two yeast enzymes prefer when building membrane fats. Phosphatidic acid is the starting point for all the glycerophospholipids that form cell membranes. It is made when enzymes of the LPAAT family attach a fatty chain to a simpler precursor.

Using lipidomic measurements, which catalog fats in bulk, plus a direct activity assay, the team characterized the substrate tastes of the yeast enzymes Slc1p and Cst26p. Knowing which chains each enzyme favors explains how yeast tailors its membrane mix. Membrane composition affects everything from drug sensitivity to stress tolerance, so enzyme preferences are levers for engineering yeast.
plos-pone-0012056:
Duncan Menge, Jeanne DeNoyer, and Jeremy Lichstein put in 2010 a neat tale about old woods to the test, and the tale failed. The puzzle is plain. Trees that make their own nitrogen with the help of root germs are rare in old woods of the mild zone. Yet those woods are often short of nitrogen. One tale blamed the family tree of the woods: no old-woods kind in these parts, it said, comes from stock that can fix nitrogen.

The team's checks show that the shape of the family tree does not in fact explain why the fixers are so scarce. With the stock tale cleared away, eyes turn back to the woods as they are: poor light and some nitrogen in the soil may make fixing not worth the cost. Tests that kill a neat tale are how field science keeps its tales true.
plos-pone-0012156:
Alexandra Le Bras, Chantal Samson, Matteo Trentini, and co-authors studied a gene switched on in blood vessel lining cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. New vessels sprout from old ones during growth, and the lining cells lead that sprouting. The gene they studied is mostly active in those lining cells, which made its control switches a natural target for study.

They found two control regions for the gene: a far-off enhancer and a nearby promoter, both directed by two vessel-cell regulators. Control maps like this show how a cell keeps the right genes on for its job. They also flag switches that vessel diseases, or vessel-growing tumors, might hijack.
plos-pone-0012256:
Frank Emmert-Streib proposed a new measure of complexity in PLOS ONE in 2010. Judging how complex an observed object or pattern is has resisted a single good answer for decades. The classic approach, based on the shortest possible description, is elegant but often impossible to compute for real data, and it treats random noise as maximally complex, which clashes with intuition.

His measure, statistic complexity, joins that classic idea with an ensemble approach that samples many descriptions. It is designed to rate structured patterns as complex and both total order and total randomness as simpler. A workable complexity measure is useful anywhere patterns must be compared, from genomes to markets to machine learning.
plos-pone-0012356:
Mykola Maydan, Paul McDonald, Jasbinder Sanghera and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2010 that a disputed cell protein truly works as a kinase. Integrin-linked kinase, or ILK, helps cells stick to their surroundings and organize their inner skeleton. Some scientists doubted that ILK could add phosphate tags to other proteins at all, which left its true job in doubt.

The team showed that ILK needs manganese to work and that it places a phosphate tag on a key target, GSK-3 beta, which controls many cell decisions. Proving ILK is a real, working kinase settles a long argument. It also makes ILK a clearer target for drugs aimed at cancer and other diseases of cell growth.
plos-pone-0012456:
Fei Wang, Shi Huang and Long Ma studied gene clusters in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In worms, some genes sit in operons, groups read together from one switch and then cut into separate messages. Splicing can also make several message versions from one gene, adding variety.

The team found operon genes carry more multi-version genes than average and use their splice sites in distinctive ways. The pattern shows operons are not plain read-through systems; they fine-tune output per gene. Worms are a basic model for gene control, so these rules inform genetics far beyond one small animal.
plos-pone-0012556:
Arno van Kuijk, Jeroen DeGroot, Rishma Koeman and colleagues measured blood markers in early psoriatic arthritis drug trials, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Drug developers want soluble biomarkers — blood signals — that show quickly whether a new treatment engages joint and bone damage, before large trials commit. The team compared the drug adalimumab with placebo in small proof-of-concept trials.

Markers of cartilage and bone metabolism shifted in informative ways under treatment. On the group level, such markers can screen candidate drugs cheaply and early. For psoriatic arthritis, where joint damage accumulates silently, fast readouts shorten the road to better therapies.
plos-pone-0012656:
Bol, Desjardins, Reusens and co-authors asked whether a mismatch between early and later diet sets male mice up for disease. Surveys and animal work link poor feeding before birth, followed by rich food later, to the metabolic syndrome. Their 2010 study tested that chain in mice, watching blood pressure and blood vessels.

The design follows pups whose early nutrition differed from their adult diet. Outcomes in such mice test whether the mismatch itself, not just rich food, drives high blood pressure and artery disease. Answers matter for advice given to mothers and infants worldwide.
plos-pone-0012756:
Hall, Espinoza, Benbow and co-authors charted HIV infection across America's large cities. The national epidemic stays centred in urban areas, yet each city has its own pattern of who is hit hardest. Their 2010 study gathered city-level data to compare those local profiles side by side.

The contrasts matter because a plan that works in one city may miss the mark in another. Prevention money and testing sites do the most good when aimed at the local pattern. Their survey gives city health departments a shared evidence base for tailoring the response.
plos-pone-0012856:
Vivithanaporn, Maingat, Lin and co-authors showed that a hepatitis C protein stirs brain immune cells and worsens HIV's brain harm. Hepatitis C genetic material and proteins are found in human brain tissue. What HIV and hepatitis C co-infection does to the brain, though, was unclear when they wrote in 2010.

Their study found the HCV core protein activates neuroimmune responses and adds to HIV-1's toxic effect on neurons. Co-infected patients face brain risks beyond either virus alone. The result supports brain screening in co-infection care.  Brain cells in culture let the team isolate the effect.
plos-pone-0326556:
Nelson Pang and Jessie Yeung traced how Canadians use four kinds of mental health providers over time: family doctors, psychiatrists, psychologists, and social workers. Seven cycles of a national health survey from 2007 to 2020 supplied the trends, and the most recent cycle supported a deeper analysis of who uses which door into care.

Family doctors were consistently the most accessed, and psychiatrists the least, while use of psychologists and social workers climbed late in the period. Women used family doctors and social workers more than men but psychiatrists less, and older adults showed their own pattern. Knowing which door each group actually uses helps planners fix the bottlenecks that matter instead of expanding the wrong service.
plos-pone-0331156:
Vanessa Mitschke, Francesco Grassi, Alperen Doğaner, and Anne Schacht wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. Their field is emotion research, and their subject is how people judge the social meaning of scenes that carry feeling. The work is built as a large-scale rating study with several dimensions rated at once.

Participants rated affective scenes, meaning pictures that stir emotions, on how socially relevant each scene feels. Gathering many ratings across many scenes lets the authors map which features make a scene feel socially important. Other researchers can use that map when choosing picture sets for experiments on emotion, attention, and social judgment.
plos-pone-0336456:
Ulla Lichtenhagen and co-authors ran two experiments in 2026 on eyewitness lineups when a crime had several culprits. Guidelines say to show suspects in separate lineups, yet seeing culprits together might jog memory through familiar faces.

Volunteers watched a staged crime video with four culprits, then faced lineups shown together or one by one. The first experiment found no clear difference in spotting that a culprit was present. Further testing probed the idea that one recognised face cues another. The question matters for police practice, where a small gain in detection must be weighed against fairness to suspects.
plos-pone-0339756:
Janerra Allen, Elliot Hong, and Fow-Sen Choa published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It works with task-based fMRI, brain scans recorded while people perform set tasks. The authors build models of the brain's energy landscape and its changing states, aiming to extract biomarkers for schizophrenia.

A biomarker is a measurable sign that can help identify a condition or track its course. Modeling brain activity as states that rise and fall may reveal patterns plain averages would hide. If such signs prove reliable, they could support earlier or more objective assessment in schizophrenia, which is still diagnosed mainly by interview and observation.
plos-pone-0340156:
Xia Guan and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about maize, the corn plant. Gibberellins are plant hormones that drive growth, and bioactive forms control height and flowering. The authors measure natural variation in these hormone levels across maize tissues in North America.

Knowing how hormone levels differ between tissues and plant lines is basic knowledge for breeding. Breeders selecting for stature or stress tolerance work with growth hormones whether they measure them or not. A map of natural variation gives them starting material and targets. Plant scientists across the maize belt are the readers for this kind of baseline survey.
plos-pone-0340256:
Leonardo Sorbelli and colleagues described a fossil bovid from an early Pliocene lake site in Catalonia, Spain, in 2026. Fourteen animals were found, several as near complete skeletons, an unusual wealth of material for sorting out tangled fossil cattle naming.

After close comparison with related fossil genera from Europe and Africa, the team placed the animal in Parabos and recognised five valid species across two genera. The skeletons point to life in wet, plant rich surroundings. Whether these animals were the first of the modern cattle line or the last of an older one remains open, and the rich material frames that question sharply.
plos-pone-0340756:
Valeria Rios Montoya and co-authors compared vaccine coverage and infant deaths across countries from twenty ten to twenty twenty-three, using World Health Organization and UNICEF records for six routine childhood vaccines. They grouped countries by income to test a blunt question: does wider vaccination lower child deaths even where poverty and weak services hold coverage back?

Richer countries had both higher coverage and far fewer infant deaths, while poorer countries lagged on both counts. Coverage dipped worldwide in the pandemic year and had only partly recovered three years later. Once income was accounted for, most links between coverage and survival faded. The team concludes that unfair starting conditions, not vaccine effort alone, drive the gap in child deaths.
plos-pone-0341756:
Ueamporn Summart and four colleagues published this 2026 study adapting a short social support questionnaire for Thai patients with blood cancers. The eight-question scale asks how much illness-specific support patients feel. The team translated it, adjusted it for Thai culture, and tested it on several hundred patients at three hospitals in the northeast.

Statistical checks on split halves of the sample confirmed the scale's structure and accuracy. Summart concludes the Thai version is a quick, valid way to gauge support, and urges cancer teams to weigh family and social backing as part of care.
plos-pone-0342856:
Shira Linsk, Anna Thonis, and Kristin M. Winchell count moths across New York City to see how city life treats them. Moths react quickly to harm in their surroundings, so they work well as warning species. Their 2026 study merges public sightings posted by residents with the team's own night sampling in twelve spots across six parks.

Moth variety fell as built-up land and night lighting rose. Places with more broad-leaf tree cover and open land held richer moth life. The public records missed some species the team caught by hand, so both data sources were needed. Keeping parks darker at night and holding on to tree cover emerge as simple ways to help city moths persist.
plos-pone-0343756:
Juan Xiang and co-authors built a cheap DNA fingerprinting kit for cowpea, an important legume grown worldwide. Breeders need fast ways to tell varieties apart, protect their rights, and check seed purity. Their 2026 study sequenced nineteen cowpea accessions and mined the results for stable genetic markers.

The scan found hundreds of thousands of variants, narrowed to a high-quality set for analysis. The accessions fell into three genetic groups. From the data, the team picked just six core markers, all inside genes, that together separated every accession. Each variety received a fingerprint profile and its own QR code. Xiang and colleagues offer the kit as a low-cost tool for breeding and seed testing.
plos-pone-0344656:
Qing He and colleagues charted the chemistry of ageing in base liquor for Sichuan's strong-aroma baijiu, sampled at one, five, ten, fifteen, and twenty years. Seventy-five flavour compounds were tracked with mass spectrometry, metabolomics, and three-dimensional fluorescence scans to see how the spirit's character is built and lost over time in storage.

Esters, the fruity backbone, fell steeply after year five. Acids peaked at five years, alcohols at ten, and polyphenols at fifteen, each then declining. Fluorescence shifted toward longer wavelengths, signalling growing molecular complexity and richer flavour. The authors say the timeline gives distillers a scientific grip on ageing and quality control.
plos-pone-0345056:
Collins Mukubesa and colleagues reviewed records of three hundred sixteen tuberculosis patients treated at a rural general hospital in Zambia, asking who dies during treatment and why. Nearly one patient in five died, a heavy toll for a curable disease. The team followed patients from the start of treatment to their recorded outcome over up to a year.

Death risk rose with age, with a diagnosis made on symptoms alone rather than lab proof, and in patients also living with HIV. Two things protected people: being watched over by family-based treatment supporters and starting treatment at a higher body weight. For rural programs, the message is plain: confirm cases in the lab, support patients at home, and treat weight loss as a warning sign, not a side note.
plos-pone-0345356:
Rayhanah Almutairi and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional study of nurses working in Saudi Arabia. The authors look at job satisfaction and burnout, and at how feeling supported and skilled at work connects with both.

The central idea is resilience, the ability to recover from strain, acting as an indirect pathway between workplace support and outcomes. Nurses who felt their skills were growing and their institution backed them are examined alongside their resilience levels. Hospital managers concerned with keeping nurses in the job are the readers most likely to use these links.
plos-pone-0345956:
Sawera Qureshi and colleagues built machine learning classifiers that read short summaries of aviation incidents and sort each as an incident or an accident, matching the official label. The dataset covers eighty years and more than fifty thousand events from Canada's transportation safety board. Manual sorting is slow and inconsistent, and wrong labels can hide safety problems.

Three classic text classifiers were compared on the same word-weighted features. Fast automatic triage can flag possibly mislabeled reports and speed severity checks when reports flood in. Aviation runs more than a hundred thousand safe flights a day, and its safety culture depends on learning from every occurrence. Studies like this test whether algorithms can shoulder the sorting work reliably.
plos-pone-0346056:
Sangrok Lee and Taehyun Jung asked if AI inventions act like the rare tools that change whole industries. Steam power and electric grids did this in the past. The pair tested the idea with patents from one firm, Samsung. They looked at filings from 1982 to 2018 and matched AI patents with like non-AI ones.

The AI patents won on all three counts. Later work built on them more. They reached into more fields. And they paired with other tech more often. The gaps held up under many checks. Lee and Jung say this helps explain why firms keep pouring cash into AI.
plos-pone-0346156:
Cristina Davino and colleagues set out to measure educational poverty, the lack of real chances to learn and grow, among teenagers in Naples, Italy. Rather than count only school results, they surveyed young people aged fifteen to nineteen about their family life, their schooling, and the world around their homes. Then they looked for the hidden patterns that tie those answers together.

Three broad forces stood out: family, school, and environment. Grouping the teenagers by these forces showed clear types, from well supported to badly deprived, and family background, language grades, gender, and school type all tracked with the groups. The authors offer their model as a first tool for spotting which young people are being left with the fewest chances.
plos-pone-0346656:
Mayuko Harada and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on the silkworm Bombyx mori, the moth whose larvae spin silk. The authors identify an atypical microRNA in it, a small gene-regulating molecule that breaks the usual pattern. The molecule also carries sequence variation between individuals or strains.

MicroRNAs fine-tune gene activity, and an unusual one can reveal new biology or serve as a marker. Silkworms are both an industrial animal and a model insect, so findings spread in two directions. Insect geneticists and sericulture researchers, who breed silkworms for silk, share the audience for this identification.
plos-pone-0346756: Blood pooling between brain and skull can return after surgery. This paper used machine learning to classify recurrence risk after surgical treatment of chronic subdural hemorrhage. The model flags high-risk patients for closer follow-up.
plos-pone-0347556:
Angela Esohe Adeoti-Lawani and colleagues measured lasting protein leakage in urine samples from children in Nigeria who live with sickle cell anaemia. Such leakage is an early warning of kidney damage that single tests often miss. Nigeria carries the world's heaviest burden of the disease. One hundred forty-nine affected children and the same number of matched healthy children gave urine samples, repeated after at least three months for those testing positive.

Nearly a quarter of the sickle cell group had persistent proteinuria, against under three percent of controls. Children with the leakage had lower levels of fetal haemoglobin, the protective form that softens the disease. The authors urge routine repeated screening so kidney damage is caught while still reversible.
plos-pone-0347656:
Lori Reider and colleagues recorded parents and young children in the United States and Hong Kong reading a picture book about snakes, spiders, lizards, and turtles, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Thirty-one families in each place took part, and the team coded how much fear and negative language crept into the talk, alongside questionnaires on fear beliefs.

Across both cultures, snakes and spiders drew more fear and harsher words than lizards and turtles. Hong Kong parents expressed more snake fear than American parents, passing a stronger signal even where children's own beliefs were similar. The study shows one quiet route by which animal fears are handed down: the words parents choose at story time.
plos-pone-0347856:
Marielle Ribeiro Feitosa, Fernanda Rebelo, and co-authors followed new mothers in a Brazilian city to find what most threatens the early bond between mother and baby. The months after birth place heavy demands on women, and a weakened bond can affect both mother and child. Their 2026 study assessed mothers at three and six months after delivery, measuring bonding quality and depression symptoms with standard questionnaires, in a group considered low risk.

Postpartum depression stood out as the strongest predictor of impaired bonding at both time points, including specific problems like damaged attachment and anxiety about the baby. Social support pulled the other way, protecting the bond. The authors argue for routine depression screening after birth and for programs that strengthen mothers' support networks, since the bond suffers most where depression goes unnoticed.
plos-pone-0347956:
Aliye Demet Demirag and colleagues examined whether hydroxychloroquine, a familiar anti-malaria drug, could block a sensor on mast cells that may help glioblastoma, a deadly brain tumor, resist treatment. They combined several methods: quantum chemical calculations of the drug's structure, light-based measurements to confirm it, and computer docking of the drug into the sensor's shape.

One hundred simulated docking runs tested how the drug might grip the receptor, checked against known reference results, and lab tests on cells followed. Standard care still leaves glioblastoma patients with a median survival of little more than a year, so repurposing known drugs is an active strategy. This study maps whether the drug-receptor pairing is plausible enough to justify deeper testing.
plos-pone-0348056:
Jun Yang and colleagues tested mycosubtilin, a ring-shaped molecule made by a common soil bacterium, against human colon cancer cells grown in the laboratory. Natural products remain a rich source of cancer drug leads, and this compound had never been tried against colorectal cancer. Computer methods first predicted its likely targets, then cell experiments measured growth, death patterns, and protein changes.

The compound slowed cancer cell growth more strongly than a standard chemotherapy drug in the same tests. Treated cells showed the classic signs of programmed death, with shrunken, fragmented nuclei, and levels of a key survival protein fell. Cell results are a first step only, but a natural molecule outperforming a frontline drug in dishes earns further study.
plos-pone-0348356:
Hong Zhang, Keqiang Dong, and co-authors proposed a new mathematical lens for spotting jet engine wear early, based on how vibration patterns shift over time. Existing entropy measures summarize which patterns occur but ignore how the system moves between them. Their 2026 method adds those transitions, building an entropy that watches pattern traffic, plus a distance measure comparing both pattern counts and transition behavior between recordings.

On simulated data and on NASA's public engine degradation dataset, the new measure caught finer chaotic changes than rival entropy methods. More usefully, it flagged abnormal shifts in pattern transitions early in components' decline, offering timelier fault warnings. Combined with a mapping technique, the distance measure also sorted engine recordings by similarity, supporting diagnosis.
plos-pone-0348956:
Sujata Kandel and Hari Prasad Kaphle survey nurses in private hospitals in Pokhara, Nepal, about how engaged they feel at work. Engaged nurses matter for patient safety and care quality, yet private-sector nursing in Nepal is little studied. Their 2026 study questions more than two hundred nurses using standard scales for engagement, job satisfaction, and plans to quit.

Engagement scores ran high on average. Nurses who saw chances to grow in their careers were far more likely to feel engaged. Feeling that the workload was manageable also helped. The findings suggest hospital managers can hold on to nurses by building clear career paths and keeping workloads sane, rather than relying on goodwill alone.
plos-pone-0349256:
Jung Won Kwak, Sung-Joon Park, and Hwan Hoon Chung checked whether a simple measuring formula can place a long intravenous line correctly at the bedside. These lines, threaded from the arm toward the heart, work best when the tip lands near a precise junction, and intensive care units often lack the navigation gadgets that guide placement elsewhere. The formula estimates length from chest X-ray landmarks such as collarbone length and spine segments.

Across more than four hundred placements at one centre, the procedure succeeded in about ninety-seven percent of cases, and roughly three quarters of tips landed in the ideal zone. Success did not depend on operator experience or which arm was used, and it held up even in patients with other complex devices in place. Two radiologists agreed on tip judgements almost perfectly. The authors recommend the formula as a dependable first safeguard.
plos-pone-0349356:
Hojun Seo, Junyeoung Ahn, and Byungseok Kang present CrossSwap, a face swapping system designed to fix the uncanny results of earlier tools, which often lost the original person's identity. Their model studies the source face's shape before blending, then uses attention blocks that adjust across scales to pour identity features into the target picture while keeping the target's pose and expression.

Against three recent rival methods, CrossSwap took first place on pose and expression accuracy and second on identity retention and overall image quality. The authors argue that respecting face shape, not just surface features, is what makes a swap look like the same person in a new scene. The work sits inside generative image research and carries the field's usual dual-use questions.
plos-pone-0349556:
Sujan Adhikari, Swagat Khanal, and Akash Adhikari reviewed research in 2026 on drug resistance hiding in livestock drinking water systems. Pipes and troughs grow biofilms, slimy layers where bacteria shelter, swap resistance genes, and survive cleaning.

Searching four databases, the reviewers found biofilms holding bacteria unlike those in water or dung passing through. Dangerous traits turned up, including resistance to last resort drugs in pig systems. Standard disinfection often failed, with resistant bacteria back within days. The authors frame farm water lines as an active reservoir that food safety and drug resistance plans must include.
plos-pone-0349656:
Mohamed Mohiya published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is an exploratory study inside a multinational energy corporation. The subject is how employees view safeguarding information, protecting company data from leaks and attacks, in their own daily work.

Security rules fail when staff see them as someone else's job, so employee perspectives are the real test of a policy. An exploratory study maps attitudes before a company tries to change them. Energy firms guard data whose loss could affect markets and infrastructure, making their staff's habits a matter of wider interest to security managers.
plos-pone-0349756:
Soichiro Takamiya and colleagues asked a pricing question: at what cost would stem cell therapy for stroke be good value in Japan? A recent combined analysis of trials found the therapy helps patients after acute or early stroke, but the treatment will not be cheap. The team built a ten-year simulation comparing stem cells plus standard care against standard care alone.

The model tracked costs and quality-adjusted life years, the standard measure blending length and quality of life. Working backward from Japan's official value threshold, they solved for the therapy price at which the extra benefit justifies the extra cost. Health systems need exactly this number before a promising therapy can be covered, priced, and offered fairly.
plos-pone-0349856:
Sileshi Demelash Sasie and colleagues evaluated the disease surveillance system of Ethiopia's Sidama Region, the network meant to spot outbreaks early. One hundred forty health workers and facilities across thirteen districts were checked against World Health Organization and national standards, covering case detection, reporting, data analysis, training, and supplies. The survey ran in late 2023.

Evaluations like this score each link in the chain, from village health posts to regional offices, against set adherence targets. Weak links, such as late reports or missing feedback, are exactly where an outbreak can slip through unseen. With few subnational evaluations published in Ethiopia, a district-by-district account gives regional managers concrete gaps to fix rather than general worry.
plos-pone-0350556:
Sorachai Kamollimsakul and co-authors followed university students through a self-guided meditation program to see if each short session lifted mood on the spot. Students report high stress, and formal services are often hard to reach. Their 2026 study had twenty-seven students complete twenty-eight sessions of a Thai mind-body practice over two weeks, rating negative mood just before and after each session.

Students stuck with the program well, finishing nearly all sessions. Negative mood dropped clearly right after every session, and that lift stayed steady across the two weeks rather than fading. Starting levels of anxiety and resilience did not change the benefit. The authors present the practice as a feasible per-session mood tool for similar student groups, while calling the evidence preliminary.
plos-pone-0350656:
Tereza Patrmanova and colleagues compared soils under native beech trees and planted spruce trees at one European site. Tree type shapes soil chemistry and microbes, which in turn steer how soil forms and stores carbon. Samples across soil layers were tested for acidity, nutrients, dissolved carbon forms, carbon makeup, and microbe communities.

Total carbon stored did not differ between forests. Carbon quality and its spread across layers did differ. Spruce soil showed acid washing changes absent under beech, and one dissolved acid ran far higher. Beech soil, milder and richer in easy carbon, hosted distinct microbe groups. Swapping tree species changes what soil carbon is, even when totals look the same.
plos-pone-0350856:
Clara L Sanchez and colleagues asked whether heart rhythm wobble can tell what kind of exercise a person is doing. Knowing dose matters when activity itself acts as treatment. Twenty six healthy volunteers cycled at two steady loads and in bursts, while chest straps logged each beat and gas and lactate measures tracked effort.

Beats from the last four minutes of each bout fed a model that sorted sessions by type. Correct sorting was strong, with hit and clear rates in the high eighties to high nineties. Simple beat spread measures and a fractal style index carried most signal. A cheap chest strap, the work hints, may reveal exercise pattern where diaries stay vague.
plos-pone-0350956:
Brooke Ike leads a team of six publishing the plan for a pilot trial of social prescribing against loneliness in cancer survivors, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Social prescribing, a British model, connects patients to community activities and support through a link worker rather than a prescription pad. The team adapted a proven version for survivors using a structured adaptation process, then designed a feasibility trial across two primary care practices serving rural patients in the American Northwest.

Thirty-six survivors who screen positive for loneliness will be assigned by chance to the enhanced program or to usual care with a brochure. The pilot's true endpoints are feasibility questions: can the practices recruit, will survivors accept the offer, and does the program run as designed? A full trial follows only if those answers are yes. The protocol matters because loneliness after cancer is common, harmful, and untouched by oncology's usual tools.
plos-pone-0351056:
Jeremy Gordon, John Chuang, and Giovanni Pezzulo asked how people plan a route before they start moving. Volunteers wore a virtual reality headset and could look around a map during a planning pause. Eye trackers recorded where each person looked, how far their gaze jumped, and how long it rested at each spot.

Early looking was wide and fast, then narrowed as a plan took shape. Fixations grew longer and jumps grew shorter near the end of planning. Spots that mattered most for joining parts of the map drew the most attention. People who planned in deeper steps did better only on the hardest maps. The pattern fits planning that breaks a big trip into smaller sub goals.
plos-pone-0351156:
Kethmany Ratsavong and colleagues studied why toddlers stay undernourished in city districts of Vientiane, Laos, where food is generally available. A survey of three hundred and thirty three mother and child pairs in two districts was followed by deep interviews with forty seven caregivers to explain the numbers.

About twenty seven percent of children under two were stunted, fourteen percent underweight, and four percent wasted, while five percent were overweight. Better nourished children had caregivers who drew advice from many sources and turned knowledge into daily practice. Caregivers of undernourished children leaned mainly on clinics. Practical demos and videos that build cooking and feeding skill may beat leaflets alone.
plos-pone-0351556:
Sex hormones shape joint health, and osteoarthritis may partly reflect their signals gone wrong. Yishu Wang and colleagues mined public gene datasets for hormone-linked genes that also change in osteoarthritic tissue, in this 2026 PLOS One bioinformatics study.

Genes altered in disease were crossed with hormone-associated candidates, then a network method picked the disease-relevant set. Three machine learning models voted for the hub genes at the center. Immune cell estimates showed how those hubs relate to the cells patrolling diseased joints. Checks against outside datasets and blood samples supported the picks. The authors offer the hubs as leads for hormone-aware arthritis research.
plos-pone-0351756:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, ask a surprising question about fat talk, the ritual of friends criticizing their own bodies to each other. Western research usually ties such talk to worse body image. Among about thirteen hundred female nursing students in Henan, China, the team measured fat talk, self-acceptance, and body image with standard scales.

All three moved together in the positive direction: more fat talk went with better body image, and with higher self-acceptance. A pathway analysis found that much of the link ran through self-acceptance, which accounted for over half of the effect, though its size was modest. The authors read the result culturally: in this setting, fat talk may work as bonding and mutual reassurance. They caution that context decides whether the same words harm or help, and that findings from one culture should not be exported carelessly.
plos-pone-0351856:
Moemen Khalifa and colleagues followed a hundred nine women through breast cancer radiotherapy that also treats nearby lymph nodes. They watched for a slow side effect: an underactive thyroid. Part of the gland sits close to the treatment field. Damage can surface months after treatment ends. Thyroid tests ran before treatment and six months after. Each woman's dose map across the gland was matched to her result.

About eight percent developed the thyroid problem in that window. Risk rose with the hottest dose to the gland. It rose most clearly with the share of the gland taking the highest dose band. Past a small share, the odds climbed steeply. A second cutoff marked the lobe nearest the treatment side. Planners now have concrete numbers for sparing the thyroid while they aim at the cancer.
plos-pone-0351956:
Mary Charlson, Martin Wells, and James Hollenberg present a population health tool in this 2026 study. The measure sums thirty-eight chronic conditions into one weighted score. It builds on the famous Charlson comorbidity tradition. Here the aim is prediction at population scale. The team calculated scores for over twenty-seven thousand Weill Cornell health plan members. Claims data covered six years, from 2016 to 2021, for employees and their families.

Scores from each year were tested against what happened next. The question was whether one number could flag future hospital admissions. Repeated admissions and the high costs that follow them counted too. A working score changes how health systems manage populations. Instead of reacting to crises, they can identify the highest-risk patients early. Interventions, from nurse check-ins to medication reviews, can then concentrate where preventable hospitalisations are likeliest. The study offers that score as a foundation for proactive, cheaper care.
plos-pone-0352156:
Manoj Kumar and Akshat Kumar Singh ask, in this 2026 PLOS One study, whether India's soaring caesarean section rates are driven by medicine or by money. Using national family health surveys across two rounds and several states, they modeled which factors predict a surgical birth, from wealth and education to where the delivery took place.

The place of delivery towered over every other factor: giving birth in a private facility multiplied the odds of a caesarean several times over, and far more in some states than others. Wealth and education mattered mainly where public medical infrastructure was weak, largely by steering women into private care. The authors blame financial incentives in private practice and call for targeted policy to curb unnecessary surgery.
plos-pone-0352256:
Lixue Yang, Jiaxin Zhu, and Zengxin Zhang compare two ways of fine-tuning a large language model for specialist translation, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Their test bed was Chinese-to-English political text, an area where general models often stumble. One method retrained every parameter of the model; the other adjusted only a small part, using far less computing power.

On genuinely new political texts, neither method beat the untuned model in any consistent way. Only on test items drawn from the training material itself did both shine — a sign they had memorised overlap, not learned the domain. The sobering lesson: fine-tuning gains can be an illusion created by leaked test data.
plos-pone-0352356:
Larry Kessler and seven colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether Americans answer national survey questions about cancer screening the same way twice. The National Health Interview Survey tracks screening for cervical, colorectal, breast, and lung cancers. Its results guide national health goals, so shaky answers would distort policy.

Nearly eighteen hundred adults from four health systems first answered the screening questions. Randomly chosen participants then repeated the survey one month or three months later. Agreement between the two rounds ranged from moderate to strong, depending on the question. Some people were set aside because they had new screening tests between rounds. Overall, the questions proved steady enough to trust for tracking national screening trends.
plos-pone-0352456:
Martina Pérez Serrano and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study of how season changes the meat of wild male red deer in Spain. Thirty-two deer, taken by selective stalking with minimal stress, were harvested in September, January, April, and June. The team measured carcass traits and the chemistry of the loin muscle, expecting diet shifts and the effort of growing antlers to leave marks on the meat.

September deer carried the heaviest carcasses and the most fat within the muscle, while January and June animals were leanest. Tenderness, acidity after storage, and fatty acid makeup also shifted across the year. Mineral patterns pointed more to bone being drawn on during antler growth than to diet. The findings matter for hunters and game sellers judging meat quality by harvest date.
plos-pone-0352756:
Sora Kang and three colleagues ask, in this 2026 PLOS One study, whether hospitals that patients rate highly are also the hospitals rated safest. The authors linked national patient experience survey results with independent safety grades for more than fourteen hundred American hospitals using 2023 data, then compared experience scores across the grade ladder.

Experience scores generally declined as safety grades worsened. Two measures stood out as independent predictors of a top safety grade: how well nurses communicated and whether patients would recommend the hospital. Scores for doctor communication oddly pointed the other way once other factors were included, which the authors treat cautiously. They conclude that patient experience and technical safety capture different but complementary sides of quality.
plos-pone-0352856:
Dominique Vincent-Genod and colleagues, including the MFM-Play Study Group, published this 2026 interview study of a therapy app for neuromuscular disease. The app turns a standard motor function test into a game, hoping children try harder and scores vary less between testers. Fourteen hospital therapists who had tried it discussed what helped and what blocked them.

Therapists liked the practical gains and the independence it gave patients, but training gaps, technical snags, and changed habits slowed adoption. Vincent-Genod concludes the app can work if hospitals support staff through a changed testing routine, not just hand over a tablet.
plos-pone-0353056:
Nishan Pokhrel and three colleagues watch four rescued tigers at Nepal's Central Zoo to see how captivity shapes their days, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Most of the zoo's tigers arrived after conflicts with people. Observers logged behaviour across summer and monsoon, during busy visiting hours and quiet ones, using scan sampling backed by camera footage.

The tigers spent most of their time asleep or resting. Visitor crowds stirred both sexes into more pacing and drinking, while quiet hours brought rest. Females explored and paced more than the largely sedentary males, and a recently rescued female played most of all. Long-term captives paced repetitively — a pattern keepers read as stress, and a prompt to enrich enclosures.
plos-pone-0353156:
Yichuang Luo, Fang Wang, and Xiaohu Liu present this 2026 PLOS One computer vision paper on following objects through video reliably, even when they are hidden briefly or move fast. Their method upgrades a leading segmentation model whose memory of earlier frames can accumulate errors. The upgrade estimates uncertainty about each object's appearance and motion and uses it to decide what the model should remember, with separate long-term and short-term memory handling.

Across five standard video benchmarks the method beat previous state-of-the-art systems, with the largest gains in scenes involving occlusion and objects reappearing after vanishing. The authors argue that tracking what a model is unsure about, not just what it sees, is the key to segmenting crowded, fast-changing video.
plos-pone-0353356:
Salem Mgammal Al-Ameri and five co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study on transformer bushings. These fittings carry wires through a transformer's wall. They are a frequent source of breakdowns. The team modeled one bushing's electrical fingerprint in software. That fingerprint is its frequency response. They then varied the model's inner capacitance to mimic three faults. The faults were wear, surface dirt, and physical damage.

Each fault left a distinct pattern in the fingerprint. The authors mapped those patterns for future diagnosis. A second, physics-based model showed how electric fields shift under each fault. That explains why the patterns form. Together, the two approaches give utilities a way to spot bushing faults early. Early warning can keep a transformer in service.
plos-pone-0353456:
Nuha Al-Aghbari authored this 2026 PLOS One study asking whether two routine blood tests taken at hospital admission can predict which COVID-19 patients will die. Albumin, a protein tied to nutrition and organ reserve, and blood urea, a kidney-related waste measure, are cheap and widely available. The analysis covered more than a thousand adults treated at a single tertiary hospital.

About a quarter of the patients died in hospital. Those who died arrived with lower albumin and higher urea, and both measures still predicted death after accounting for age, other illnesses, and inflammation markers. Each step up in urea raised the odds of death, while higher albumin was protective. The author argues these simple tests add useful warning information beyond the usual inflammation measures.
plos-pone-0353556:
Tae Wan Kim and seven colleagues ask a stark question. Do patients who reach intensive care already in shock fare worse when their lungs fail? Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It came from South Korea. They reviewed nearly three thousand five hundred adults. All had acute respiratory failure. All were treated at one major hospital between 2019 and 2023. Shock meant needing drugs to support blood pressure on arrival.

Nearly one in five patients arrived in shock. Their intensive care death rate was close to half. For the others it was under a fifth. The gap survived statistical adjustment for other risks. The pattern held across illness severity. It held across breathing-support types too. Shock on arrival, the authors argue, is a simple early warning sign.
plos-pone-0353756:
Limin Fang and four colleagues survey shoppers about what makes them buy plant-rich foods, in this 2026 PLOS ONE pilot study. Drawing on three theories of consumer behaviour, they modelled seven influences, from personal attitude and cultural setting to packaging design and the information on the label. Survey answers were fitted into a structural model linking each factor to buying intention and to healthy eating behaviour.

All seven factors pushed buying intention upward, but packaging's practical features pulled hardest, ahead of personal needs and food information. Product-side variables beat consumer-side ones overall. Intention then carried part of the effect into actual healthy eating. For food brands, the lesson is blunt: the packet may matter as much as the pitch.
plos-pone-0353856:
Mats Eriksson and four colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for watching the brains of newborns and their mothers at the same moment, during a routine painful procedure. Babies in intensive care endure repeated blood tests, and parents soothe them with skin contact, breastfeeding, and singing — but what that comfort does inside the brain is unknown. Twenty mother-baby pairs will be studied during a planned heel or vein blood draw.

Light-based scanners on both heads will record whether their brain activity synchronises, while heart rhythms, skin conductance, and the mother's gaze are tracked too. Pain will be scored from the baby's behaviour. The study aims to explain, in brain terms, why a parent's presence is medicine.
plos-pone-0353956:
Wen-Yu Jao and three colleagues compare two modern diabetes drug families for an unexpected side benefit, in this 2026 PLOS ONE database study. Both drug types control blood sugar and calm inflammation, which made researchers wonder whether they also protect joints. Using a huge multi-hospital record system, the team matched over four hundred and fifty thousand new users of one family against the same number starting the other.

Users of the first family, the SGLT2 blockers, developed osteoarthritis less often over five years than users of the GLP-1 medicines, especially in the knee. They also needed fewer major joint injections, though joint replacement rates matched. The authors call for trials to test whether the difference is real.
plos-pone-0354156:
Khadivi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, survey wild Persian irises growing in the mountains of Markazi Province, Iran. This ornamental flower is prized by gardeners, yet how much its wild plants vary from place to place was little known. Knowing that variation helps protect the species and pick the best plants for breeding.

The team measured dozens of traits, from flower size to color, in seventy-eight plants gathered from seven areas. Variation was wide: flower width, petal length, and other features differed a lot between plants. Statistical grouping sorted the plants into four clear families of form. Traits tied to flower size moved together closely, and a few traits best predicted overall flower width. Ten standout plants with fine flowers are named as breeding candidates. The survey gives growers and conservation workers a first map of what this wild iris has to offer.
plos-pone-0354256: Diabetic wounds in Duhok, Iraq — Pseudomonas aeruginosa lurking in them. This paper measured prevalence and risk factors. The findings guide wound care where resistant bacteria threaten limbs — and lives.
plos-pone-0354356:
Klinga and colleagues, in a 2026 interview study in Sweden, follow health and social care leaders through a training program in person-centred leadership. Such leadership, which treats staff and patients as partners, is meant to spread person-centred care, but evaluations of the training are scarce. Thirteen leaders were asked what changed in how they lead.

Leaders described growth on three levels: leading themselves, leading their teams, and developing their workforce, all in a more person-centred direction. Three themes named the shift: enable co-creation, live as you learn, and strive for equal relations. None of it happened automatically. Leaders needed backing from their own bosses, time to coach, and work methods that share power, both during the course and after. The authors argue training budgets are wasted if organizations do not also build those surrounding conditions.
plos-pone-0354456:
Partho Bosu and co-authors run a computer-only search for drug leads against acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer where faulty cell growth crowds out healthy blood making. Starting from a public gene dataset, they found hundreds of genes behaving differently in the disease and mapped which ones sit at network hubs. Two hub proteins with known shapes became their docking targets.

Virtual screening built shape models for compounds that might block those targets, then filtered candidates for drug-like behavior and safety before detailed docking. A couple of compounds bound tightly in simulation and stayed stable in motion tests. Bosu and colleagues stress that these are candidates for lab testing, not proven drugs, and offer them as starting points for chemists.
plos-pone-0354756:
Caoyan Xu and seven co-authors published a pig genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They compared Chinese pig breeds with Western breeds, which differ in how much fat is marbled through the meat. Fat inside the muscle shapes taste, and breeders care about what controls it at the gene level.

Xu's team combined gene activity data with protein data to trace the control networks behind that marbling. The two breed groups turned out to use different sets of switches. Knowing which networks differ gives breeders clearer targets when they select animals, and it helps explain why the same feed can yield lean meat in one breed and rich meat in another.
plos-pone-0354856:
Alexa Pohl and co-authors scoped the research on how transportation shapes cancer screening and the stage at which cancer is found. Millions of Americans miss care each year for want of a ride. Their 2026 review searched five databases for quantitative patient-level studies across two decades and kept about one hundred after quality checks.

Screening studies slightly outnumbered stage studies in the final set. Measures of transport exposure fell into families: travel time and distance, help needed to make the trip, public transit, vehicle access, and patients' own sense of distance. Comparing those families exposed inconsistent measurement across the field. Pohl and colleagues recommend shared measures so future studies can actually be combined.
plos-pone-0355056: Sequencing short synthetic DNA strands quickly accelerates synthetic biology. OligoSeq enables rapid nanopore sequencing of single-stranded oligonucleotides. The streamlined method turns around oligo reads fast enough to keep pace with high-throughput DNA synthesis.
plos-pone-0355156:
Agnieszka Drozdowska-Szymczak and co-authors outline in 2026 a study of whether a brain injury protein in cord blood can flag oxygen shortage in babies whose growth slowed late in pregnancy. The protein rises after injury to the central nervous system from low oxygen. Full term pregnancies with slowed growth will be compared with normally grown pregnancies after delivery.

Cord blood will be tested for the protein plus acidity and related measures, and blood flow scans just before birth will add context. The team will check whether protein levels track flow and blood gas results. As a protocol, it reports plans and approvals, not findings.
plos-pone-0355556:
Esther Ríos-Albert and co-authors analysed how key university figures across six European countries talk about sexual harassment. How leaders define the problem shapes whether victims report it and how institutions respond. Their 2026 study interviewed ninety informants, from student representatives to equality officers, and read the transcripts with critical discourse methods.

Informants described harassment as many-sided, spanning physical, verbal, non-verbal, and online acts. Accounts returned again and again to crossed boundaries, missing consent, and power gaps. The quoted title line calls it a hierarchical transgression. Definitions ranged from rule-based to experience-based to mixed, varying with gender and job role. The authors argue shared language is a first step toward shared response.
plos-pone-0355856:
Patrinee Traisathit and colleagues examined whether dirty air shortens survival for leukaemia patients in northern Thailand. They studied just over six hundred people with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia diagnosed across two decades. Their 2026 analysis split patients into children, adolescents and young adults, and older adults.

Survival fell steeply with age: about two-thirds of children lived five years, against very few older adults. Patients who died had breathed higher levels of fine particles and other pollutants, most clearly among children. High fine-particle levels were tied to greater death risk in the youngest group. Traisathit and colleagues argue air quality belongs in leukaemia care planning for the region.
plos-pone-0355956:
Joshua De Soyza leads a team of five checking whether a standard lung severity score works in a genetic lung disease, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency damages lungs and often brings bronchiectasis, chronically widened airways. A widely used severity index predicts death, hospitalization, and flare ups in ordinary bronchiectasis, but it had never been tested in this population. The team applied it to one hundred ninety-eight registry patients in Birmingham, nearly all with the severe genotype and most with COPD alongside.

The index sorted patients meaningfully. Survival differed significantly across its severity bands, exactly what a prognostic tool must do. The team also probed whether scores tracked lung function decline and quality of life measures. Validation in a rare disease subgroup matters because trials and clinics borrow tools from common diseases on faith. Here, at least for prognosis, the borrowed tool earned its place.
plos-pone-0356056:
Yaseen Al-Mulla mapped frankincense trees in Oman's Dhofar region using satellite images and the trees' light fingerprints. Frankincense resin is valuable, and the source tree matters ecologically and commercially, yet its spectral signature was barely studied. The 2026 study gathered field spectra across the visible and infrared range and matched them to high-resolution satellite bands.

A spectral matching method separated frankincense from surrounding vegetation far better than a simple greenness cutoff, which overstated cover. Overall mapping accuracy passed ninety percent. Three deep learning detectors were also tried on the imagery; the best found about seven hundred trees with strong precision and recall. Al-Mulla presents the workflow as a base for monitoring this prized species.
plos-pone-0356356:
Xinyuan Wang and Zhenyang Zhang examine what makes software developers in China actually follow data protection rules, in this 2026 survey study. Working from deterrence theory, they asked whether developers' awareness of data law shapes their compliance directly. They also asked whether it works indirectly, through how certain and how severe developers believe punishment to be. The analysis used structural models fitted to survey responses. Workplace compliance culture was tested as a further influence on those pathways.

Legal awareness promoted compliant behavior both directly and through perceived sanctions, with the certainty of being caught mattering more than the severity of the penalty. A strong compliance culture boosted awareness's effect on perceived certainty, though its boost to perceived severity was weakly supported. The authors advise regulators to invest in visible, consistent enforcement and companies to build cultures where rules feel real, rather than relying on harsh penalties.
plos-pone-0357156:
Chunmeng Wang and three colleagues fuse several photographs into one image that keeps both shadow and shine, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Scenes with bright skies and dark corners defeat a single exposure. Their system, MEF-TBN, splits the work among three cooperating branches. One reads fine local detail. One models the whole scene's structure with a transformer. The third restores natural color, which fusion methods often bleach or distort.

The branches produce weight maps that decide, pixel by pixel, which exposure should speak. A merging stage refines the local and global judgments together before the final blend. Against nine established fusion methods, the system topped most technical sharpness measures and swept the human perception oriented scores, while placing second on structural similarity. For phone cameras and medical imaging alike, the work shows that giving color its own dedicated branch pays off in pictures that look right, not just measure well.
plos-pone-0357756:
Emmanuel Daniel, Saada A. Seif, and Walter C. Millanzi published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on how new mothers in Tanzania's Kilimanjaro region keep their babies warm. Newborns lose heat fast in their first month, yet most research describes facility routines rather than what mothers do. The authors interviewed twelve post-natal mothers in depth at public facilities in 2024 and analyzed conversations for themes.

Four practice themes emerged. Mothers wrapped babies in multiple layers of cotton cloth and prepared clothing before delivery. They warmed rooms with heating or even lighting. They kept babies in constant skin-to-skin contact and breastfed promptly. And they massaged babies with oil and delayed bathing, both believed to protect warmth. These home-grown practices, the authors say, largely match clinical guidance, so health education should reinforce rather than replace them, and facilities should support skin-to-skin care and warm rooms.
plos-pone-0357956: Costa and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how the brain reacts to faces within fractions of a second. They recorded early electrical responses from the scalp.
